The machines also vary enormously. One manufacturer's machines may work across 100 or more job sites and applications, most platforms have 10 or more critical operating scenarios, and sensor types, numbers and mounting positions differ by platform [Introduction]. Wheeled, tracked and articulated machines stop differently, and the brake standards treat them in separate documents [Chapter 8].
terms.why: Everything about validating an automatic brake on these machines follows from their mass, their ground and their close-contact work: stopping distances are long, brakes are limited by heat and torque, loads shift, and many real tasks look like a collision to a sensor. The booklet marks evidence proven only for road vehicles as "on-road evidence" because the step from a highway to a quarry is one of the central uncertainties of the program [Introduction].

terms.title: Wheel loader
terms.oneSentence: A wheel loader is a four-wheeled machine with a large bucket at the front that scoops up loose material and tips it into a truck or onto a pile.
terms.explained:
Picture a very large shovel on wheels. The operator drives forward into a pile of gravel or broken rock, fills the bucket, backs away, turns, and lifts the bucket to empty it into a waiting truck. In the United States the same machine is called a front-end loader. Its day is spent in short forward and reverse moves with people, trucks and piles close by.

That pattern shows in the accident record: in US surface-mine fatality reports from 2000 to mid-2006, front-end loaders were involved in 33% of 22 blind-area deaths, second only to dump trucks [Chapter 4].

The first commercial automatic braking on earth-moving machines was fitted to wheel loaders, and all of it is narrow. Volvo CE's system (January 2023) brakes only in reverse, between 3 and 15 km/h, for 2 to 3 seconds, and remembers the last slope climbed so that reversing down a stockpile does not trigger it. Caterpillar's and Liebherr's loader systems also act in reverse only. None publishes weather limits, false-intervention rates or validation methods [Chapter 2].
terms.why: The wheel loader is the clearest case of a machine whose normal job is also what a sensor sees as a collision risk, so it is the hardest place to avoid nuisance braking. Every fielded off-road braking product launched on loaders in reverse only at low speed, the narrow operating domain the booklet expects this program to follow [Chapters 1, 2].

terms.title: Haul truck
terms.oneSentence: A haul truck is a very large off-road dump truck that carries rock or ore from where it is dug to where it is dumped or processed.
terms.explained:
A haul truck is a road dump truck scaled up many times. Most have a single stiff frame, so they are also called rigid dump trucks. The largest, often called ultra-class trucks, carry roughly 300 t or more; the booklet quotes a Caterpillar 797F with a 363 t payload and about 624 t gross weight [Chapter 8]. The operator sits high up in a cab on one side.

Because the truck is so tall and long, its blind areas are huge: the front-right blind area of a 50 t haul truck extends 18 m or more and grows with size [Chapter 4]. In 54 US haul-truck deaths from 2005 to mid-2021, 21 involved berms, 13 were collisions with people or vehicles, 12 happened at dump points and 8 had other causes. Of the 13 collisions, 12 involved a truck moving forward, and four began with a truck starting to move while people were within about 15 m [Chapter 4].

Haul trucks also stop differently. On long downhill roads they slow mainly with a retarder, a braking effect from the drivetrain, whose power is limited, so available deceleration falls as speed and mass rise [Chapter 8].
terms.why: The haul truck has the clearest fatality evidence, and its deadliest pattern is forward motion or starting from rest, not reversing. The plan therefore needs separate forward, reverse, start-from-rest, turning and swing scenarios rather than one generic proximity zone [Chapter 4].

terms.title: Articulated hauler (ADT)
terms.oneSentence: An articulated hauler, also called an articulated dump truck (ADT), is an off-road dump truck whose front and rear halves are joined by a hinge so it bends in the middle to steer.
terms.explained:
Imagine a dump truck cut in two behind the cab and reconnected with a large pivot. The front half carries engine and cab; the rear half carries the load. To turn, the two halves swing toward each other. This lets the truck work on rough, soft, twisting ground, which is why ADTs are common on construction sites and in quarries.

The hinge changes braking. In a straight stop on level ground an articulated hauler behaves like a simple mass, but braking while turning, on a side slope or at a large articulation angle can make the two halves push on each other, roll or swing [Chapter 8]. The booklet quotes a Volvo A60 at about 44 t empty and 99 t loaded, and a New South Wales brake example in which a 25 t ADT at 50 km/h needs 3.13 m/s² of deceleration to stop in about 31 m [Chapter 8]. The forthcoming ISO/PRF 21815-5 treats articulation as its own form of collision-relevant motion [Chapter 8].
terms.why: Construction-site ADTs have only aggregate accident statistics behind them, and published data on jackknife or roll events during automatic braking of articulated off-road machines were not found [Chapters 4, 8]. The hinge is one place where a simple braking model is not enough.

terms.title: Excavator
terms.oneSentence: An excavator is a digging machine with a long jointed arm and a bucket, mounted on a body that can rotate a full circle on top of its tracks or wheels.
terms.explained:
An excavator usually works from one spot. It digs with the arm, then swings its upper body round to drop the material into a truck. The swing is the dangerous movement: the counterweight at the back and the arm at the front sweep a wide circle, and a person or truck inside it can be struck without the machine moving forward or backward at all.

The standards treat rotation separately. ISO 21815-4, under publication in October 2026, covers swing and rotation and relies mainly on preventing the rotation from starting when something is in the way, rather than braking during the swing [Chapter 4]. No agency statistics were found that separate out how often swing strikes cause serious collisions [Chapter 4].

One product shows the shape of the problem. Komatsu's KomVision on hydraulic excavators detects people with cameras and stops the machine when travel or swing starts, but not during an ongoing swing, and it must be switched off during trailer loading because a rapid stop "can make the machine unstable" [Chapter 2].
terms.why: The excavator shows that a job-site collision is not only driving into something; rotating motions need their own detection zones and their own kind of intervention, and an automatic stop can itself create a stability hazard.

terms.title: Dozer and grader
terms.oneSentence: A dozer pushes earth and rock with a wide blade at the front, and a grader levels and shapes road surfaces with a long angled blade under its body.
terms.explained:
A dozer (bulldozer) usually runs on tracks and pushes material into place, builds and repairs dump areas and clears ground; the booklet quotes a Caterpillar D11 at about 107 t [Chapter 8]. A grader is a long wheeled machine with a blade between its front and rear wheels; on a mine it keeps haul roads smooth and sloped. Both move slowly, work close to other machines and reverse often.

They appear in the record where machines share tight spaces. At a tip head a dozer pushes material while loaded trucks drive up, turn and back in. New Zealand's regulator described a D10 dozer reversing into the wheel of a loaded 777 truck at a tip head, and a reversing truck clipping a dozer at night [Chapter 4]. In New South Wales a light vehicle entering a tip-head area was struck by a reversing dozer, and the driver died [Chapter 4]. A grader and a haul truck collided with "major damage to both machines" [Chapter 4]. Tracked machines also brake differently: tracks keep more grip in soft soil than tires, and slow crawlers have their own brake standard, ISO 10265 [Chapter 8].
terms.why: Dozers and graders are typical of heavy-machine-to-heavy-machine contacts, which the booklet ranks as the most frequently reported collision type even though it is usually property damage [Chapter 4]. A braking system must handle a tracked machine's stopping behavior and must not treat every nearby truck at a tip head as an emergency.

terms.title: Load-haul-dump machine (LHD)
terms.oneSentence: A load-haul-dump machine (LHD) is a low, long loader built for underground mines, where it scoops broken rock, carries it along narrow tunnels and dumps it into a truck or a chute.
terms.explained:
Underground tunnels are low and narrow, so the machines in them are flat and long. An LHD, also called a scoop or underground loader, is a wheel loader stretched out and squashed down. The operator sits sideways in a low cab, and the load in the bucket can block the view ahead.

New South Wales recorded 30 collisions involving LHDs and personnel transports in underground coal mines in the 12 months to mid-2025, often with the LHD carrying bulky loads such as concrete kibbles that block the operator's view [Chapter 4]. In New Zealand an underground loader loading from a stockpile caught the body of a reversing truck with its bucket and tipped onto its side [Chapter 4]. Collision systems sold for underground machines slow and stop the machine but depend on every person and machine carrying a tag [Chapter 2].
terms.why: Underground speeds and tunnel geometry differ from surface haul roads, so evidence from one does not transfer automatically to the other [Chapter 4]. The LHD is also the clearest case of a machine whose own load creates the blind spot.

terms.title: Trackless mobile machinery (TMM)
terms.oneSentence: Trackless mobile machinery (TMM) is the South African legal term for any self-propelled mining machine that does not run on rails, from haul trucks and loaders to light vehicles.
terms.explained:
"Trackless" does not mean without crawler tracks; it means not on railway tracks, unlike the rail-bound locomotives still used in some mines. So a TMM is any free-moving machine on a mine. The term matters because South Africa wrote it into law.

Regulations under the Mine Health and Safety Act (published 2015, in force from 21 December 2022 with no transitional period) require that where a diesel-powered TMM is heading for a collision and the operator takes no action, the machine is slowed to a safe speed and then braked automatically, and that the system fails to safe without human intervention [Chapters 2, 3]. This is the only legal mandate for automatic braking on heavy mining machines the booklet found, and it came before any validation standard; industry then wrote performance requirements and, in 2025 and 2026, independent verification test specifications for surface TMM collision prevention systems [Chapters 1, 2]. South Africa recorded nine TMM-related deaths in 2024, up from six [Chapter 4].
terms.why: South Africa is the booklet's main real case of a market forced to deploy intervention first and refine afterward, and its verification documents are among the few off-road test specifications that exist [Chapters 1, 2].

terms.title: Light vehicle
terms.oneSentence: On a mine site, a light vehicle is an ordinary pickup, four-wheel-drive or van used by supervisors, maintenance crews and visitors to move among the heavy machines.
terms.explained:
A light vehicle is anything roughly car-sized. It shares haul roads with trucks that weigh a hundred times more, so sites fit it with tall flags, flashing strobe lights and radios, and set rules for where it may park and how it may approach a machine.

The size mismatch makes light vehicles the most common victims in the deadliest surface-mine collisions. Five of the 13 US haul-truck collision deaths from 2005 to 2021 involved light vehicles, and an earlier analysis found victims were "primarily light vehicle occupants." Two cases involved a truck driving over a parked pickup whose strobe light was switched off; in one, the pickup was momentarily hidden by the truck's cab pillar [Chapter 4]. In New South Wales a light vehicle entering a tip-head area was struck by a reversing dozer [Chapter 4].
terms.why: The booklet ranks a haul truck crushing a light vehicle in front of it as the number-one harm scenario [Chapter 4]. The system must see a car-sized object in front of a tall truck, often while the truck is stationary and about to move, which is the situation where a time-to-collision calculation gives no answer [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Operator and cab
terms.oneSentence: The operator is the person who drives and controls a machine, and the cab is the enclosed compartment where that person sits.
terms.explained:
On a heavy machine the operator steers, works the bucket or blade, watches mirrors and camera screens, listens to the radio and decides when to move and when to wait. The cab is a glass and steel box high above the ground, often on one side, with pillars that can hide a pickup [Chapter 4]. Vibration, dust, radio traffic and production pressure are normal.

Two facts about the operator run through the booklet. The standards keep responsibility with the operator, because ISO 21815-1 states that the technology cannot cover every situation [Chapter 4]. And the operator is the least understood part of the system: no field-measured distribution of how fast heavy-machine operators react to proximity warnings was found [Chapter 4]. The cab also matters during an automatic stop. MSHA (the US Mine Safety and Health Administration) estimates that three to four miners' lives a year could be saved by adequate seat belts, and seven of 12 drivers killed at dump points were unbelted [Chapter 4].
terms.why: An automatic brake acts when the operator has not, so validating it means assuming something about what the operator does and when. The booklet advises treating operator response as an uncertain quantity and testing how sensitive results are to it [Chapter 4].

terms.title: Job site
terms.oneSentence: A job site is any place where heavy machines work, and the booklet is concerned with four main kinds: surface mines, underground mines, quarries and construction sites.
terms.explained:
Each kind has its own shape, traffic and dangers.

A *surface mine* (open pit) is a huge stepped hole. Material is dug at the bottom, carried up ramps by haul trucks along haul roads, and dumped on waste piles or taken to a plant. Loaded trucks can reach 40 to 50 km/h, and the worst accidents are trucks running over light vehicles, trucks going through edge barriers, and trucks reversing over dump edges [Chapters 4, 8].

An *underground mine* is a network of tunnels. Machines are low and long, speeds are lower, roadways are confined, and workers are often on foot close to machines. The booklet's underground evidence concerns continuous mining machines, shuttle cars and LHDs striking or pinning people [Chapter 4].

A *quarry* produces stone, sand and gravel, with a rock face, crushers, stockpiles and loading areas, usually with smaller trucks and loaders. British guidance says transport accounts for 40% of quarry accidents and 60% of quarry deaths, and reversing over people is the classic quarry accident [Chapter 4].

A *construction site* mixes machines with public traffic, delivery trucks and many workers on foot in confined space. At US road construction sites, being struck by a vehicle or machine was the most common cause of death from 2005 to 2016 [Chapter 4].

The challenge statement says one machine type may work across 100 or more job sites and applications [Introduction]. For simulation, the booklet turns this into operating-domain parameters: site type (pit, quarry face, stockpile yard, road works, building site, forest, field), surface (gravel, mud, snow, ice, paved), slope, object classes, weather and light, machine model and sensor pose [Chapter 5].
terms.why: The same braking algorithm gives different safety results at sites with different traffic separation, intersection rules and pedestrian controls, so site type is a main dimension the virtual program must cover [Chapter 1]. The booklet concludes that no single method can produce valid virtual environments for all site types in the time available, and that a library of parameterized representative site types anchored to a few surveyed real sites is the realistic route [Chapter 5].

terms.title: Haul road, berm, bench and pit wall
terms.oneSentence: These are the built features of a surface mine or quarry: the haul road is the internal road the trucks use, a berm is a ridge of material piled along an edge as a barrier, a bench is one horizontal step of the pit, and the pit wall is the steep face between benches.
terms.explained:
A surface mine is dug as giant steps. Each flat step is a bench; the steep face to the next step is the pit wall. Haul roads run along benches and up ramps, with grades that can exceed 9% [Chapter 4]. Along road and dump edges, crews pile up a ridge of earth or rock called a berm (in Australia a windrow or bund). It is meant to stop a drifting truck going over the edge, and drivers also use the dump berm as a bump stop [Chapter 4].

These features cause many deaths that are not collisions with people or vehicles: of 54 US haul-truck deaths from 2005 to mid-2021, 21 were berm-related and 12 were at dump points, where 10 involved an absent or inadequate berm [Chapter 4]. For a sensor, berms and walls are large, solid, legitimate objects. The NIOSH radar study deliberately did not count berm detections as nuisance, because driving over a dump edge is deadly [Chapter 4]. Regulators propose false-activation tests for berms and windrows [Chapter 3].
terms.why: A system that only sees people and vehicles addresses an incomplete part of the fatal-risk picture, and one that brakes for every berm would be unusable [Chapter 4]. Virtual sites must place berms accurately: an edge modeled tens of centimeters out of place can corrupt a stopping-distance test [Chapter 5].

terms.title: Stockpile, dump point and tip point
terms.oneSentence: A stockpile is a pile of loose material waiting to be used, a dump point is where a truck tips its load, and a tip point or tip head is the active edge of a dump where trucks and a dozer work together.
terms.explained:
A loader drives into a stockpile to fill its bucket. A truck backs up to a dump point, often at the edge of a slope, and raises its body. At a tip head a dozer pushes the dumped material over the edge while the next loaded trucks drive up, turn and reverse in. All of this means machines deliberately driving close to large objects and to each other.

These places concentrate both deaths and nuisance alarms. Of 12 US dump-point deaths, six were trucks reversing over the edge and six were ground failures [Chapter 4]. At the same time, backing toward a rock pile for loading is the textbook nuisance detection: a real object, a slow intended approach, a driver who knows it is there [Chapter 4]. South African guidance says that with a fixed stop distance, machines being loaded could not come close enough and the system would have to be switched off [Chapter 4]. Volvo's loader system remembers the last slope climbed precisely to avoid braking when reversing down a stockpile [Chapter 2].
terms.why: The system must tell an intended approach to a pile from an intrusion into the same space by a second truck or a person, and must not "learn away" repeated berm alarms at a dump edge, where the object really is dangerous [Chapter 4]. Loading and dumping are separate validation scenarios.

terms.title: Spotter and pedestrian
terms.oneSentence: A pedestrian is any person on foot near a working machine, and a spotter is a person whose job is to stand where the operator can see them and guide a reversing or maneuvering machine by hand signals or radio.
terms.explained:
On a job site "pedestrian" means ground crew, surveyors, mechanics, blast crews, supervisors and visitors. They are the most vulnerable things a machine can hit, and they are often close on purpose. A spotter is a formal role: US rules accept an observer as an alternative to a reverse alarm [Chapter 3], and Queensland requires an authorized pedestrian approaching a machine to communicate with the operator and have that communication confirmed [Chapter 4].

People on foot dominate the clearly addressable deaths: 67% of 22 US surface-mine blind-area deaths were people behind reversing machines, and underground, 39 miners were struck or pinned by continuous mining machines from 1984 to 2015 [Chapter 4]. The same closeness creates the design problem. Mechanics remove wearable tags to work inside the danger zone, and an untagged contractor is invisible to a tag-based system [Chapter 4]. A system that applies the same exclusion zone to a walking worker, an authorized spotter and an intruder will either stop work constantly or need a controlled task-and-mode concept [Chapter 4]. On the road, pedestrian detection remains weak at night, and in a 2025 test high-visibility clothing caused a complete loss of detection in some systems [Chapter 10].
terms.why: Protecting people on foot is the main purpose of the system, and legitimate close work by ground crew is what makes the detection zones so hard to design [Chapter 4].

terms.title: Blind spot and operator visibility
terms.oneSentence: A blind spot is any area around a machine that the operator cannot see from the seat, and operator visibility is the overall picture of what the operator can and cannot see with eyes, mirrors and cameras.
terms.explained:
Sit in a haul-truck cab, high on the left, with a huge engine hood in front and a load body behind, and most of the ground around you disappears. The front-right blind area of a 50 t haul truck extends 18 m or more and grows with truck size [Chapter 4]. A pickup or a person there does not exist for the operator. Cab pillars, raised buckets and bulky loads add more hidden zones.

Blind areas are the single most important factor in the deadliest collisions. NIOSH counted 22 blind-area deaths in US surface mines from 2000 to mid-2006; dump trucks were involved in 38% and front-end loaders in 33%, and 67% of victims were in the rear blind area of reversing equipment [Chapter 4]. Standards approach visibility from two sides: ISO 5006 defines how to measure what an operator can see, and ISO 16001 covers detection systems and visibility aids such as cameras and mirrors; the booklet notes that these visibility-type methods let blind zones be computed per machine model from its geometry before hardware arrives [Chapter 7]. Both the existing warning system and the new braking system exist to cover the ground the operator cannot see.
terms.why: Scenarios should be built around where each machine model's blind areas are, because that is where the victims are. Blind-area geometry changes with every model and sensor position, one reason evidence does not transfer freely between models [Chapter 1].

terms.title: Reversing and reverse alarm
terms.oneSentence: Reversing (backing up) is driving a machine backward, and a reverse alarm is the loud beeping a machine makes automatically while it does so.
terms.explained:
Heavy machines reverse constantly: a loader backs away from a pile, a truck backs up to a dump edge, a dozer backs off the material it has pushed. The view to the rear is usually the worst, so for decades the standard protection has been a reverse alarm. US mine rules require horns and backup alarms or an observer, and US surface-coal rules accept instead a detection device using infrared, ultrasonic, radar or "another effective device" whose sensing area gives a person enough time to escape. None requires automatic braking [Chapter 3].

Reversing is the classic fatal pattern for smaller machines. British guidance says nearly a quarter of workplace-transport deaths happen during reversing, and 67% of US surface-mine blind-area deaths were behind reversing equipment [Chapter 4]. But the booklet warns that "reversing is the main fatal mode" is true for some machine populations and not others: very large haul trucks kill mostly while moving forward [Chapter 4]. All the off-road automatic braking products the booklet found work in reverse only or mainly in reverse, at low speed [Chapter 2].
terms.why: Low-speed reversing is where automatic braking already exists off-road and where a first release is most likely [Chapters 1, 2]. A plan that covers only reversing misses the deadliest haul-truck scenario, so forward, reverse, start-from-rest, turning and swing each need their own scenarios [Chapter 4].

terms.title: Vehicle interaction
terms.oneSentence: Vehicle interaction is the mining industry's term for any situation in which a moving machine comes close to another machine, a person or a fixed feature of the site, whether or not contact happens.
terms.explained:
The phrase is deliberately wider than "collision." It covers near misses and everyday close approaches as well as crashes, because the industry wants to manage the whole situation. The booklet uses the three classes that regulators and the industry group EMESRT (Earth Moving Equipment Safety Round Table) use: vehicle to vehicle, vehicle to person, and vehicle to environment (berms, edges, walls, structures) [Chapter 4].

Two findings shape the booklet. Regulators say the problem is not going away: New South Wales reported "no meaningful reduction" in reported vehicle interactions year on year (2023), and Queensland reports mobile plant collisions at the top of its high-potential incident list (2024) [Chapter 4]. And research and reality are mismatched: a NIOSH review found most published work targets vehicle-to-vehicle interactions, while accident records contain many vehicle-to-environment events such as berm deaths [Chapter 1]. EMESRT's performance requirement PR-5A turns vehicle interactions into a catalog of standard scenarios and a nine-level model of controls [Chapters 1, 5].
terms.why: The vehicle-interaction scenarios are the closest thing the off-road world has to a ready-made test catalog, and the booklet recommends building the operating-domain definition on ISO 21815 and the EMESRT scenarios [Introduction, Chapter 1]. The three classes also remind the planner that a system detecting only vehicles and people leaves the environment class unaddressed.

terms.title: Collision
terms.oneSentence: A collision is a machine striking a person, a vehicle, another machine or a fixed object, and on job sites a small number of collision types cause most of the deaths.
terms.explained:
In this booklet the word is used precisely and separated from two neighbors: a near miss (no contact) and a non-collision accident such as a truck going through a berm or rolling over. The separation matters because an object-detecting system can only address the first group.

The booklet ranks collision situations by harm, using fatality data from several countries [Chapter 4]:

A large haul truck crushes a light vehicle in front of it, often when starting from rest (5 of 13 US haul-truck collision deaths, 2005 to 2021).

A smaller dump truck or loader reverses over a worker on foot or a small vehicle (67% of 22 US blind-area deaths, 2000 to 2006).

A person on foot is struck or pinned in other movements, above all underground (39 continuous-miner deaths, 1984 to 2015).

and 5. Loss of control through a berm, and reverse-overs or ground failure at a dump point: the largest group of haul-truck deaths (33 of 54), but not object collisions.

A worker on foot struck at a road construction site (131 backing deaths, 1992 to 2010).

Heavy machine against heavy machine at tip heads, loading areas and haul roads: mostly property damage, and the most frequently reported collision type in regulator data.

Lower come underground LHD collisions, collisions during an intentional loading approach, contact with fixed structures, and swing strikes, for which frequency data were not found [Chapter 4].

Two warnings accompany the ranking. Databases record deaths far better than damage-only collisions, and agencies use different categories, so numbers from different countries must not be added into one international rate [Chapter 4]. And the scale is real but partly outside the system's reach: in 2025 powered haulage caused 13 of 33 US mining deaths (39%), a category wider than object collisions [Chapter 4].
terms.why: The ranking tells the program which scenarios to prioritize: a truck starting forward with a light vehicle in front, a loader or truck reversing over a person, and close machine-to-machine work. It also warns that a system detecting only vehicles and people "addresses an important but incomplete part of the fatal-risk picture" [Chapter 4].

terms.title: Fatality, serious injury and property damage
terms.oneSentence: Accidents are counted in three bands of severity, deaths, serious injuries and damage to equipment or structures, and the records get thinner and less reliable as severity goes down.
terms.explained:
A fatality is a death. A serious injury causes lost working time or permanent harm, and agencies define it differently (lost-time injury, reportable injury, high-potential incident). Property damage is harm to machines, vehicles or structures with no one hurt. Only deaths are investigated and published case by case.

The result is a lopsided evidence base. Accident databases record fatalities far better than property-only collisions, near misses, nuisance alarms or events the operator prevented [Chapter 4]. Some figures show the scale: in US mining in 2025, powered haulage caused 13 of 33 deaths and 426 of 4,792 nonfatal injuries; in US construction in 2020, struck-by incidents caused 150 deaths and 14,000 nonfatal injuries with 1.4 billion dollars in direct compensation costs [Chapter 4]. For damage, regulators describe frequent collisions such as a grader and haul truck with "major damage to both machines," but no source quantified property-damage cost or ranked damage by collision type [Chapter 4]. Agencies also use categories such as "powered haulage" or "struck by moving vehicle" that do not line up, and none publishes operating hours alongside counts [Chapter 4].
terms.why: The system is meant to prevent all three bands, but the evidence for what to test is strongest for deaths. The booklet advises using fatality patterns for scenario priorities and treating frequency and damage estimates as much weaker [Chapter 4].

terms.title: Exposure
terms.oneSentence: Exposure is the amount of opportunity for something to happen, measured in units such as hours of machine operation, kilometers driven, loading cycles or number of close approaches, and it is the denominator that turns a count of events into a rate.
terms.explained:
Saying "there were 30 collisions" means little until you know whether they happened in 30 hours or 30 million hours. A rate is a count divided by exposure:

`rate = number of events / amount of exposure`

For example, 3 unnecessary automatic stops in 600 operating hours is 0.5 per 100 hours. The choice of unit matters. The booklet argues that for operator acceptance the useful measures are unnecessary warnings or interventions per operating hour, per loading cycle, per reverse maneuver and per legitimate close approach, broken down by task, rather than false positives per detection [Chapter 4]. A system can have an excellent overall false-positive rate and still be unusable if nearly every loading cycle contains one unwanted intervention [Chapter 4].

Exposure data are scarce off-road. None of the accident sources gives operating hours, kilometers or cycles alongside collision counts, so no rate can be computed and no country or machine type compared like for like [Chapter 4]. The one field study with a clean denominator is small: a radar warning system on a haul truck alarmed in 94% of 618 reverse movements over seven days [Chapter 4].

Exposure also decides how much testing proves anything. A RAND study found that showing the safety of self-driving cars by driving alone would take hundreds of millions, sometimes hundreds of billions, of miles; off-road machines accumulate far less exposure per unit than cars, so the problem is worse on a job site [Chapter 1]. Statistical shortcuts that concentrate tests on rare dangerous situations need a known exposure distribution, which does not exist for 100 or more site types [Chapter 1]. An exposure model is therefore one of the first things the booklet asks the program to build, by recording from the existing warning fleet how often each task, approach and environment actually occurs [Chapters 1, 9].
terms.why: Without exposure the program cannot say how often the new system will brake unnecessarily, cannot weight test results to the real world, and cannot claim a rate of anything. The booklet names exposure denominators as a gap in all the accident data [Chapter 4].

terms.title: Near miss
terms.oneSentence: A near miss is an event that could have caused a collision or injury but did not, usually because someone stopped, swerved or was lucky.
terms.explained:
Two haul trucks meeting on the wrong side of a dark haul road and making emergency stops 15 m apart is a near miss [Chapter 4]. Nobody is hurt, so such events often go unrecorded. Queensland's regulator warns that collision near misses in surface mines are under-reported, and New Zealand's said its incident data were incomplete because few quarries reported [Chapter 4]. Where counted, they are many: Queensland recorded 48 mobile-equipment collisions and near misses at open-cut coal mines in five months of 2017 [Chapter 4].

Near misses are precious for an automatic-braking program because fatal accidents are far too rare to tune a system on. The booklet recommends logging every warning and intervention with machine state, load, grade, speed, target class, weather, light, operator response, whether braking was necessary, and task phase [Chapter 4]. It also warns of a bias in existing logs: an existing warning may make the operator brake, so the data contain few natural examples of what would have happened without it, and the near misses where the warning was ignored, the most valuable records, are often not logged with ground truth [Chapter 10].
terms.why: Near-miss and intervention logs are the main source of realistic test scenarios and of the exposure model, and the four-month campaign should be seen as the start of a living evidence base fed by field near misses, not a one-time dataset [Chapter 9].

terms.title: Collision Mitigation System (CMS)
terms.oneSentence: A Collision Mitigation System (CMS) detects an object close to a machine, warns the operator, and if the operator does not react, applies the brakes automatically to avoid the collision or make it less severe.
terms.explained:
"Mitigation" is chosen carefully. To mitigate is to reduce the harm, not necessarily to prevent it: a system that brakes late may still make contact, but at lower speed. Volvo CE and Caterpillar both use the name for their wheel-loader functions [Chapter 2]. In this booklet, "the CMS" means the manufacturer's next-generation system that is the subject of the whole program.

The manufacturer already sells a proximity awareness system that warns the operator when the machine gets too close to an object, much like parking sensors on a car. Getting it to an acceptable balance between detecting hazards and crying wolf took years of calibration, and each platform needed its own tuning [Introduction]. The CMS keeps the warnings and adds the automatic brake. Prototype hardware and software are expected in mid-2027, and validation must then finish in under four months, where the last comparable function took three to four years [Introduction].

Technically the CMS is a chain, and validation must cover all of it: the environment, the sensor, the perception software that recognizes objects, the threat logic, the warning and the operator's chance to act, the decision to intervene, the interface to the machine's controls, the brake or retarder, the machine's real motion, and the resulting distance or collision [Chapter 1]. The governing standard, ISO 21815, limits intervention to reducing speed, stopping or preventing motion from standstill, never automatic steering [Chapters 1, 8].

The booklet also says what the CMS is not. It is not a replacement for site design, traffic rules or operator skill: in the industry's nine-level model it is the top level, intervention, which works only on a sound baseline of the lower levels [Chapters 1, 4]. And it is not proven anywhere to be validatable in four months: the research found no case in any industry of a new automatic braking function going from first representative hardware to accepted validation in about that time [Introduction, Chapters 1, 2, 13].
terms.why: The CMS is the product the plan must validate. The booklet's central conclusion is that the four months cannot be compressed but most of the work can be moved in front of them: build the scenario catalog, the data pipeline on the existing fleet, the simulation and bench tools and the credibility evidence before the prototype arrives, so the four months become a confirmation and calibration campaign [Introduction, Chapters 1, 10, 13].

terms.title: Collision Warning System (CWS) and Collision Avoidance System (CAS)
terms.oneSentence: A Collision Warning System (CWS) only alerts the operator to a nearby object, while a Collision Avoidance System (CAS) also acts on the machine, slowing or stopping it.
terms.explained:
The difference is who acts. With a CWS a light flashes or a buzzer sounds and the operator decides. With a CAS the machine itself slows, stops or refuses to move. The booklet's Collision Mitigation System is a CAS in this vocabulary. Standards and researchers write CWS/CAS, or use the umbrella term CXS for both [Chapters 1, 3]. ISO 21815-1 covers detection, operator warning, automatic intervention and test procedures for both kinds [Chapter 3].

The manufacturer's current product is a warning system; the new one is an avoidance system, and the industry is in the same transition. A NIOSH review of 97 haul-truck collision-system cases from 2000 to 2020 found 37% were warning systems and only 10% avoidance systems, most at low technology-readiness levels [Chapter 8]. The step changes the safety problem: a wrong warning costs annoyance, while a wrong intervention is a command that stops a machine weighing tens or hundreds of tons [Chapter 4].
terms.why: The plan can reuse much of what the warning system taught (sensors, scenarios, false-alarm history) but must add new evidence for everything after the brake command, which the warning system never exercised [Chapters 1, 7].

terms.title: Proximity Detection System (PDS)
terms.oneSentence: A Proximity Detection System (PDS) senses when a person or machine comes within a set distance of a machine and warns or stops it; the term is used mainly in US underground coal mining and in South Africa.
terms.explained:
The idea is a protective bubble around the machine. Many PDS designs are tag-based: workers wear a small transmitter and the machine measures how close each tag is. A 2015 US rule requires proximity detection on continuous mining machines to stop the machine before it contacts a miner [Chapter 3].

The underground PDS record is the richest field evidence of what happens when a system can stop a machine. Workers at seven coal mines said mobile PDS "unnecessarily shut down vehicles anywhere from once a day up to 15 times during a single cut of coal," and nearly 70% worried about "how and when the mobile PDS takes control" [Chapter 4]. At one mine the emergency-stop override had become routine and had been used 87 times by a worker before his fatal accident in 2017 [Chapter 4]. On the positive side, NIOSH judged that 82% of 39 continuous-miner deaths might have been prevented by proximity systems [Chapter 4], and developed "intelligent" PDS that blocks only the motions that could pin a worker [Chapter 8].
terms.why: PDS is where the industry has already lived through nuisance stops, overrides and bypasses, so its record is the booklet's main warning about what an automatic brake must avoid [Chapter 4]. Its tag dependence also shows the limit of cooperative systems: an untagged person is invisible.

terms.title: Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB) and Advanced Emergency Braking System (AEBS)
terms.oneSentence: Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB), called an Advanced Emergency Braking System (AEBS) in United Nations vehicle regulations, is the function on modern cars and trucks that brakes by itself when a crash with the vehicle or person ahead is about to happen.
terms.explained:
Sensors watch the road ahead; if the gap closes too fast and the driver does nothing, the car warns, then brakes hard. The road rules are precise. UN Regulation No. 152 for cars and vans requires a braking demand of at least 5.0 m/s², far above what heavy machines reach; UN Regulation No. 131 covers heavy road vehicles; and the US rule FMVSS 127 requires AEB on all new light vehicles by 1 September 2029, with tests for unwanted braking [Chapters 2, 3, 8].

Road AEB is the booklet's richest source of measured effects, always marked as on-road evidence. Front warning plus AEB cut rear-end striking crashes by 50%; rear AEB cut backing crashes by 78%; but it also raised the rate of being struck from behind by 20% [Chapter 4]. What does not transfer is equally clear: road AEB assumes a hard, known surface, a vehicle that should stay away from everything, and speeds where time to collision works, and heavy machines break all three [Chapter 8]. Regulators accepted virtual testing for car AEB only after years of correlation work, with physical tests retained [Chapter 10].
terms.why: Road AEB is the closest precedent for both the function and the use of simulation as evidence, so the booklet mines it for methods while refusing to copy its numbers [Chapters 2, 8, 10].

terms.title: Forward Collision Warning (FCW)
terms.oneSentence: Forward Collision Warning (FCW) is the car and truck function that warns the driver of an imminent crash ahead but leaves the braking to the driver.
terms.explained:
FCW is the warning-only half of road collision safety: a sound, light or vibration when the vehicle ahead is too close for the speed. It is the road cousin of the manufacturer's existing proximity warning, and the booklet uses FCW research for what it shows about how people respond to imperfect warnings.

The findings are mixed, and all are on-road evidence. An 18% false alarm rate was linked to truck drivers ignoring FCW (12%) or giving up on it (11%) [Chapter 4]. Yet in simulators, warnings with 20 to 33% false alarms still shortened brake reactions, and a 2025 study found no "cry wolf" effect at 33% false alarms, though it caused unnecessary braking [Chapter 4]. In real driving, false alerts were 12% when turning against 2% in lane keeping, and drivers turned sensitivity down over time [Chapter 4]. Unnecessary alarms with a visible cause hurt trust less than alarms with no visible cause [Chapter 4].
terms.why: FCW research is the best available evidence on how false alarm rates affect whether warnings are heeded, but it comes from drivers on highways. An accepted false alarm rate for off-road machines was not found [Chapter 4].

terms.title: Pedestrian AEB (PAEB)
terms.oneSentence: Pedestrian Automatic Emergency Braking (PAEB) is the version of car AEB that detects people on foot and brakes for them.
terms.explained:
Detecting a person is harder than detecting a car. People are small, come in all shapes and clothing, stand, crouch or lie down, and are hard to see at night. PAEB uses cameras, often with radar, and machine-learning software trained to recognize human shapes. The US rule FMVSS 127 requires pedestrian AEB to work between 10 and 73 km/h, in daylight and darkness [Chapter 2].

Independent testing shows how far it has to go. In an October 2025 test of four recent cars at 40 km/h, nighttime impact avoidance had improved from 0% in 2019 to 60% in 2025, still roughly 40% failures under ideal conditions, and high-visibility clothing caused a complete loss of detection in some systems [Chapter 10]. Caterpillar's own literature says its camera-based people detection "may not detect people... lying down or crouching, or when cameras are impaired by low light conditions (dusk, dawn, overcast), inclement weather (snow, rain, fog)" [Chapter 2].
terms.why: People on foot are the main victims the CMS must protect, they wear high-visibility clothing on every site, and much work happens at night. The road record warns that pedestrian detection is the weakest and most condition-dependent part of the function, which argues for keeping physical night and weather tests where simulation is weakest [Chapters 6, 10].

terms.title: Intervention
terms.oneSentence: An intervention is what a collision system does to the machine itself when the operator has not acted: it reduces speed, stops the machine, or prevents it from starting to move.
terms.explained:
A warning talks to the operator; an intervention talks to the machine. ISO 21815-1 allows exactly three kinds for earth-moving machinery: speed reduction, stopping, and motion inhibit (refusing a command to move from standstill). Automatic steering is never allowed [Chapters 1, 8]. ISO/TS 21815-2 defines the digital messages a collision system sends to the machine to "slow down, stop or prevent motion" [Chapter 8]. South African law describes the same sequence: detect, warn, then if no operator action, slow to a safe speed, then apply the brakes [Chapter 2].

Intervention changes the nature of a mistake. With a warning-only system an unnecessary detection costs annoyance and distraction. Once the system can intervene, a false or nuisance classification becomes a machine-motion command, so the same error turns from a human-factors problem into a human-factors and vehicle-dynamics hazard [Chapter 4]. Underground workers describe "jarring and jolting" stops, and mine leaders preferred systems that slow the machine to a crawl before setting the brake [Chapter 4].
terms.why: Intervention is the new element in the CMS. Everything the warning system proved stops at the first brake command; after that the recorded past no longer tells you what the machine would do, and new evidence from closed-loop simulation, bench tests and proving-ground tests is needed [Chapters 1, 7].

terms.title: Staged intervention
terms.oneSentence: Staged intervention means that a collision system acts in steps of increasing force, from a quiet information signal through warnings and gentle slowing to hard braking and a locked stop, rather than jumping straight to an emergency stop.
terms.explained:
Think of a driving instructor watching a learner head toward a parked car: first a word, then a sharper warning, then a hand toward the brake, then the brake itself. A staged system gives the operator every chance to act and, when it does act, begins gently and escalates only if the situation keeps getting worse.

The booklet assembles the ladder for earth-moving machines from the standards and the field evidence [Chapter 8]:

*Information signal.* An object is present but the stopping margin is healthy; a visual indication only.

*Urgent warning.* Risk is rising while the operator still has time; a distinct sound, light or vibration.

*Automatic slowing.* The operator does not react and margin remains; the drive request is reduced or the retarder slows the machine smoothly.

*Partial braking.* The safe margin is approaching its minimum; controlled braking below the limits of stability and traction.

*Maximum safe braking.* A collision is otherwise unavoidable; the hardest braking the current stability and control limits allow. No universal maximum deceleration for off-road machines was found.

*Stopped-state hold.* The machine is at zero speed and the hazard remains; the brake is held and released only after an operator action where rolling away is possible.

*Motion inhibit from standstill.* Something is already in the path before the machine moves; the move command is rejected. This covers the start-up hazard that time to collision cannot see.

Road AEB uses a shorter version: warning, brief brake jerk, partial braking, full braking [Chapter 8]. ISO 21815-3 requires distinguishable warning levels and places automatic action at collision-risk level 4 or above [Chapter 8]. The step from partial to maximum braking should depend on the remaining stopping margin and its uncertainty, not on distance alone: a well-seen wall on dry ground is not the same as a half-hidden person on a downhill mud slope at the same distance [Chapter 8].

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Monitoring"] --> B["Information signal"]
    B --> C["Urgent warning"]
    C --> D["Automatic slowing"]
    D --> E["Partial braking"]
    E --> F["Maximum safe braking"]
    F --> G["Stopped-state hold"]
    G --> A
    A --> H["Motion inhibit at standstill"]
    H --> A
```

*The intervention ladder: each step is taken only if the operator has not reduced the risk and the stopping margin keeps shrinking.*

Each stage has a cost. Frequent signals overload the operator; slowing may be too weak downhill; partial braking may keep the machine in the hazard zone longer and conflict with following machines; maximum braking risks rollover, articulation instability, load shift and sliding; motion inhibit disrupts close work [Chapter 8].
terms.why: Staging is how the system can be both safe and tolerable: mine leaders preferred a system that slowed to a crawl before braking, and underground workers rejected abrupt stops [Chapter 4]. Each stage needs its own thresholds, tests and evidence, which multiplies the validation work but also lets a first release use the gentler stages while the harder ones are still being proven [Chapters 1, 8].

terms.title: Nine levels of control
terms.oneSentence: The nine levels of control are the mining industry's ladder of defenses against vehicle interactions, running from how a site is designed (Level 1) to a machine that brakes by itself (Level 9), with warning technology at Levels 7 and 8.
terms.explained:
The model comes from EMESRT (the Earth Moving Equipment Safety Round Table), a group of mining companies, in its performance requirement PR-5A, and it is used by the ICMM (International Council on Mining and Metals), regulators and suppliers worldwide [Chapters 1, 3, 5]. The levels are [Chapter 5]:

Site requirements: the layout and rules of the site itself.

Segregation controls: keeping people, light vehicles and heavy machines apart.

Operating procedures: the written rules for how work is done.

Authority to operate: who may drive what.

Fitness to operate: fatigue, health, impairment.

Operating compliance: whether the rules are actually followed.

Operator awareness: technology that helps the operator see and know, such as cameras and proximity displays.

Advisory controls: technology that advises the operator to act.

Intervention controls: technology that acts on the machine, slowing and stopping it.

Levels 1 to 6 are about people, places and procedures. Levels 7 to 9 are technology and form a ladder of their own: awareness, advice, action. The manufacturer's existing proximity warning sits at Levels 7 and 8; the Collision Mitigation System is a Level 9 control.

```mermaid
flowchart BT
    L1["Level 1: Site requirements"] --> L2["Level 2: Segregation controls"]
    L2 --> L3["Level 3: Operating procedures"]
    L3 --> L4["Level 4: Authority to operate"]
    L4 --> L5["Level 5: Fitness to operate"]
    L5 --> L6["Level 6: Operating compliance"]
    L6 --> L7["Level 7: Operator awareness"]
    L7 --> L8["Level 8: Advisory controls"]
    L8 --> L9["Level 9: Intervention controls"]
```

*The EMESRT ladder: Levels 1 to 6 are design, people and procedures; Levels 7 to 9 are technology, ending with the machine acting on its own.*

The industry is firm that the top rung does not replace the others. ICMM and EMESRT state that implementing Level 8 and 9 controls well requires first understanding the effectiveness of the Level 1 to 7 baseline for normal operations, and that "there are no silver bullets" [Chapter 1]. Regulators differ in emphasis: New South Wales and NIOSH favor the lower levels with Levels 7 to 9 as backup, while South Africa has made Level 9 intervention a legal requirement since December 2022 [Chapter 4]. The Australian ACARP test framework follows the same logic in two tiers: prove object detection first, then Level 8 or 9 intervention [Chapter 1].
terms.why: The nine levels explain why the same braking algorithm can be safe at one site and troublesome at another: the site's own Level 1 to 6 controls decide how often people and machines legitimately get close [Chapter 1]. They also give the plan its vocabulary for staged release, which is how Epiroc describes running its system on site "without immediately enforcing level-9 intervention" [Chapter 1].

terms.title: Nuisance braking
terms.oneSentence: Nuisance braking is an automatic brake application that was not needed, either because there was no real object (a false intervention) or because the object was real but posed no danger (an unnecessary intervention).
terms.explained:
The vocabulary comes from a NIOSH field study of a radar warning system on a haul truck, and the booklet carries its definitions over to braking [Chapter 4]. A *false* alarm occurs when the sensor reports an object that is not significant: a rut, a rock, a bush, or the truck's own tires. A *nuisance* alarm is technically correct, the object is there, but there is no urgent danger because the operator knows about it and the task requires the approach, for example backing toward a rock pile to be loaded. In that study 18% of alarms were false, 42% were nuisance and 40% warranted action [Chapter 4]. Nuisance braking is what happens when the first two categories drive the brakes instead of a buzzer.

The field record shows how destructive that is. Underground, stop-capable proximity systems "unnecessarily shut down vehicles anywhere from once a day up to 15 times during a single cut of coal"; workers reported jarring and jolting stops; a manufacturer reported 5 to 10% production loss while proximity detection was active, although two mine operators said production recovered [Chapter 4]. The chain the booklet draws runs from unnecessary interventions to annoyance, lost production and new hazards, then to bypass, override, tag removal and widened zones, and finally to protection being lost when it is needed [Chapter 4]. Chapter 8 calls nuisance interventions the main documented field failure of deployed proximity systems [Chapter 8].

A better sensor alone does not fix it. In the haul-truck study most unwanted alarms were nuisance, not false, so the task, the intention and the kind of object had to be understood [Chapter 4]. Nor can it be measured on a test track with staged targets; it needs real operations, measured as unnecessary interventions per operating hour, per loading cycle and per reverse maneuver, by task [Chapter 4]. The booklet's planning advice is to run the new software in shadow mode (computing but not executing brake commands) on fielded machines so the nuisance-brake rate is measured before braking is enabled [Chapter 1], and to make the nuisance-intervention rate an acceptance metric equal in weight to missed interventions [Chapter 8]. How much a nuisance brake should "cost" relative to a miss when tuning is a safety-policy decision to be written down, not hidden in a formula [Chapter 9].
terms.why: Nuisance braking is the most likely way for the CMS to fail in service: not by missing a hazard, but by stopping machines so often that people switch it off [Chapters 4, 8]. The manufacturer's own experience that balancing detection against false positives took years is the reason the program exists [Introduction].

terms.title: False alarm and alarm accuracy
terms.oneSentence: A false alarm is a warning given when nothing dangerous is there, a nuisance alarm is a warning about something real that is not dangerous in the situation, and alarm accuracy is the share of all alarms that deserved a response.
terms.explained:
Imagine a smoke detector. One that goes off with no smoke gives a false alarm. One that goes off every time you make toast gives a nuisance alarm: there is smoke, but you know why. One that never catches a real fire has a miss. Alarm accuracy asks: of all the times it sounded, how often was it right to?

The best off-road numbers are still from a 2004 field test, published in 2006, of a radar warning system on a Caterpillar 793B haul truck over seven days at a US copper mine [Chapters 4, 7]. Of 580 alarms, 102 (18%) were false, 243 (42%) were nuisance, and 235 (40%) warranted action. There were no missed detections. False alarms came from ruts, rocks, foliage and the truck's own rear tires, and the audible alarm was found switched off after shifts [Chapter 4]. No study defines a false alarm rate that off-road operators will accept; an 18% rate caused problems, but it does not follow that 17% is acceptable or that 5% would be [Chapter 4].
terms.why: The old system's false and nuisance rates are the baseline the new system must beat, and they can only be measured fairly against an independent record of what was really there [Chapter 7]. That the 2006 figure is still the best hard number shows how thin the independent off-road data are [Chapter 7].

terms.title: Alarm fatigue
terms.oneSentence: Alarm fatigue is the state in which a person has heard so many alarms that did not matter that they stop reacting to alarms at all, including the one that does matter.
terms.explained:
This is the "cry wolf" effect. In hospitals, nurses exposed to constant monitor alarms learn to ignore them; on a job site, operators warned on every loading cycle do the same. The warning still sounds, but it no longer changes behavior. ISO 21815-3 notes that false positives "could create alarm fatigue" [Chapter 3].

The booklet looked for direct measurements in mining, such as the probability of ignoring the nth warning, and found none [Chapter 4]. It found the precursors and the outcomes: very high exposure to unnecessary alarms, annoyance, degraded trust, disabling and overriding [Chapter 4]. NIOSH warned that operators may "lose confidence in the system and start to ignore alarms altogether" [Chapter 4]. Road and aviation evidence is mixed: a cry-wolf effect was strong in some truck warning data, absent in air-traffic-control alerts with 45% false alarms, and absent in some driving-simulator studies [Chapter 4].
terms.why: Operators of the existing warning fleet may already have learned to ignore frequent warnings, and will meet the first automatic stops with that habit [Chapter 1]. A warning stage in the intervention ladder only buys time if the warning is still believed.

terms.title: Switching off and bypassing
terms.oneSentence: Switching off and bypassing means defeating a safety system on purpose, by turning it off, overriding it, removing the tag it tracks, or redesigning its zones so it no longer protects what it should.
terms.explained:
When a protective system gets in the way of the job, people find ways around it. Researchers found the audible alarm of a haul-truck warning system switched off after shifts [Chapter 4]. Mechanics removed wearable tags to diagnose leaks inside the danger zone; mines asked for a "temporary bypass" feature; zone redesigns removed coverage at a hauler's rear corners [Chapter 4]. At one underground mine the emergency-stop override had become common practice, and the investigation of a fatal accident in June 2017 recorded 87 prior activations of the dead worker's own override [Chapter 4]. South African guidance warns that false slow-downs and stops can "disrupt production to a point where the systems must be switched off" [Chapter 4].

Rules try to make this harder. ISO 16001 forbids disabling a detection system with a single action, and South African industry guidance limits emergency and maintenance overrides by time and speed and forbids routine use [Chapter 3]. Regulators in the United States, Australia and South Africa agree that alarm burden leads people to ignore, bypass or switch off systems [Chapter 4].
terms.why: A system that is switched off protects no one, so bypass resistance and task compatibility belong in the safety case, and the real rate of bypassing is something only field monitoring can reveal [Chapter 4]. The design target the booklet names is calibrated trust, not maximum trust.

terms.title: Operator reaction time
terms.oneSentence: Operator reaction time is the time between a warning (or the appearance of a hazard) and the moment the operator begins to act, for example by pressing the brake.
terms.explained:
During the reaction time the machine keeps moving at full speed, so the distance it covers is speed multiplied by time:

`d_reaction = v * t`

where `d_reaction` is the distance traveled before anything happens, `v` is the speed and `t` is the reaction time. At 40 km/h (about 11.1 m/s) a reaction time of 2 s means 22.2 m before braking even begins. Queensland guidance uses this example as a combined operator-plus-mechanical delay for illustration, not as a measured human value [Chapter 4].

The booklet's main finding is a gap: no representative, field-measured distribution of heavy-machine operators' reaction times to proximity warnings was found [Chapter 4]. The values in use are borrowed or illustrative: 0.5 to 1 s from road research, about 1 s in a US regulatory brake-test table, 1 to 3 s as a margin in a mining-truck patent, 2.5 s in road-design manuals [Chapters 4, 8]. Road research adds that brake responses depend on how fast the gap is closing, and that the estimated benefit of a warning system ranged from 53% to 96% depending on which driver model was chosen [Chapter 4].
terms.why: A Collision Mitigation System acts when the operator has not, so the time the system waits is a bet on the operator's reaction time. The booklet advises treating that time as an uncertain parameter and running sensitivity analyses, not presenting one average as validated [Chapter 4].

terms.title: Human factors
terms.oneSentence: Human factors is the field that studies how people perceive, decide and act when working with machines, and designs the machine so that real people, tired or busy or distracted, can use it safely.
terms.explained:
A sensor can be perfect and the system can still fail if the operator does not notice the warning, does not understand it, does not trust it, or has learned to work around it. Human factors covers attention, workload, trust, habit, fatigue, how information is presented, and how behavior changes over months of use.

The booklet's human-factors evidence is thin where it most needs to be thick. The strongest off-road study placed drivers in a haul-truck simulator and showed that a richer proximity display reduced collision risk and braking force; the effect was smaller with less experienced drivers, a warning against assuming one generic operator [Chapter 4]. Industry guidance notes that "Human Performance can change both positively and negatively after technology is introduced" [Chapter 1]. No validated model of an off-road operator exists [Chapter 4]. The booklet therefore asks the plan to keep three uncertainties separate: sensor uncertainty, operator-response uncertainty and machine-response uncertainty [Chapter 4]. It also gives human factors its own question in the allocation of evidence: does the complete intervention improve rather than degrade real operations, answered by operator simulation, nuisance-intervention testing, shadow operation and staged deployment [Chapter 1].
terms.why: A vehicle-and-environment simulator does not represent adaptation, over-reliance, override behavior or mode confusion, so human-in-the-loop evidence may be required for any safety claim that depends on what the operator does [Chapter 10].

terms.title: Human-machine interface (HMI)
terms.oneSentence: The human-machine interface (HMI) is everything through which the system and the operator communicate: the screens, lights, sounds, vibrations and buttons in the cab.
terms.explained:
When the system detects something, the HMI is how the operator finds out. A good HMI makes the urgent warning unmistakable, shows where the object is, and lets the operator acknowledge or override without fumbling. A poor one is a buzzer that sounds the same for a rock pile and a person.

ISO 21815-3 requires warning levels that can be told apart [Chapter 8]. The Australian ACARP project tested visual and auditory proximity interfaces in a haul-truck simulator and found that a schematic display helped drivers reduce collision risk [Chapters 1, 4]. People on foot responded fastest to vibration, then visual signals, then sound [Chapter 4]. Workers rated underground proximity systems well on training, ease of use and feedback, and poorly on reliability and fit with the task [Chapter 4]. The continuous audible warning in the haul-truck radar study was annoying enough to be switched off [Chapter 4]. For testing, every warning should be logged with its level, time stamp, audio, visual or haptic state and acknowledgement; otherwise it is impossible to tell afterward whether a warning was given, seen and ignored [Chapter 7].
terms.why: The HMI decides whether the warning stage of a staged intervention buys the operator real time, and whether an automatic stop surprises the operator. The booklet recommends sorting out basic HMI problems in a simulator before expensive prototype tests [Chapter 1].

terms.title: Operator behavior change
terms.oneSentence: Operator behavior change is the way people start to work differently once a protective system exists, including risk compensation (taking more risk because they feel protected) and over-reliance (letting the system do the watching).
terms.explained:
Give a person a safety net and some will climb higher: that is risk compensation. Give a person a machine that brakes by itself and some will stop checking the mirrors: that is over-reliance. The opposite also happens: a system that is wrong too often is distrusted and disabled. The goal the booklet names is calibrated trust, trusting the system exactly as much as it deserves [Chapter 4].

Off-road, the evidence is qualitative only. Underground workers changed where they stood, removed tags and asked for bypasses; regulators worry about a "silver bullet" mindset; an MSHA commenter said miners "have taken higher risks because of a false sense of security" [Chapter 4]. The booklet rates four adaptations: learning the zones and changing close-proximity tasks (moderate evidence), overriding or disabling (strong that it occurs, frequency unknown), relying too much (reported, not quantified), and driving faster or following closer because the machine will brake (not found in surface-mining data) [Chapter 4]. On the road, drivers who trusted other vehicles' automatic braking braked later themselves, a possible parallel for ground crew who assume a machine will stop for them [Chapter 4].
terms.why: Behavior change cannot be seen in a four-month window or in a simulator; it needs months of field time, so the booklet lists it as uncompressible and assigns it to staged release with field monitoring [Chapter 1]. The missing numbers should be collected during pilot deployment rather than assumed [Chapter 4].

terms.title: Tasks that look like a collision risk to a sensor
terms.oneSentence: Many normal, intended parts of the job, such as loading a truck, bumping a dump berm or working beside ground crew, put a large object close to the machine in exactly the way a sensor is designed to flag.
terms.explained:
A sensor measures distance and closing speed; it does not know what the operator intends. The booklet collects the documented cases where ordinary production looks dangerous to a simple sensor [Chapter 4]:

*Loading a truck.* Backing toward a rock pile is the textbook nuisance detection. Yet the loading zone cannot be ignored, because a second truck or a person can enter it.

*Dump berms as bump stops.* Safe practice, but the berm is also the edge reference that keeps the truck from going over, so berm detections should not be treated as nuisance.

*Tip heads shared by dozers and trucks.* Machines must work close together.

*Walls, ribs and stockpiles.* Small clearances; underground, some tasks need miners closer than 3 ft (about 0.9 m) to the machine.

*Ground crew and maintenance.* Mechanics inside the danger zone, spotters, authorized pedestrians.

*Parking and workshops.* Small clearances and many fixed objects.

*The machine itself.* The truck's own rear tires triggered false alarms.

*Swing and rotation.* Excavators strike without any travel.

Komatsu's excavator system must be off during trailer loading, and Volvo's loader system remembers the last slope so it does not brake when reversing down a stockpile: product-level fixes for single tasks [Chapter 2].
terms.why: These tasks are where nuisance braking will come from, and each should be a separate validation scenario rather than a slower version of haul-road driving [Chapter 4]. Neither "always alarm when close" nor aggressive suppression works across all tasks; the system needs context and the plan needs per-task metrics [Chapter 4].

terms.title: New risks created by automatic braking
terms.oneSentence: An automatic stop can itself cause harm, through the jolt to the operator, a shifting or spilled load, loss of stability on a slope, a following machine running into the stopped one, or the machine rolling back once the brake is released.
terms.explained:
Stopping a car hard is uncomfortable. Stopping a loaded 100 t truck hard on a wet downhill ramp is a different matter. The booklet lists the secondary hazards found in the sources and notes that most are reported but not measured [Chapters 4, 8]:

*Operator injury from a sudden stop.* Underground workers report "jarring and jolting" stops; MSHA says it knows of no injuries from them. No safe jerk limit was found.

*Spilled or shifted loads.* Mechanically credible; no quantified data found.

*Loss of stability on slopes.* Braking hard uses up the grip needed for steering; a rollover caused by automatic braking: not found.

*Being struck from behind.* On the road, automatic braking raised the rate of being hit from behind by 20%; off-road, not found.

*Rollaway after the stop.* ISO 21815-3 recommends an operator action, such as setting the parking brake, before the brake is released.

To keep the stop safe, the booklet reports the published position that the commanded deceleration should be the smallest of several limits:

`a_command = min(a_need, a_traction, a_stability, a_machine, a_load)`

where `a_need` is the deceleration needed to avoid the collision, `a_traction` is what the ground can provide, `a_stability` comes from the roll, pitch and articulation state with the payload, `a_machine` is what the brakes can deliver, and `a_load` is the limit set by payload or attachment. The deceleration should ramp up gradually and end in a held state [Chapter 8].
terms.why: The program must test not only whether the machine stops short of the object but also deceleration and jerk, stability on grades, laden and unladen states, and behavior after the stop [Chapters 4, 8]. The booklet places this in the hazard analysis rather than assuming a machine is safe because it "stops sooner" [Chapter 1].

terms.title: Warning-system fleet
terms.oneSentence: The warning-system fleet is the set of machines the manufacturer has already sold with the proximity warning system, and its field history is the record of what those machines have detected, warned about and got wrong in real use.
terms.explained:
Before any prototype of the new system exists, the manufacturer already has machines in the field with sensors watching their surroundings. The booklet treats this fleet as the program's most valuable early asset, with conditions.

The opportunity: the existing machines can start recording now, in October 2026, including through the winter that the later validation window will never see [Introduction, Chapter 1]. Replaying those recordings through new software measures detection and false-alarm behavior on real data, and the recorded false-alarm history is the best available data for setting intervention thresholds [Chapters 1, 7]. The fleet is also the natural source for an exposure model, and the booklet says estimating that distribution from it should start now [Chapter 9].

The conditions: what is established is that a warning system exists, not that it keeps raw sensor data, machine signals, accurate time stamps or labels. A record worth replaying needs all of these plus an independent record of what was really there; labeling dominates the cost [Chapter 1].

The limits: field history can validate inputs and parts of the simulation, not the new closed-loop braking chain. The logs are open-loop (the world did not react to the new software), censored by the operator (a warning that made the operator brake hides what would have happened otherwise) and biased toward normal operation [Chapter 10].
terms.why: "Start recording now" is one of the few unconditional recommendations in the booklet, because the fleet's winter data cannot be collected later and because the baseline the new system must beat can only be measured from it [Introduction, Chapters 1, 7].

terms.title: Sensor and prototype freeze
terms.oneSentence: The sensor freeze is the project milestone at which the sensor types, numbers and mounting positions are fixed, and the prototype freeze is the milestone at which the first representative hardware and software are fixed; the booklet uses "before freeze" and "after freeze" to divide the work.
terms.explained:
In engineering a "freeze" is a decision that will not be reopened. Until the sensors are frozen, nobody knows whether the system will use cameras, radar, lidar, ultrasonic sensors or a mix, or where on each machine they will sit; the booklet had to cover all options for that reason [Chapter 1]. The prototype, due in mid-2027, is the first hardware and software built the way the product will be built.

The freeze divides what can be done early from what cannot. Before it, a program can build everything that does not depend on sensor physics: hazard analysis, scenario catalog, acceptance metrics, safety-case structure, simulation architecture and the data pipeline on the existing fleet [Chapters 1, 2]. After it, the sensor-specific work starts: matching simulated sensors to real ones, bench testing with the real controller, choosing test targets that look right to the chosen sensor [Chapters 1, 6].

A late change is costly. A sensor change in 2027 invalidates the sensor-model correlation, the bench stimulation assumptions, the detection-range evidence, the mounting analysis and parts of the case for reusing evidence across models [Chapter 1]. Standards are moving too: several ISO parts were due to change in late 2026, so the plan should re-baseline on the editions actually published [Chapter 3].
terms.why: The freeze dates set the critical path. The booklet's advice is to build the architecture sensor-interface-neutral but not sensor-physics-neutral, so final sensor models drop in as replaceable modules, and never to claim a validated sensor digital twin before hardware and mounting are frozen and correlated [Chapters 1, 2].

terms.title: Validation window
terms.oneSentence: The validation window is the period of less than four months after the prototype arrives in mid-2027 in which the Collision Mitigation System must be validated.
terms.explained:
Validation means showing, with evidence, that the system does what it is supposed to do safely in the conditions it will meet. The last comparable function at this manufacturer took three to four years, mostly through physical testing and tuning on each machine model [Introduction]. The new target is under four months, in the second half of 2027 [Chapter 2].

The booklet's answer is consistent across chapters. No case was found, in any industry, of a new automatic braking function going from first representative hardware to accepted validation in about four months; every documented reduction in physical testing rested on years of earlier investment, a narrow operating domain, or both [Introduction, Chapters 1, 2, 13]. So the four months cannot be compressed, but most of the work can be moved in front of them: the scenario catalog, the data pipeline on the existing fleet, the simulation and bench tools and the credibility evidence can all exist before the prototype arrives [Chapter 1].

The window then has a fixed shape: correlate (measure latency, detection range and stopping on the real prototype), multiply (re-run the correlated scenarios virtually), confirm (whole-machine tests of the worst cases), then shadow mode (live operation with braking disabled) [Chapter 1]. It is a final validation window, not a capability-construction window [Chapter 2]. Two things sit awkwardly inside it: it contains no northern winter [Chapter 13], and the EU Machinery Regulation applies from 20 January 2027, so if the perception uses machine learning, the lead time for a notified body alone could exceed the window [Chapter 1].
terms.why: The window is the constraint the whole plan is built around. The booklet's reframing, that it should be a confirmation and calibration campaign for a method already proven before the prototype arrives, is its most repeated conclusion [Introduction, Chapters 1, 6, 10, 13].

terms.title: Site type and the "100+ site types" claim
terms.oneSentence: A site type is a class of job site with a characteristic layout, surface and traffic (an open pit, a quarry face, a stockpile yard, a road works), and the "100+ site types" claim is the challenge statement that one machine may work across 100 or more job sites and applications.
terms.explained:
The challenge statement lists job sites and applications as the first variable that makes validation hard [Introduction]. Taken literally, that would mean validating on 100 different places. The booklet argues that the number is not meaningful until the organization defines what it counts: individually validated sites, parameterized classes of environment, or customer configurations inside a validated envelope [Chapter 13].

The booklet replaces counting with coverage. No standard sets a required number of virtual job sites; teams argue sufficiency through coverage of a defined operating domain and its parameters, because two hundred nearly identical dry pit roads give less coverage than a small set that spans different geometry, materials and conditions [Chapter 5]. Site type becomes one parameter among many, alongside surface, slope, object classes, weather and light, machine model and sensor position [Chapter 5]. As planning assumptions rather than evidence, the booklet mentions 15 to 30 parameterized site archetypes anchored by 3 to 5 surveyed real sites as one possible starting point [Chapter 5]. Every off-road product the booklet found launched much narrower than its full market [Chapters 2, 13].
