The booklet's allocation principle assigns "did the software decide correctly?" to SIL, "did the machine execute safely?" to HIL and whole-machine tests, and "did the sensor perceive correctly?" to replay, sensor simulation and physical tests [Chapter 1].

terms.title: Model-in-the-loop (MIL)
terms.oneSentence: Model-in-the-loop testing runs a model of the control logic against a model of the machine and its surroundings, with no real software or hardware yet.
terms.explained:
Before any code is written for the real controller, engineers draw the decision logic as a block diagram in a modeling tool: if the object is closer than this and the speed is above that, warn; if there is no reaction after so many milliseconds, brake. Model-in-the-loop (MIL) runs that diagram in the same tool against a simple machine model, so the designers can see whether the rules behave sensibly long before anything is built. It is the cheapest and earliest rung of the ladder.

The booklet mentions MIL as part of the volume end of the pipeline, "model-in-the-loop and software-in-the-loop for volume (thousands of runs per night on cloud or on-premise compute)" [Chapter 9], and the model-based tool chain it describes at the middle cost level supports MIL, SIL and HIL from the same models [Chapter 11]. Nothing about sensors or real timing can be learned here; the value is in catching logical mistakes, such as a warning zone that never triggers when the machine is articulated, while a fix costs minutes.
terms.why: The decision logic of a warn-then-brake function is far simpler than an automated-driving planner [Chapter 7], so much of it can be designed and checked at MIL level in late 2026, before the sensor is chosen.

terms.title: Software-in-the-loop (SIL)
terms.oneSentence: Software-in-the-loop testing runs the real braking software, compiled for an ordinary computer, inside a simulated machine on a simulated site, so that thousands of scenarios can be tried without any hardware.
terms.explained:
The software that will one day run inside the machine's controller is built instead for a desktop or cloud computer. It receives inputs from a simulator (object positions, or synthetic sensor data, plus machine speed and state), makes its decisions and sends brake requests back to the simulated machine, which slows down according to its model. The scene evolves, the software sees the new situation, and the loop continues. Because the real world is absent, time can run faster than real time and hundreds of copies can run in parallel.

Chapter 7 lists what SIL needs: a scenario or world model, an environment simulation with sensor models (ideal, phenomenological or physics-based) or semantic object inputs, a machine-dynamics model that includes braking, articulation and load, and a test oracle that scores each run [Chapter 7]. It proves logic correctness, timing in simulated time, boundary exploration, requirements tests, very high-volume regression and closed-loop coverage of large scenario sets; the booklet calls it "the right tool for sweeping the 100+ site types and 10+ scenarios parametrically" [Chapter 7]. It cannot prove real sensor physics in dust, snow or glare unless the sensor models are validated, nor the timing, processor and input-output faults of the final controller, nor the real brake hardware. "It is only as credible as its models" [Chapter 7].

A name clash: in functional-safety standards, SIL also means Safety Integrity Level, a grade of how reliable a safety function must be. The two have nothing in common; context tells them apart.

Standard support is thin. ISO 18497-4:2024 for agricultural machines explicitly lists simulation beside measurement, test and analysis as a verification method, the closest off-road support found [Chapter 7]. ASAM states that no standardized metrics exist to assess sensor-simulation quality [Chapter 7]. The booklet's pre-hardware advice is to run SIL first with ideal or semantic sensors to debug threat assessment and braking logic, then add realistic sensor error models for each candidate sensor type, validated against recordings from existing machines [Chapter 7].
terms.why: SIL is where the statistics become feasible: a 1% miss-rate claim in each of 20 critical strata needs about 6,000 zero-miss trials, "which is only feasible in simulation or hardware-in-the-loop" [Chapter 9]. But SIL results are trusted only after replay and sensor-model correlation, the first of the booklet's three ordering rules [Chapter 1].

terms.title: Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) with data injection
terms.oneSentence: Hardware-in-the-loop testing connects the real electronic control unit, with its real wiring and network messages, to a simulator that runs in real time and feeds it the data a real machine would produce.
terms.explained:
Imagine taking the brain of the machine, the electronic control unit (ECU), out of the machine and placing it on a laboratory bench. Instead of real sensors and a real engine, it is wired to a powerful computer that pretends to be the rest of the machine: it sends the messages a camera, radar or speed sensor would send, listens for the brake request the ECU sends back, and moves the virtual machine accordingly. Because the ECU cannot tell the difference, it must respond within the same milliseconds as on a real machine, which is why the simulator must keep hard real time.

"Data injection" means that the simulated sensor data are fed in electrically, behind the sensor's own optics or antenna: raw camera data behind the imager, radar detections at the detection level, or recorded machine-network traffic (CAN, the controller area network bus, and the SAE J1939 message set used on heavy vehicles) [Chapter 7]. Chapter 7 lists what HIL needs: a real-time simulator with deterministic timing, a machine-dynamics model, electrical input-output and sensor-interface emulation, "restbus" models that imitate the rest of the machine network, and the ISO/TS 21815-2 brake-request interface [Chapter 7].

HIL proves the real-time behavior of the production ECU and its software, communication and interface timing, diagnostics and fault behavior, fail-to-safe behavior, and decision logic under repeatable scenarios. South Africa's MOSH regime (Mining Industry Occupational Safety and Health learning hub), for example, requires that a disconnection between the detection device and the machine be detected within 500 ms and that the machine reply within 50 ms; such limits are tested on a bench [Chapter 7]. HIL cannot prove sensor front-end behavior, because injection bypasses the lens, imager or antenna, nor true machine and brake behavior when these are only modeled [Chapter 7]. Fault injection (stale messages, dropped frames, corrupted data, disagreement between sensors) is far faster and safer here than waiting for faults in the field [Chapter 1].

The rig can be commissioned before the final processor exists, using a virtual or development ECU, and only that surrogate is swapped when production controllers arrive [Chapter 7]. Integration effort is real: the booklet ranks raw-signal sensor HIL as the highest-effort integration type and warns that a renderer accurate offline may not meet ECU timing deterministically [Chapter 11].
terms.why: HIL is the natural home for the J1939 intervention interface of ISO/TS 21815-2 and for the laboratory stage of the South African verification regime; it finds timing, bus and integration faults without occupying a machine, which the four-month window cannot spare [Chapters 1, 7].

terms.title: Direct digital or raw signal injection
terms.oneSentence: Raw signal injection feeds simulated or recorded sensor data into the sensor's electronics at a defined electrical point, so that everything downstream of that point is tested and everything upstream is not.
terms.explained:
A camera is a chain: lens, imager chip, serial link, image-processing unit, detection software. Instead of showing the camera a picture, an injection device plugs into the link and sends the frames directly. The booklet treats this as a method in its own right because "its value depends entirely on the insertion point" [Chapter 7]. Inject after the imager and you test the processing chain, bandwidth, timing, the handling of corrupted frames and interface faults; you do not test the lens, exposure control, dirt on the glass, vibration or sun glare. Inject a radar object list onto the vehicle network and you test only the decision software.

The same principle governs replay: re-injecting recorded frames into the image electronic control unit (ECU) "tests everything downstream of that point, but it does not retest the old lens, exposure control, imager, lens contamination, vibration or sun-glare response" [Chapter 7]. Camera raw-image injection is commercially implemented, and one vendor argues that it avoids the screen-synchronization and field-of-view problems of showing a camera a monitor [Chapter 7].
terms.why: Injection makes high-volume HIL and replay possible, but the booklet insists that the injection boundary be stated with every result, so that evidence about the processing chain is never mistaken for evidence about the sensor in dust or glare [Chapter 7].

terms.title: Over-the-air sensor stimulation (sensor-in-the-loop)
terms.oneSentence: Over-the-air stimulation presents a real, complete sensor with artificial light, radio waves or sound generated from the virtual scene, so that the whole sensor, including its optics or antenna and its firmware, is in the loop.
terms.explained:
Instead of injecting data behind the sensor, the test rig makes the sensor "see" something. For radar, a target simulator receives the radar's transmitted signal and sends back echoes with a chosen delay, speed shift and strength, so the radar believes a worker is 8 m away and approaching. For a camera, a screen or projector shows the rendered scene. For lidar, an emulator returns delayed light pulses. For ultrasonic sensors, an echo generator does the same with sound [Chapters 6, 7]. The rig needs a shielded or echo-free room, calibrated signal losses and real-time synchronization with the scene, and it usually runs closed-loop [Chapter 7].

The physical limits bite at close range. Digital radar target simulators have a minimum simulated range set by their processing delay: each 6.67 nanoseconds of delay adds 1 m of apparent distance. A 2021 peer-reviewed review gives about 20 to 30 m as a typical minimum for digital systems, with a single-digit number of targets, at a cost of "hundreds of thousands of dollars"; vendors claim minimums of 0.6 m or 1.5 m and from five to several hundred objects [Chapters 6, 7]. Camera stimulation suffers from screen frame-rate mismatch and wide fields of view; lidar stimulation, especially for solid-state lidar, is identified as a remaining gap; ultrasonic stimulation exists only for automotive parking functions [Chapter 7]. None of these devices reproduces terrain clutter, berms, dust plumes or radio reflections from steel structures.
terms.why: Workers at 0.5 to 5 m behind a machine are exactly where digital radar simulators are weakest, so the booklet rates over-the-air stimulation low for close-range off-road use and reserves it for sensor and ECU (electronic control unit) regression, timing tests and supplier-independent characterization [Chapters 6, 7].

terms.title: Vehicle-in-the-loop (VIL) and mixed reality
terms.oneSentence: Vehicle-in-the-loop testing drives the complete real machine on a safe, empty test area while virtual hazards are fed to its sensors or controller, so that it brakes for a worker who exists only in the simulation.
terms.explained:
The machine is real: real brakes, real hydraulics, real controller delays, real operator seat. The danger is virtual: a simulated worker steps behind the machine, the simulated detection reaches the braking system by injection or over-the-air stimulation, the machine really brakes, and its real position and speed are fed back into the simulation so that the next stimuli match. Because the machine moves through an empty area while reacting to virtual objects, this is also called mixed reality or augmented-reality testing; one cited approach injects virtual hazards into a real vehicle's controller on a test track, and an augmented-reality proving-ground platform was published in 2024 [Chapter 1].

VIL proves real braking dynamics, real actuator and controller delays, real end-to-end latency and the real operator interface without endangering people or targets; "it is the bridge between simulation and field" [Chapter 7]. It cannot prove perception of the injected objects unless they are stimulated over the air, and a bench cannot reproduce soft soil, grades, sinkage, articulated dynamics, payload behavior, vibration, dust or weather; the size of heavy machines makes facilities difficult [Chapter 7].

The evidence is on-road only. A 2024 survey reports limitations in testbench fidelity, multi-target radar simulation, multi-camera systems and especially lidar stimulation, and did not identify a full-scale VIL platform ready for comprehensive industrial testing; off-road VIL on production-scale haul trucks, loaders, dozers or excavators was not found [Chapters 1, 7].
terms.why: The booklet's hierarchy uses VIL "only where its extra physical fidelity justifies the investment" and treats it as emerging and capital-intensive rather than a proven shortcut for heavy machines [Chapter 1].

terms.title: Driver-in-the-loop (DIL), operator-in-the-loop and the machine simulator
terms.oneSentence: Driver-in-the-loop or operator-in-the-loop testing puts a real person in a simulator cab, with screens, controls and sometimes motion, to study how operators react when the machine warns, waits and then brakes.
terms.explained:
Everything in the ladder so far asks whether the machine detects and stops. This rung asks a different question: what does the human do? Machine simulators used for operator training (a realistic cab in front of large screens, often on a motion platform) can present a warning, a delay and then an automatic stop, while recording the operator's hands and feet, eye movements and comments. The booklet lists the questions such studies can answer: warning timing, whether automatic intervention surprises the operator, nuisance-warning workload, simultaneous manual braking, override behavior, trust and understanding of the interface [Chapter 1].

Evidence is thin. A University of Queensland and ACARP (Australian Coal Association Research Program) project used a haul-truck simulator (about 2017) to evaluate visual and sound proximity interfaces, but for advisory warnings, not automatic braking; no off-road study of operators experiencing automatic braking in a simulator was found [Chapter 1]. Road-vehicle simulator studies found that warnings with 20 to 33% false alarms still shortened brake reaction times, and that drivers who trusted other vehicles' automatic braking braked later [Chapter 4]. No validated operator model for off-road machines exists; mining studies use fixed reaction delays [Chapter 4]. The booklet names human-in-the-loop simulators at research institutes and machine manufacturers as possible resources [Chapter 11].

Simulators cannot validate real sensors or brakes, reproduce motion cues perfectly, or reveal long-term complacency and risk compensation after months of nuisance interventions [Chapter 1].
terms.why: The booklet schedules operator studies before prototype safety testing, so that basic interface problems are not discovered during expensive machine tests, and reminds that human performance "can change both positively and negatively after technology is introduced" [Chapter 1].

terms.title: Real time (hard real time)
terms.oneSentence: A simulation runs in real time when one simulated second takes exactly one real second, and in hard real time when every computing step is guaranteed to finish within its deadline, every time.
terms.explained:
A weather forecast may take an hour to compute tomorrow's weather; nobody minds. A flight simulator must draw the next frame before the pilot notices a lag. That is real time: the computer keeps pace with the clock on the wall. Hard real time is stricter: not on average but at every single step, because a late result is a wrong result. A controller that expects a radar message every 50 ms and receives one 80 ms late behaves differently from the real machine.

Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) needs hard real time because the real electronic control unit on the bench runs at its own pace and cannot wait for a slow simulator [Chapter 7]. That is why HIL uses dedicated real-time computers with deterministic operating systems and input-output hardware, and why the booklet's compute table says that for HIL "deterministic real time matters more than throughput" [Chapter 11]. The conflict with fidelity is direct: a neural scene of 23 million elements rendered at 17 frames per second, or a soil model running 50 to 200 times slower than real time, cannot drive a HIL bench; the booklet advises keeping separate offline high-fidelity models and real-time models where needed [Chapters 5, 11].

The real-time factor (simulated time divided by wall-clock time) also decides cost: a simulator at 10 times real time costs one tenth per simulated hour of one at real time, and no generic factor should be assumed without benchmarking on the actual machine geometry and sensor set [Chapter 11].
terms.why: Milliseconds in sensing, networking, decision and actuation move the stopping point; timing can only be tested where the simulator keeps real time, and real-time limits cap the sensor fidelity available on the bench [Chapters 5, 7].

terms.title: Open loop versus closed loop
terms.oneSentence: In an open-loop test the system's output does not change what happens next, while in a closed-loop test the system's actions feed back and alter the situation it then sees.
terms.explained:
Watching a recording of a reversing loader and asking "would the new software have braked here?" is open loop: the recording continues as it was, whatever the software decides. Putting the software in a simulation where its brake request actually slows the virtual loader, so that the worker is now farther away and the next camera frame looks different, is closed loop. Open loop is cheap and uses real data; closed loop is the only way to see consequences.

Chapter 7 defines "the first-divergence point" precisely. Before the new system commands braking, the recorded machine pose, object poses and sensor measurements are valid historical evidence. At the first brake command that did not occur in the original run, the counterfactual machine begins to differ from the recorded one. After that instant, feeding the original sensor record while pretending the machine has slowed is physically inconsistent [Chapter 7]. Recorded data can therefore answer "would the new system have detected the object and requested intervention before time t?"; they cannot answer "would the machine actually have stopped safely, what would the next measurements have been, or would the worker have reacted?" [Chapter 7].

The danger of ignoring this is documented. On-road research (2024) showed that open-loop planning scores could be matched using the vehicle's own state alone, giving "a misleading impression" [Chapter 7]. Teams therefore split the metrics: perception and trigger timing open loop on logs; braking consequences in closed-loop simulation, hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) and vehicle-in-the-loop (VIL); selected stopping outcomes on a proving ground. A "log-to-simulation switch" branches from the recorded prefix into simulation at the intervention point, with a machine model consuming the brake command and a sensor model regenerating the observations [Chapter 7]. After the branch, the evidence is only as good as the machine, terrain, actor and sensor models, a warning the booklet calls more serious off-road, where soil, grade, payload and dust are more variable than paved-road dynamics [Chapter 7].

Shadow mode and replay are open loop; software-in-the-loop (SIL), HIL and VIL are normally closed loop; semantic replay can be either [Chapters 1, 7].
terms.why: The existing warning fleet can supply enormous open-loop evidence from today, but the new function changes machine motion, so three evidence classes must be kept apart: the recorded prefix (measured), post-intervention simulation (model-dependent), and selected real stops (measured, few cases) [Chapter 7].

terms.title: Replay and re-simulation of recorded data (open-loop replay)
terms.oneSentence: Replay feeds sensor data recorded on real machines back into the software, exactly as recorded, to see what the software would have detected and decided.
terms.explained:
A machine with the existing warning system drives a shift with cameras, radar, machine speed and gear all recorded with precise time stamps. Months later, a new version of the perception software is run against that recording, frame by frame, and its detections are compared with an independent ground truth of where the workers and vehicles really were. Re-simulation is the same idea with more processing: the recording may be re-rendered or partly modified before it is fed in.

Replay proves detection rate, false-alarm rate and warning timing for the sensor set, mounting positions and situations that were actually recorded; it gives repeatability, regression across software versions, the baseline of the old system, and a fair old-versus-new comparison when both accept the same inputs [Chapter 7]. It can reproduce a rare recorded event indefinitely [Chapter 1]. It cannot show the effect of any action that differs from the recording (braking, steering, an operator reaction), anything about sensor types or positions that were not recorded, conditions not in the logs, or physical sensor effects upstream of the injection point [Chapter 7]. Its fidelity "is defined by the point at which data are re-injected" [Chapter 7]. Neural re-simulation of camera and lidar logs from nearby new viewpoints exists but degrades once the viewpoint moves 1 to 4 m from the recorded path, which matters for new mounting positions [Chapter 7].

A useful replay record needs synchronized raw sensor streams, machine speed, gear, steering and articulation, brake state, calibration, weather and site metadata and a defensible ground-truth channel; without that, large volumes of logs have little validation value [Chapter 1]. The common mistakes (recording only object lists, missing calibration, unsynchronized clocks, lossy compression, event-triggered recording only) fill a page of Chapter 7. Labeling capacity dominates the cost [Chapter 1].
terms.why: Replay and shadow mode are the cheapest large-volume methods, and the company already owns the right fleet; recording must start in October 2026, through the winter, not when the prototype arrives [Chapters 1, 7]. The booklet's first ordering rule is that replay and sensor-model correlation come before simulation results can be trusted [Chapter 1].
aliases: Replay and re-simulation of recorded data

terms.title: Semantic or object-list replay
terms.oneSentence: Semantic replay feeds the decision software not with raw sensor data but with a list of objects (type, position, speed), either recorded or taken from ground truth, so that only the warning and braking logic is tested.
terms.explained:
Perception turns pixels and radar echoes into an object list: "person, 11 m behind, moving left at 1 m/s". Semantic replay skips perception and supplies that list directly, in common coordinates together with machine state. The decision logic, warning stages and brake-request rules are then exercised independent of any sensor type. It can run open loop (lists as recorded) or closed loop (lists regenerated as the virtual machine slows) [Chapter 7].

It is the cheapest way to sweep very large scenario sets, because no rendering or ray tracing is involved; the booklet's compute table rates "logic and object-list braking tests" as processor-dominant with very high parallelism, suited to commodity servers [Chapters 7, 11]. It proves thresholds, warning logic, threat assessment and brake-request logic. It cannot prove perception, and it can hide sensor latency, occlusion, false detections and range or classification errors, because it assumes perception has already succeeded [Chapter 7]. ASAM OSI (Open Simulation Interface) provides standard interfaces between environment, sensor, fusion and function models, including ground-truth interfaces, for exactly this kind of test [Chapter 7].
terms.why: The first level of the booklet's multi-fidelity architecture is "deterministic functional and object-list tests for millions of braking-logic combinations" [Chapter 11], and semantic inputs are where the booklet says software-in-the-loop (SIL) testing should start, before realistic sensor error models are added [Chapter 7].

terms.title: Shadow mode (silent testing)
terms.oneSentence: In shadow mode the new braking software runs live on working machines, sees everything the sensors see and decides when it would brake, but its brake commands are disconnected, so it only records what it would have done.
terms.explained:
It is like a trainee sitting beside an experienced operator and saying quietly "I would brake now", while the operator keeps control. Every such moment is logged together with the sensor data, and later compared with what really happened: was there a person, did the operator brake anyway, was it a pile of gravel? Automotive literature calls this silent testing and treats it as open loop, because the candidate software produces setpoints "which are not executed by the actuator system" [Chapter 1].

Shadow mode produces evidence that nothing else can at this scale: the rate of false hypothetical interventions, that is, the nuisance-brake rate measured over real operating hours; missed threats; detection range in real dust, light and weather; the effect of mounting differences; previously unknown scenario classes; and how often each situation occurs on each site type [Chapter 1]. It cannot establish whether a real automatic stop stays stable on a wet decline with a full load, whether a false stop causes the following truck to collide, whether the load shifts, whether the operator fights the brake, or whether the actuator has an integration fault; and operator behavior changes once braking becomes real [Chapter 1]. Evaluating many software candidates at once becomes inefficient [Chapter 1].

The precedents are thin for mining. Road programs describe daily shadow-mode deployment before roll-out, and the nearest off-road analogue is a supplier's statement that its system can run on site "without immediately enforcing level-9 intervention"; a publicly documented heavy-off-road shadow-mode program was not found [Chapter 1]. Recording the old and the new system in parallel on the same machine is the fairest basis for comparing them [Chapter 7].
terms.why: The booklet's third ordering rule is that shadow mode should run before braking is enabled, so that the nuisance-brake rate is measured while braking is still disabled; false alarms need exposure hours, not staged targets, and 300 hours with no unnecessary brake supports a claim of fewer than one per 100 hours [Chapters 1, 9]. The nuisance rate is also the number that decides whether operators accept the system or switch it off [Chapter 4].

terms.title: Proving ground, track test and whole-machine test
terms.oneSentence: A proving ground is a closed, controlled area where the complete real machine, with its real sensors, is tested against physical targets; a track test is one such test, and a whole-machine test is any test in which nothing is simulated.
terms.explained:
This is the top rung of the ladder: a real loader, a real operator or a robot driver, a real test body standing where a worker would be, and measuring equipment that records exactly when the machine warned, when it braked and where it stopped. ISO 21815-1 includes test procedures for collision warning and avoidance systems, and ISO 16001 defines a test body, a detection zone and a detection time [Chapter 7]. The South African MOSH regime (Mining Industry Occupational Safety and Health learning hub) moves from laboratory tests to a proving ground and then to a cordoned-off area of a working mine [Chapter 7].

Whole-machine tests are the end-to-end reality anchor for actual stopping behavior and for sensor behavior in a real environment, but they are expensive, have low coverage, cannot control the weather, and hazardous edge cases are hard to execute [Chapter 7]. The one published independent verification regime for mining shows the price: first-pass rates of 62% for detection devices and 42% for machine-side systems across 189 tests, at 1.6 tests per week with an 18-week lead time; every machine type, model and serial number with different braking characteristics must be verified separately; and the published stopping tests cover gradients of 1% or less, unloaded [Chapter 7].

The booklet's rule for the role of the track is that track tests should confirm predictions from simulation rather than explore [Chapter 1]. The first six weeks after hardware delivery are a physical anchor campaign that answers three questions: are this machine's parameters inside the family model, are the predicted bounds conservative, and where does the model fail [Chapter 8].
terms.why: No framework in any industry lets simulation remove physical testing; the question for the four-month window is which physical tests give the most information for correlating the models and confirming the worst cases [Chapters 2, 10].

terms.title: Soft target, robotic target and target platform (ISO 19206)
terms.oneSentence: A soft target is a dummy of a person or vehicle that a machine can hit without damage, a robotic target or target platform is a low, self-driving carrier that moves the dummy along a programmed path, and ISO 19206 is the standard series that specifies such targets for road-vehicle testing.
terms.explained:
To test whether a system brakes for a worker, somebody must stand behind the machine. Nobody will. So road-vehicle testing developed foam and fabric dummies that look like a pedestrian to a camera, reflect radar like a human body and return laser light like clothing, mounted on flat robotic platforms that drive repeatable paths at set speeds. The ISO 19206 series specifies these pedestrian, bicycle and vehicle targets, and the Euro NCAP protocols reference Parts 2 and 4 [Chapter 3]. Robots and soft targets automate approach speeds, crossing paths and repeated near-collision runs, as a 2021 report by the United States road-safety regulator describes [Chapter 1].

The off-road picture is different. These platforms are built for passenger-car speeds and shapes; no off-road equivalent of a Euro NCAP protocol and no publicly documented high-throughput robotic-target system for heavy machines were found, so the booklet treats robotic automation as a candidate investment, not a proven shortcut [Chapter 1]. Off-road surrogates must represent people in protective clothing, light vehicles under the nose of a haul truck, machines and fixed obstacles, with camera appearance, radar cross-section, lidar reflectivity and ultrasonic response matched to each sensor: an optically realistic dummy may have the wrong radar signature [Chapter 3]. The South African test specification uses light vehicles for the controller test on a proving ground [Chapter 7].
terms.why: Targets must be realistic to the chosen sensors, which is one more reason the booklet says the sensor decision cannot wait [Chapter 1].
aliases: Soft target, robotic target and target platform

terms.title: Correlation test
terms.oneSentence: A correlation test is a physical test run specifically to check whether the models predicted what the real machine did, and by how much they were wrong.
terms.explained:
Correlation here means agreement between simulation and reality. Before the prototype arrives, every model (braking, sensor, terrain) is a prediction. The first tests on the real machine should therefore not be the full scenario matrix but a small set of carefully chosen measurements that the models have already predicted: end-to-end latency, detection range, brake-command timing, stopping dynamics and repeatability on each representative machine variant. The differences become the models' error bounds, and the error bounds define the envelope within which virtual results may be trusted [Chapter 1]. "If the virtual and bench models are wrong, millions of virtual scenarios produce false confidence" [Chapter 1].

The booklet repeats the idea at every level. Sensor models are correlated against measurements on existing machines in dust, rain and darkness in 2026 and 2027, before the prototype [Chapter 11]. Every high-value simulator phenomenon (dust, fog, glare, wet surfaces, reflective objects, occlusion) gets a smaller physical reference set, and simulation is credible only in the dimensions where these paired tests agree [Chapter 9]. The physical anchor campaign in the first six weeks after hardware delivery asks whether the machine's parameters are inside the family model, whether the predicted bounds are conservative, and where the model fails [Chapter 8]. Reviewers demand blind correlation, with withheld physical data never used for tuning [Chapter 13].

Agreement is never one number; Part G covers the metrics.
terms.why: Correlation is the booklet's first ordering rule and the step that turns the prototype from the only place to run scenarios into a model-correlation asset; the four-month window is a confirmation and discrepancy-resolution campaign only if the correlation plan exists beforehand [Chapters 1, 10].

terms.title: Regression testing and continuous integration (CI/CD) for simulation
terms.oneSentence: Regression testing re-runs old tests after every software change to make sure that nothing which used to work now fails, and continuous integration is the automated factory that does this on every change.
terms.explained:
Software changes constantly: a threshold is tuned, a filter is improved, a bug is fixed. Each change can quietly break something else. A regression is exactly that: a case that used to pass now fails. Regression testing keeps every important case and re-runs it automatically. Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) is the software-industry practice of building and testing automatically whenever a developer submits a change, so that a problem is found within hours rather than at the end of the project.

The booklet maps this onto the validation program [Chapter 9]. Build a change-impact graph: a change to sensor mounting selects the scenarios that cover that sensor's field boundaries and occlusions; a brake-model change selects stopping-margin scenarios; a perception change selects all downstream braking scenarios. Run a fast "smoke" subset of software-in-the-loop (SIL) runs on every submitted change, a small mandatory safety regression set on every eligible build, larger virtual campaigns overnight or at release gates, and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) and physical confirmation selected by risk. Keep every past failure as a permanent regression test. And never continuously rerun the frozen estimation set and optimize to its failures; it is reserved for release candidates [Chapter 9].

Road-autonomy programs turn every captured or synthesized scenario into a permanent test. The booklet's caution: running millions of tests does not show that the test set represents the real operating domain [Chapter 1]. Simulator upgrades themselves need regression tests before adoption [Chapter 11].
terms.why: In a four-month window, the only affordable way to prove that a tuning change late in the campaign did not break an earlier result is an automated pipeline that already exists [Chapter 9].

terms.title: Test management, versioning and the traceability chain
terms.oneSentence: Test management is the record-keeping that lets thousands of runs be planned, reproduced and traced from the hazard they address to the evidence they produce, and versioning gives every ingredient of a run a fixed identifier.
terms.explained:
With thousands of virtual runs per night, "we tested that" is meaningless unless each run can be found again and repeated exactly. The booklet's rule is to treat every executed run as a reproducible experiment with an unchangeable manifest [Chapter 9]. The chain runs: hazard, then safety requirement, then functional performance requirement (for example an objective from the mining industry's EMESRT PR-5A requirement or an ISO 21815 risk level), then logical scenario, then test case, then run, then result, then evidence item in the safety case [Chapter 9].

The minimum manifest stored with each run lists the requirement and hazard identifiers, the scenario family and its version, the concrete parameter values, operating-domain tags, machine and sensor configuration, calibration, software build, simulator or rig version, random seed, raw-data identifiers with checksums, verdict and deviations [Chapter 9]. Versioning means that everything that can change a result gets an identifier recorded with the run, including machine-learning model weights, terrain assets and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) rig configuration, typically as content hashes (fingerprints computed from the file itself) [Chapter 9].

Neutral standards exist: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 for test documentation, ASAM MDF for measured signals, ASAM ATX for test specifications and results. The implementation can be commercial, open-source or in-house; "the important property is a stable machine-readable data model with immutable IDs, not the brand" [Chapter 9]. Site models need the same discipline, with a capture date, a coordinate reference and a revision history [Chapter 5].
terms.why: Once braking affects motion, reproducible configuration control is a safety obligation rather than a convenience; a result that cannot be tied to an exact product state is not evidence [Chapter 7].

terms.title: Cloud execution and compute budget
terms.oneSentence: Cloud execution means renting computers by the hour from a data-center provider to run many simulations in parallel, and the compute budget is the money and machine-hours set aside for that.
terms.explained:
A campaign of thousands of runs per night needs far more computers than an office owns. Cloud providers rent them. In the prices the booklet found, a machine with one graphics processing unit (GPU) suitable for sensor rendering cost about USD 1.73 to 1.86 per hour on demand; a one-year commitment lowers that, and "spot" capacity sold at discounts of up to 90% suits work that can be interrupted and restarted, such as statistical regression, but not deterministic hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) tests or long irreplaceable jobs [Chapter 11].

The arithmetic matters more than the price. Ten such GPU machines running 24 hours a day for 122 days cost about USD 54,490 and deliver at most about 29,000 GPU-hours. Sensor-realistic runs typically go at about real time per GPU, so a four-month window caps how many of the 100-plus sites times 10-plus scenarios times weather times machine variants can run at full sensor fidelity, which forces a tiered strategy [Chapter 11]. Cost per simulated hour equals the cloud price per wall-clock hour divided by the real-time factor; no generic factor should be assumed [Chapter 11].

Compute is cheap relative to engineering labor: the booklet's labor floor is roughly USD 150,000 to 260,000 per specialist per year, which is why "free" software can still mean a seven-figure annual program [Chapter 11]. High-resolution site scans and machine data are commercially sensitive, and cloud terms were not reviewed [Chapter 11].
terms.why: The GPU-hour ceiling is what makes "do not make one simulator carry every test" a necessity rather than a preference [Chapter 11].

terms.title: Headless simulation versus rendered simulation
terms.oneSentence: A headless simulation runs without drawing any picture, computing only the numbers a test needs, while a rendered simulation produces images or sensor views, which costs far more computing.
terms.explained:
"Headless" is software jargon for running without a screen. A braking-logic test with an object list does not need to see anything: the machine is a point with a speed, the worker is a point with a position, and the result is a stopping distance. Such runs use ordinary processors, run far faster than real time and spread across thousands of cheap processor cores [Chapter 11]. Rendering is needed only when a camera, lidar or radar model must be fed with a view of the scene; then a graphics processing unit (GPU) traces rays through geometry and materials, and the run slows toward real time or below [Chapters 5, 11].

The booklet's compute discussion makes the choice explicit: in a four-month window, tests per wall-clock hour matter more than real-time rendering, lower-fidelity models can screen the broad space, and high-fidelity rendering is reserved for perception-sensitive subsets [Chapters 5, 11]. The word "headless" itself does not appear in the booklet; the distinction does.
terms.why: Most of the millions of braking-logic combinations should run headless; rendered runs are the scarce, expensive resource to be spent on the cases that correlation and sensitivity work identify [Chapter 11].

terms.title: Sim-to-real gap
terms.oneSentence: The sim-to-real gap is the difference between what a system does in simulation and what it does in reality, caused by everything the models leave out or get wrong.
terms.explained:
A photograph of a meal is not the meal. A simulated quarry, however convincing on screen, differs from a real one in ways that matter to sensors and brakes: the exact way wet rock returns laser light, the radar echoes bouncing between steel structures, the real dust plume, the real sinkage of a loaded tire. A detector trained or tested in simulation can therefore score well there and fail in the field, and a stopping distance predicted in simulation can be shorter than the real one. That difference is the gap. In machine learning it is also called the domain gap.

The booklet documents the gap for every sensor type, almost all on road data: radar simulation that narrows but does not close detection gaps, lidar detection accuracy shifting between simulated and real point clouds, camera benchmarks motivated precisely by the mismatch under extreme weather, and a 2025 study still developing the metrics to measure the gap, "which means there is no consensus yet on how to quantify it" [Chapter 1]. Specific numbers show its size. Ray-traced radar reproduced about 12% of the real point density. A neural scene scored 22.99 on an image-similarity scale (PSNR, in decibels, where higher means closer to the real image) from the recorded lane and 17.05 from the next lane, and a scene built from drone images fell from 29.13 to 10.36 when viewed from a car [Chapter 5]. An agricultural procedural generator achieved a 9.9% gap on a segmentation task, which counts as a good result [Chapter 5]. No accepted method was found for qualifying sensor models in dust, snow or fog on off-road sites, and no validation of simulated braking distance on gravel, mud, ice or slopes for heavy machines was found [Chapters 1, 5].

The gap is managed, not removed: physical anchor sites and correlation tests measure it; validity envelopes record where it is small enough; mixing even a few real images with synthetic data improves transfer; and the Columbia shuttle accident is the booklet's warning about trusting a model outside the range where its gap was measured [Chapters 5, 10]. A pretty image is not a small gap: fidelity should be judged per tested requirement, since photorealism is nearly irrelevant to radar, ultrasonic and braking physics [Chapter 5].
terms.why: The booklet's largest single risk is "model-confidence risk": a simulation can produce millions of repeatable but systematically wrong tests, and without correlation data the results may not be accepted by the safety case, by customers or by regulators [Chapter 11]. Measuring the gap is covered in Part G.

terms.title: Domain randomization
terms.oneSentence: Domain randomization deliberately varies the appearance and conditions of simulated scenes at random (lighting, colors, textures, object positions) so that software trained or tested on them does not depend on details that will differ in reality.
terms.explained:
If every simulated quarry has the same gray gravel and the same noon sun, a detector may learn "gravel and noon sun" instead of "a person". Randomizing the sun angle, the rock color, the ground texture, the camera noise and the pose and scale of objects from run to run forces the software to rely on what stays constant, the shape and motion of a human, and makes the real world look like just one more random variation. It is a way of shrinking the sim-to-real gap for machine-learning perception without having to model reality exactly.

The booklet mentions it twice. One simulator's data-generation tool provides programmable domain randomization of pose, scale, lighting and material appearance (a vendor statement), and a 2022 construction study estimated excavator poses from synthetic images generated with domain randomization [Chapter 5]. Chapter 9's finding about synthetic training data applies: mixing synthetic and real images helps, training on synthetic data alone leaves a persistent gap, and no peer-reviewed demonstration was found that synthetic-only training or validation establishes collision-avoidance reliability for heavy off-road machines [Chapter 9].

Randomization is not validation: random appearance says nothing about whether radar physics or braking distance is right, and randomized runs must still freeze their random seeds to be reproducible [Chapter 5].
terms.why: It is a training-side tool for a machine-learning detector, useful for robustness, not a source of safety evidence about the function.

terms.title: "Do not make one simulator carry every test" (multi-simulator architecture)
terms.oneSentence: This is the booklet's recommendation to spread the test program across several levels of simulation fidelity and several tools, each used for the questions it answers well, instead of running every case in one maximum-fidelity simulator.
terms.explained:
It is tempting to buy or build one simulator that does everything: photorealistic cameras, physics-based radar, grain-by-grain soil, every weather, all 100 sites, every machine model. The booklet calls the alternative a "fourth architecture", valid at any cost level [Chapter 11]:

Deterministic functional and object-list tests for millions of braking-logic combinations.

Medium-fidelity closed-loop dynamics with ideal or noisy sensors for broad regression.

High-fidelity rendering, radar and lidar for perception-sensitive subsets.

High-fidelity soil simulation for braking- and traction-sensitive subsets.

Hardware-in-the-loop for timing, controller and interface behavior.

Targeted physical tests for correlation and final evidence.

"The allocation of cases to each level must come from sensitivity and correlation work, not from assumption" [Chapter 11]. The reasons are practical. The market itself is modular, with road-vehicle tools strong in sensors and scenarios and heavy-machine tools strong in terrain and hydraulics, and nobody has both [Chapter 11]. High-fidelity soil runs 50 to 200 times slower than real time and cannot be used for every regression case [Chapter 11]. The GPU-hour ceiling of a four-month window caps full-fidelity runs [Chapter 11]. And fidelity should be decomposed by the tested requirement rather than ranked by how convincing the screenshots look [Chapter 5]. Chapter 8 gives the same advice for machine models: layered models per machine family rather than one "ultimate" digital twin [Chapter 8]. The price is integration work, which open standards reduce but do not remove [Chapter 11].
terms.why: This architecture is how a program starting from zero can cover the combinatorial space inside the window while spending its scarce high-fidelity and physical resources only where correlation shows they are needed [Chapter 11].
aliases: "Do not make one simulator carry every test"

terms.title: Mass, payload and gross vehicle weight (GVWR)
terms.oneSentence: Mass is how much matter a machine contains, payload is the load it carries, and the gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR) is the maximum total of machine plus load that the manufacturer allows.
terms.explained:
In everyday speech "weight" and "mass" mean the same thing. In engineering, mass is measured in kilograms (kg) or metric tons (t, 1,000 kg), and weight is the force gravity exerts on it. For this glossary the difference does not matter: a heavier machine is harder to get moving and harder to stop.

Whatever the machine carries, rock in a truck body or gravel in a loader bucket, is the payload. Machine plus payload is the gross mass, and the GVWR is the manufacturer's upper limit for it. On heavy machines the payload can exceed the empty machine: the booklet quotes a Volvo A60 articulated hauler at about 44 t empty and 99 t gross, and a Caterpillar 797F mining truck at about 624 t gross with a 363 t payload [Chapter 8]. A loaded machine can be twice as heavy as an empty one, and its center of gravity (the point where its mass balances) sits higher and further back.

In a simple textbook model, mass cancels out: a heavy object and a light one with the same tire grip stop in the same distance. Real machines break that rule. Brakes produce only a limited force and absorb only so much heat, so a heavier machine with the same brakes decelerates less. Payload also shifts load between the axles, changes how much braking force each wheel or track can transmit, and brings the machine closer to tipping [Chapter 8]. The brake standard ISO 3450 therefore tests a machine in the configuration "having the most adverse effect on braking", with dumpers at maximum payload [Chapter 8].
terms.why: The automatic brake must know, or assume the worst about, how heavily the machine is loaded, because payload changes both how far the machine travels before it stops and whether hard braking is safe. The booklet concludes that "one vehicle mass" is an inadequate description, that payload must be a variable in the stopping model, and that machines whose mass changes a lot belong in a different model family from machines of nearly fixed mass [Chapter 8].
aliases: Mass, payload and gross vehicle weight

terms.title: Speed, acceleration and deceleration
terms.oneSentence: Speed is how fast something moves, acceleration is how quickly its speed increases, and deceleration is how quickly its speed decreases.
terms.explained:
Speed is distance per unit of time. Road signs use kilometers per hour (km/h); engineers prefer meters per second (m/s) because the formulas then work out simply. To convert, divide km/h by 3.6: 15 km/h is about 4.2 m/s, 30 km/h about 8.3 m/s, 50 km/h about 13.9 m/s. A brisk walk is about 5 km/h, or 1.4 m/s. The machines in the booklet mostly work between 3 and 15 km/h, and haul trucks reach 30 to 50 km/h on haul roads.

Acceleration is the rate at which speed changes, so its unit is meters per second, per second, written m/s². A deceleration of 2 m/s² means the machine loses 2 m/s of speed every second: from 4.2 m/s it would stand still after about 2.1 seconds. Deceleration is simply negative acceleration; the booklet uses both words.

A second unit appears constantly: g, the acceleration of a freely falling object, about 9.81 m/s². A car braking at "0.8 g" decelerates at about 7.8 m/s². The road-car automatic braking regulation UN Regulation No. 152 demands at least 5.0 m/s², about 0.5 g [Chapter 8]. Heavy off-road machines are far below that. New South Wales guidance proposes a minimum in-service deceleration of 0.60 m/s² (about 0.06 g); the US mining rule in MSHA Table M-1 (MSHA is the US Mine Safety and Health Administration) assumes a constant 9.66 ft/s², about 2.94 m/s² or 0.3 g; and a South African industry specification sets an emergency-stop deceleration of 1.9 m/s² for machines faster than 20 km/h and 1.0 m/s² for slower ones [Chapters 7, 8]. A loaded haul truck may decelerate at less than a third of the rate of a car.

Two more ideas help. Force equals mass times acceleration, `F = m x a`, with F in newtons (N), m in kg and a in m/s². To decelerate a 40 t machine at 3 m/s² the brakes must supply 40,000 x 3 = 120,000 N, or 120 kN, roughly the weight of a 12 t object; that is why brake torque and brake heat limit heavy machines. And jerk is the rate of change of acceleration: how suddenly the braking comes on. The booklet recommends ramping deceleration up gradually, with a jerk limit, because sudden stops jolt operators and shift loads [Chapters 4, 8].
terms.why: Every stopping-distance calculation in the booklet is built from speed, deceleration and time, so misreading a unit (km/h for m/s, or g for m/s²) produces errors of a factor of three or ten. The booklet also warns that the regulatory sources mix definitions of deceleration: a commanded braking demand (UN R152), a mean deceleration computed from stopping distance (ISO 3450), a constant deceleration with separate response times (MSHA) and a net deceleration on grade (New South Wales). A program that pools them must first convert them to one definition [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Stopping distance
terms.oneSentence: Stopping distance is how far a machine travels from the moment a stop becomes necessary until it stands still.
terms.explained:
A driver sees a child step onto the road. The car keeps rolling while the driver notices and moves a foot to the pedal, keeps rolling while the brakes take hold, and still covers ground while slowing. Stopping distance is the sum of those parts.

The slowing part has a simple formula: `d = v^2 / (2a)`. Here d is the braking distance in meters, v the speed in meters per second and a the deceleration in m/s². Speed is squared, so doubling the speed quadruples the braking distance; halving the deceleration doubles it. ISO 3450, the US mining rule (MSHA Table M-1) and the New South Wales guidance all write stopping performance with this formula, and ISO 3450 uses it backwards, `a = v^2 / (2d)`, to turn a measured stopping distance into a "mean deceleration" [Chapter 8].

Before the slowing starts, the machine travels at full speed for every second of delay: `d_delay = v x t`. For a human driver t is reaction time; for an automatic brake it is sensing, deciding, sending the command and the brake system's own dead time. The full picture is `d_total = v x t_delay + v^2 / (2a) + d_safe`, where d_safe is the clearance left when the machine stops.

A worked example: a loaded 40 t machine at 15 km/h on a 10 percent downgrade (the road drops 1 m for every 10 m forward).

Convert the speed: 15 / 3.6 = 4.2 m/s.

Choose the level-ground deceleration the brakes can give. Suppose 3.0 m/s², close to the 2.94 m/s² the US rule assumes. That takes 40,000 kg x 3.0 m/s² = 120 kN of braking force.

Correct for the slope. Gravity pulls the machine downhill with an acceleration of about g x 0.1 = 9.81 x 0.1, roughly 1.0 m/s². (Strictly it is g x sin θ, with θ the slope angle; for job-site grades this is almost the grade fraction.) Net deceleration: 3.0 - 1.0 = 2.0 m/s². In force terms, 39 kN of the 120 kN is spent holding the machine against gravity.

Braking distance: 4.2² / (2 x 2.0) = 17.4 / 4 = about 4.3 m. On level ground it would be 17.4 / 6 = 2.9 m. The slope adds about half again.

Add the delay. Suppose the chain from object appearing to brakes biting takes 1.0 s. Distance at full speed: 4.2 x 1.0 = 4.2 m.

Total: 4.2 + 4.3 = about 8.5 m before the machine stands still. With 1 m of clearance wanted, the object must be detected at least 9.5 m away, before any sensor error is added.

The delay term (4.2 m) is as large as the braking term (4.3 m). With 2.0 s of total delay, which the US rule assumes for very heavy equipment, the delay term alone would be 8.3 m. The booklet's finding is exactly this: at 5 to 15 km/h "the latency term can be half or more of the stopping distance" [Chapter 8]. Mass does not appear in the formula, but it decides whether the brakes can deliver the 3.0 m/s² assumed in step 2. The booklet's regulatory examples use the same arithmetic, for instance a 25 t articulated dump truck at 50 km/h needing 3.13 m/s² to stop in 30.82 m on level ground, which is the pure v²/(2a) value [Chapter 8].
terms.why: Stopping distance is the quantity the whole system is built around: the sensor must see at least that far, the warning must come earlier, and the brake must be commanded no later. The booklet concludes that a calibrated point-mass model, this formula with measured delays, a brake build-up lag and a worst-case deceleration that depends on grade, payload and surface, is the right core model for stopping distance, and that higher fidelity is needed only in specific places [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Brake dead time and brake build-up time
terms.oneSentence: Brake dead time is the pause between the brake command and the first braking effect, and build-up time is the further period until the brakes reach their full force.
terms.explained:
Open a garden hose: water does not arrive at once. The hose must fill, and then the flow grows to full strength. Brakes on heavy machines behave the same way. Most are hydraulic (oil under pressure) or pneumatic (compressed air). When a command arrives, valves open, fluid flows into cylinders and pressure rises. Until the pressure is high enough for the brake pads to grip, nothing happens: that is the dead time, also called brake-fill time or response time. Then the force rises over a fraction of a second to its full value: the build-up time. Engineers model the build-up as a ramp or as a "first-order lag", a curve that rises quickly at first and then flattens.

The booklet collects published figures, each specific to one architecture: pressure response under 0.3 s for a tracked vehicle's electro-hydraulic brake (2026); 0.41 s to reach the design value for a mining electric vehicle's brake-by-wire (2025); about 0.5 s inherent delay for road-truck air brakes (1989); and the US mining rule's assumed system response time of 0.5 s for equipment up to 36,000 lb, rising in steps to 2.5 s above 400,000 lb (about 181 t). A historic US mining study reported 1 to 2 s of additional lag for retarders on large haul trucks, and a road simulation round robin prescribed 0.2 s of actuator delay and 0.4 s of build-up [Chapter 8].

Test conventions matter. ISO 3450 measures stopping distance from the moment the brake control is actuated to standstill, so it includes dead time and build-up but excludes the operator's reaction. South African guidance measures brake response time from brake application to the moment deceleration reaches 10 percent of g, about 1 m/s² [Chapter 8]. A validation program should state which convention it uses.

Dead time is not a fixed number. It changes with oil temperature, with how much the accumulators (pressure reservoirs) are charged, with wear, and on the automatic path with the electronics between the collision system and the brake valve. The booklet stresses that measurements "must be done for the automated brake path, not just the pedal path", that tests should identify dead time, rise time, gain, saturation, hysteresis and release time, and that the spread of the delay matters as much as its average [Chapter 8].
terms.why: At work-site speeds the delay term can equal or exceed the braking term, so an error of half a second in the assumed dead time is an error of about 2 m at 15 km/h. The booklet found no published delay distributions for production wheel loaders, articulated haulers or haul trucks across hydraulic, pneumatic, hydrostatic, wet-disc and blended brake systems: "they must be measured". It recommends a latency sweep with at least 10 repetitions across oil temperatures per machine family among the first physical tests after the prototype arrives [Chapter 8].

terms.title: End-to-end latency budget
terms.oneSentence: The end-to-end latency budget is the list of every delay between an object appearing and the machine standing still, with a time allowance for each.
terms.explained:
A household budget divides income into rent, food and so on, and the total must not exceed what is available. A latency budget does the same with time. The "income" is the time between an object becoming visible and the moment a collision would occur, and each stage of the system spends part of it.

The stages, in order: the sensor captures the object (sensing); the software decides it is real, usually after seeing it in several consecutive frames (detection and confirmation); the decision logic computes the risk and chooses an action (determination); the command travels over the machine network to the brake controller; the brake system fills and begins to grip (dead time); the force rises to full (build-up); and the machine decelerates to a stop. The international standard ISO 21815-3 describes the same chain as the parts of its "collision-system distance", detection, determination, action, machine stopping and a safe distance, and requires the system manufacturer to communicate the typical delays in the system [Chapters 3, 8].

The booklet's reference figures come from different sources. The object-detection standard ISO 16001 allows at most 300 ms for detection [Chapter 3]. A road study reported about 170 ms of sensing plus 50 ms of detection error for an automated brake, against about 700 ms for a human driver [Chapter 8]. Brake response figures run from under 0.3 s to 2.5 s depending on the machine [Chapter 8]. A realistic chain therefore spends roughly one second before full deceleration, and at 15 km/h each second is 4.2 m of travel.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Object appears"] --> B["Sensing and detection (ISO 16001 allows up to 0.3 s)"]
    B --> C["Confirmation over several frames, then risk determination"]
    C --> D["Brake command sent on the machine network"]
    D --> E["Brake dead time (published values 0.3 s to 2.5 s by machine)"]
    E --> F["Build-up to full force (0.4 s in one road round robin)"]
    F --> G["Physical stopping: v squared over 2a, corrected for grade and surface"]
    G --> H["Machine stopped, residual safe distance left"]
```

*The chain from object to standstill; the time figures are those the booklet quotes, and the real values must be measured on each machine [Chapter 8].*
terms.why: The budget connects the sensor team, the software team and the brake team: each owns one segment, and the sum sets the required detection range. The booklet lists an end-to-end latency test, injecting a known object event and time-stamping every stage from detection to measurable deceleration, among the physical tests the program needs, and notes that if perception delays eat the budget, no brake model can recover the lost margin [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Grade (slope) and its effect on braking
terms.oneSentence: Grade is the steepness of the ground; going downhill reduces how hard a machine can slow down, and going uphill helps it.
terms.explained:
Grade is usually given as a percentage: a 10 percent grade rises or falls 1 m for every 10 m traveled, and 20 percent, common on haul roads and ramps, is 1 in 5. Pushing a loaded wheelbarrow downhill shows the effect: gravity pulls it forward, and you must hold back harder to stop it.

In numbers, gravity adds or removes an acceleration of g x sin θ along the slope, where g is 9.81 m/s² and θ is the slope angle. For job-site grades sin θ is almost the grade fraction, so a 10 percent downgrade costs about 1.0 m/s² and a 20 percent downgrade about 1.9 m/s². Compare that with the 0.6 to 3 m/s² heavy machines can deliver at all: grade and payload "shift available deceleration by the same order as the deceleration itself" [Chapter 8]. In the New South Wales 100 t truck example the grade correction alone is about 1.04 m/s², larger than the 0.75 m/s² net safe deceleration being tested [Chapter 8].

The booklet quotes two warnings. A NIOSH stopping model (NIOSH is the US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health) found combinations where the downhill pull exceeded brake capacity and the simulated machine did not stop at all. A road simulation from 2015 compared a braking trigger that ignored grade with one that included it: the grade-blind trigger avoided the collision on level ground and collided at 11 and 17 percent [Chapter 8]. Slopes also bring rollback: a machine stopped on a grade can move again when the automatic brake releases, so ISO 21815-3 recommends an operator action, such as applying the parking brake, before release [Chapter 8]. Side slopes add a tipping risk during braking.
terms.why: Grade must be an input to the braking decision, not a correction applied afterwards: "grade belongs in the trigger model" [Chapter 8]. The published South African closed-loop test specification is run on gradients of 1 percent or less and unloaded, so slope and loaded cases are not covered by any published specification [Chapter 7].

terms.title: Surface and traction
terms.oneSentence: Traction is the grip between a tire or track and the ground, and on loose, wet or soft surfaces there is less of it, so braking is limited by the ground rather than by the brakes.
terms.explained:
Walk on dry pavement, then on wet ice: your shoes are the same, the ground is different. Engineers describe grip with the friction coefficient, written µ (the Greek letter mu): the ratio between the braking or sideways force a surface can transmit and the weight pressing on it. Dry asphalt under a car tire gives about 0.8 to 0.9; wet ice can be below 0.1. The largest deceleration friction allows on level ground is about µ x g, so µ = 0.3 limits a machine to about 3 m/s² however strong its brakes. On a slope the booklet writes the traction limit as `a_traction = µ_min x g x cos θ - g x sin θ`, where µ_min is the lowest friction expected and θ the slope angle [Chapter 8].

Job sites make this harder than roads. Loose aggregate, mud, soft soil, snow and wet clay do not just lower µ; the ground itself deforms. Tires sink in, material piles up in front of the wheel, and the force depends on how much the wheel slips and on soil type, contact area and load. The booklet reports that tracks keep more shear force than tires in soft soil, that a 2023 soil model predicted forces well in sand but its tuning parameters changed with slip angle, and that all of this was tested on single-wheel rigs and sand, not full machines [Chapter 8]. Two things were searched for and not found: a reliable table of friction values for wet dirt, gravel or mud good enough to set braking thresholds, and any published full-machine braking distance on wet clay or loose gravel [Chapter 8].
terms.why: Available braking has to be treated as a distribution over machine, terrain and state, measured or estimated conservatively, rather than read from a handbook coefficient [Chapter 8]. The booklet recommends a low-speed surface matrix (hard, loose and wet) per machine family, with detailed soil modeling only where such simple envelopes fail to transfer [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Wheels versus tracks
terms.oneSentence: Wheeled machines roll on rubber tires, tracked or crawler machines run on steel or rubber belts, and the two grip, steer and stop differently.
terms.explained:
A wheel loader, haul truck or articulated hauler runs on large tires; a dozer, most excavators and some loaders run on tracks, long belts of linked plates that spread the machine's weight over a big footprint. Tracks sink less in soft ground and keep more grip in mud, which is why crawlers do the heavy pushing, but they are slow. The brake standards draw the line at 20 km/h: ISO 3450 covers wheeled and fast rubber-tracked machines, ISO 10265 covers crawlers at 20 km/h or less [Chapter 8].

For a wheeled machine the booklet says the essential quantities are wheel slip, the load on each wheel and the forward and sideways tire forces. For a crawler the force is spread along a long contact patch, and sinkage, the shearing of soil by the grousers (the ridges on the track plates), differential track speed, skid steering (one track faster than the other) and counter-rotation (tracks turning in opposite directions to spin the machine in place) all matter [Chapter 8]. A crawler can therefore collide while turning on the spot with no forward speed at all; the forthcoming standard ISO/PRF 21815-5 names differential speed, skid turning and counter rotation as collision-relevant motions [Chapter 8].
terms.why: Wheeled versus crawler is the first discriminator the booklet uses to divide the product range into machine families with separate braking models, because the physics, the brake standard and the test methods all differ [Chapter 8]. The fastest brake-response figure the booklet quotes, under 0.3 s, is for a tracked vehicle's electro-hydraulic brake, measured on one machine [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Articulated steering
terms.oneSentence: Articulated steering turns a machine by bending it at a hinge between its front and rear halves, which suits rough ground but makes the machine swing and pitch when it brakes.
terms.explained:
A car steers by turning its front wheels. An articulated hauler or wheel loader is built in two parts joined by a large vertical pivot behind the cab; hydraulic cylinders push the halves to an angle, and the machine goes round the corner like a bending caterpillar. The angle between the halves is the articulation angle.

Braking in a straight line on flat ground, such a machine behaves much like a single block. Braking while turning, on a side slope or at a large articulation angle, the two halves push on each other through the hinge: the front may be pushed sideways (yaw), the body may lean (roll), load moves between the axles, and the hinge angle itself can change. A loaded rear half pushing a lighter front half is the off-road cousin of a truck and trailer jackknifing. The booklet reports that academic models of articulated wheel loaders with 7 and 8 degrees of freedom treat roll instability as the critical mode and were validated on scaled models, and that published data on jackknife or roll events during automatic braking of articulated off-road machines were not found [Chapter 8]. ISO/PRF 21815-5 treats articulation as its own collision-relevant motion and distinguishes articulation of a stationary machine, where the rear swings although the machine is not traveling, from ordinary steering during travel [Chapter 8].
terms.why: Articulated and high-center-of-gravity stability during hard braking is one of the four places where the booklet says a point-mass model is not enough and a multibody model is needed; the deceleration the automatic brake may command has to be capped by the articulation and roll state [Chapter 8]. The test matrix therefore includes stops at the articulation limit and on a side slope for articulated machines [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Hydrostatic drive, retarder and service brake
terms.oneSentence: Heavy machines slow down in three ways: with friction brakes (the service brake), with a retarder that uses the drivetrain to hold speed on long descents, and on many machines with a hydrostatic drive that brakes by itself when the operator eases off.
terms.explained:
The service brake is what the pedal operates: friction pads pressed against discs, usually by hydraulic pressure, often running in oil ("wet disc") to carry heat away. It is the brake the collision system commands. The secondary brake is a backup and the parking brake holds the machine still; ISO 3450 treats the three functions separately [Chapter 8].

A retarder slows the machine without friction pads by making the engine, the transmission or an electric motor work against the wheels; large haul trucks descend long haul roads on the retarder so the service brakes do not overheat. Its power is limited, so the deceleration it gives falls as speed and mass rise. The booklet quotes a patent formula for this case, `a = P / (v x m) - g x sin θ`, where P is retarding power in watts, v speed in m/s, m mass in kg and the last term the downhill pull; historic mining studies reported 1 to 2 s of extra lag for retarders [Chapter 8].

A hydrostatic drive, common on wheel loaders and tracked machines, uses an engine-driven pump to push oil through motors at the wheels or tracks. When the operator lets go of the drive pedal the motors turn into pumps and the machine slows: dynamic braking. Some compact machines list this as their auxiliary brake, and ISO 3450 allows the service-brake function to involve the propel control, but continuous "back throttling" is not a substitute for a parking brake [Chapter 8]. How much braking it gives depends on oil viscosity, pressure, pump speed and displacement and engine braking torque, so it changes with temperature and operating state [Chapter 8].
terms.why: On these machines the step from brake command to deceleration is a blend of hydrostatic slowing, driveline effects, friction braking and anti-lock behavior that changes with state. The booklet concludes that a service-brake model which ignores hydrostatic slowing can trigger too early or too late, that hydrostatic braking capacity must be modeled as a function and not a constant, and that friction-brake-dominant machines and hydrostatic or retarder-blended machines belong in different model families [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Load shift and stability
terms.oneSentence: Stability is a machine's resistance to tipping, sliding or losing control, and hard braking is itself a hazard because it throws the load forward and can push the machine past its limits.
terms.explained:
Stand on a bus that brakes hard: you lurch forward. A loaded haul truck or a loader with a raised bucket feels the same lurch, with bigger consequences. During braking the load on the front axle rises and the load on the rear falls (longitudinal load transfer); on a side slope or in a turn, load also moves to the outer wheels. The higher and heavier the load and the rougher the ground, the closer the machine comes to tipping. Rock can spill from a body, a suspended load can swing, and a bucket held high raises the center of gravity exactly when the machine pitches forward.

There is a second effect. The ground can transmit only so much force in total. If all of it is used to brake, nothing is left to steer, so "brake as hard as physically possible" can mean sliding straight on in a corner. The New South Wales brake formulas assume no skidding, ISO 3450 includes controllability requirements during braking, and near a dump edge braking loads ground that is already marginal [Chapter 8].

The booklet's list of hazards from an automatic stop: rollover or unloading instability, articulation and yaw instability, loss of directional control or runaway on grade or loose ground, payload movement or spill, sliding or ground failure near edges, operator injury from sudden stops, secondary collisions, and rollaway after the intervention [Chapter 8]. Underground workers describe "jarring and jolting" stops, and mine leaders preferred systems that first slow to a crawl and only then set the brake [Chapter 4]. One wheel loader manufacturer's documentation warns that the machine "may stop abruptly and become unstable" and tells users to switch its stop function off on steep slopes, on slippery or soft ground and with suspended loads [Chapter 13].
terms.why: The automatic brake must command the smallest deceleration that avoids the collision, limited by traction, stability, brake capability and the load. No published universal safe maximum deceleration for earth-moving machines was found, so these limits must be derived per machine family, with stability tests (braking with steering or articulation, on cross-slope, at relevant payloads) in the physical campaign [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Vehicle dynamics model
terms.oneSentence: A vehicle dynamics model is a set of equations that predicts how a machine moves, slows, turns, leans and pitches in response to brake, drive and steering inputs.
terms.explained:
The simplest model treats the whole machine as a single dot with mass: a point-mass model. It knows speed, deceleration and grade, and it predicts stopping distance well in a straight line. It cannot say anything about tipping or swinging, because a dot has no shape.

The next step is the single-track or "bicycle" model. Imagine the machine squashed sideways so that each axle becomes one wheel, like a bicycle; the model then has a front wheel that steers, a rear wheel, a length between them and a center of gravity somewhere along it. With three to eight degrees of freedom (the independent movements it can represent, such as forward motion, sideways motion, yaw, roll and pitch) it predicts how the machine turns and how load moves between the axles. The booklet reports rigid models of 3 to 8 degrees of freedom for articulated loaders that "reasonably agree" with scaled-model tests [Chapter 8].

A multibody model goes further: every major part, front frame, rear frame, axles, wheels, boom and bucket, is a separate body connected by joints, and the software computes the forces between them, including contact with the ground. It shows roll, articulation and load transfer in detail, but it needs many parameters. The booklet notes a wheel-loader digging model that had to use a tire-ground friction coefficient of 2.0, a physically implausible value, to match measurements [Chapter 8].
terms.why: The booklet separates a small, conservative model used at runtime to decide when to brake from a richer offline model used to challenge it. Multibody models are needed where lateral stability, articulation, individual axle or track loading or deformable terrain matters; elsewhere a calibrated point-mass model is enough, and a simulation round robin showed that complex vehicle models can disagree more than simple ones [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Tire model and tire-soil interaction
terms.oneSentence: A tire model is a formula or table that gives the forward, braking and sideways force a tire produces for a given load, slip and surface; tire-soil interaction is the harder case where the ground deforms under the tire.
terms.explained:
A tire does not grip like glue. It grips by slipping a little: braking force rises as the tire turns slightly slower than the ground passing beneath it (slip), reaches a peak, and falls off if the wheel locks. Tire models capture this curve. Several named families appear in the booklet: Fiala, a simple physical model; the Magic Formula, also called Pacejka, an empirical curve fitted to test data and widely used for road vehicles; and TMeasy [Chapters 8, 11]. The articulated-loader studies the booklet cites used Fiala tires [Chapter 8].

These models assume a firm surface. On soft ground the tire sinks, pushes soil ahead of it, and the force depends on soil type, contact area, load, slip ratio and slip angle. A 2023 soil-wheel model covering all slip and skid states predicted forces well in sand, but some of its tuning parameters changed with slip angle, and a 2026 model shows soil building up in front of the wheel during braking [Chapter 8].
