In at least one open-source tool, the developers report that the handling tire models do not work with deformable terrain at all; only rigid or finite-element tires and tracked vehicles do [Chapter 11].
terms.why: Tire parameters on unpaved ground must be fitted from tests on the real machine; they cannot be copied from road-car values [Chapter 8]. The booklet counts the tire-ground interface among the places where simple models fail, and recommends a low-speed friction matrix (hard, loose, wet) per machine family rather than a site-by-site soil survey [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Terramechanics (SCM, DEM, SPH, CRM, FEM)
terms.oneSentence: Terramechanics is the science of how wheels and tracks interact with soil, and SCM, DEM, SPH, CRM and FEM are five ways of computing that interaction, from a fast approximate formula to very slow grain-by-grain simulation.
terms.explained:
Pavement is solid; soil is not. Under a heavy machine, soil compresses, shears and flows, and terramechanics supplies the rules. The classic approach, developed by Bekker and Wong in the middle of the twentieth century, uses a few measured soil parameters to relate pressure to sinkage and shear stress to slip. From these one can estimate how far a wheel sinks, how much rolling resistance holds it back, and how much braking or pulling force it can transmit. The booklet's qualitative result: tractive and braking force depend on soil type, contact area, load and slip, and tracks keep more shear force than tires in soft soil [Chapter 8].

Five computational methods appear in the booklet. Note that DEM here means discrete element method; elsewhere in the glossary DEM also means digital elevation model, a map of ground heights, which is unrelated.

| Method | What it does | Speed and cost | Where the booklet places it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Soil Contact Model (SCM) | Applies Bekker-Wong rules over a deformable surface | Fast, close to real time | The practical soft-ground option; its authors claim fidelity "comparable" to DEM; under 10 percent force error in some single-wheel studies, tuning varies with slip angle [Chapter 8] |
| Discrete element method (DEM) | Simulates soil as millions of grains that collide | Very slow; high-performance computing | Selected limit cases such as berms, deep aggregate and severe track-soil interaction; "unusable for scenario sweeps" [Chapter 8] |
| Smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) | Treats soil as a fluid-like cloud of particles | Very slow | Same class as DEM for this program [Chapter 8] |
| Continuum model (CRM) | Soil as a continuous deformable material, solved with SPH-type numerics | 50 to 200 times slower than real time in one open-source tool, which also needs a graphics processor from one specific vendor | Best used selectively to derive and calibrate simpler terrain models [Chapter 11] |
| Finite element method (FEM, or FEA for the analysis) | Divides soil or a tire into a mesh of small elements and solves stress and strain | Slow, parameter-heavy | Research-level terrain and flexible-tire modeling [Chapters 8, 11] |

The booklet's verdict is blunt. Evidence that DEM, SPH or FEM terrain is required to predict automatic-braking thresholds across production machines was not found; these methods are "far too costly for exhaustive scenario sweeps, and uncertain soil inputs can overwhelm the fidelity" [Chapter 8]. All published accuracy figures come from single-wheel rigs and sand, and soil parameters vary across and within a site and over time with water and traffic [Chapter 8]. The recommended approach is multi-fidelity: use detailed soil simulation to learn how stopping distance responds to soil, slope, payload and tire or track interaction, fit simpler parameterized models for the large scenario runs, and confirm the parameter envelopes with targeted physical tests [Chapter 11].
terms.why: Soft or deformable ground is one of the four places where the booklet says simple stopping models are not enough. But site-wide soil modeling is unnecessary if crawler and soft-ground tests identify a conservative "available deceleration versus state" envelope; detailed terramechanics is needed only where such envelopes fail to transfer [Chapter 8]. In a four-month window the terramechanics budget should go to a few deliberately chosen limit cases, not to modeling 100 sites [Chapters 8, 11].

terms.title: Brake model and powertrain model
terms.oneSentence: A brake model predicts how much braking force arrives, and how quickly, after a command; a powertrain model predicts how the engine, transmission and drive add to or fight that braking.
terms.explained:
The brake model sits between the decision ("brake now") and the vehicle dynamics ("the machine slows at 2 m/s²"). At its simplest it is a dead time, a build-up ramp and a maximum force. A fuller "lumped hydraulic" model represents the valve, the accumulator (pressure reservoir), the lines and the cylinder volume, and computes pressure over time. The booklet quotes a 2026 digital model of a tracked vehicle's hydraulic brakes that matched brake pressure to more than 96 percent and response time to more than 95 percent, on one machine, with temperature and wear effects not shown [Chapter 8]. Brake torque also depends on temperature: repeated downhill stops heat the discs and reduce the force, called fade, which constant-braking calculations cannot capture [Chapter 8].

The powertrain model covers everything that drives the wheels or tracks. It matters for braking because the drive can slow the machine (retarder, hydrostatic dynamic braking, engine braking) or keep pushing it (a transmission still in gear, or a downhill machine that accelerates after the throttle is released). For a hydrostatic machine the booklet says the model needs pump and motor displacement, pressure limits, engine and pump speed and controller transitions, not a single pedal-to-torque gain [Chapter 8].
terms.why: The brake-actuation hydraulics set the latency and its spread, which is one of the four places where the booklet says extra model fidelity pays off; the models should be built from component tests (bench pressure traces) and checked on the full machine, for the automated brake path specifically [Chapter 8]. The booklet also warns that the automatic system should not assume nominal brake performance after heat, wear or a detected degradation [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Model fidelity levels for braking
terms.oneSentence: Model fidelity is how much physical detail a model includes; for braking, the levels run from a lookup table or single formula, through a point-mass model with measured delays, to a full multibody simulation with soil.
terms.explained:
A map can be a sketch on a napkin, a road atlas or a satellite survey. Each is right for a purpose, and the survey is not better for finding the nearest cafe. Model fidelity works the same way: more detail costs more time, more data and more chances to be wrong, and it pays off only when the extra detail changes the answer.

The booklet's ladder for stopping distance, from simplest to richest [Chapter 8]:

Constant-deceleration equation, `d = v^2 / (2a)` plus grade and mass terms. Hours of effort. The basis of ISO 3450, the US mining rule and the New South Wales formulas. Good for sanity checks and conservative envelopes; misses delay, build-up, variable traction and stability.

Point-mass transient model with measured latency, a brake build-up lag and deceleration maps (lookup tables of available deceleration by grade, payload, surface and drive state). Low to moderate effort. The booklet's choice for the runtime trigger and for large Monte Carlo sweeps.

Point-mass plus lumped brake hydraulics: adds the pressure build-up and its spread. Days to weeks.

Hydrostatic drivetrain model: braking capacity as a function of operating state. Weeks.

Rigid multibody, 3 to 8 degrees of freedom, with tire models: roll, yaw, jackknife and pitch under braking; used to derive deceleration caps for turning and cross-slope. Weeks.

Full multibody with contact and detailed hydraulics or hydrostatics: design exploration and difficult transitions. Months; parameter-heavy.

Semi-empirical terramechanics (Soil Contact Model): soft-ground braking force and sinkage.

DEM, SPH or FEM terrain: selected limit cases only.

Reduced-order or surrogate models fitted to the richer ones: millions of evaluations, but unsafe outside the range they were trained on.

Two findings shape the choice. First, the right fidelity is "the lowest model that predicts every safety-relevant output within a validated uncertainty envelope" [Chapter 8]. Second, complexity is not accuracy: in a 2026 simulation round robin on a road braking case, the point-mass implementations reproduced the prescribed deceleration exactly, while the more complex vehicle models formed the extremes of a 0.033 s and 0.314 m spread [Chapter 8]. Higher fidelity pays off in four places: brake-actuation hydraulics (latency and its spread), articulated and high-center-of-gravity stability during hard braking, hydrostatic drives whose capacity varies with state, and soft or deformable ground [Chapter 8].
terms.why: The booklet recommends layered models per machine family rather than one "ultimate" digital twin: a fast threshold model for very large parameter sweeps, a stability challenge model to derive deceleration caps, and a high-fidelity model for the selected edge cases that could invalidate the simpler ones, with sensor simulation feeding detection delay and error into the braking simulation [Chapter 8]. No published source gives a universal off-road prediction error for any level, so each must be calibrated and checked against the program's own physical tests [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Physical tests needed to build and check a braking model
terms.oneSentence: These are the measurements on a real machine that give a braking model its numbers (calibration) and then show whether its predictions hold on cases it has not seen (validation).
terms.explained:
A model is only as good as the numbers inside it. Two kinds of test supply them. Calibration tests measure parameters: how heavy the machine is, how long the brakes take to bite, how hard they can decelerate it on gravel. Validation tests then run situations the model was not tuned on and compare prediction with measurement. The booklet's rule: "never use the same stop to both tune and claim validation" [Chapter 8].

The test types the booklet lists [Chapter 8]: mass, geometry and load-state characterization at several payloads; brake-actuator identification (time-stamped command, pressure and deceleration to find dead time, rise time and release time, on the automated path); propulsion and retarder identification; straight-line stops at several speeds, payloads, brake temperatures, grades and surfaces, measuring distance both from the collision-system command and from brake-force onset; stability tests braking while steering or articulating and on cross-slopes; crawler and soft-ground identification; hot-brake, downhill and repeated-stop tests; hold and restart tests on grade; and end-to-end latency tests.

How many? No standard or study gives a number [Chapter 8]. The booklet offers an indicative matrix per machine family and brake architecture: a latency sweep with at least 10 repetitions across oil temperatures; stops at three speeds, two payloads, level and maximum design grade, three repetitions each; one surface matrix (hard, loose, wet) at low speed; and for articulated machines stops at the articulation limit and on a side slope. That is roughly 60 to 100 instrumented runs per family, "achievable in the window only if families share instrumentation" [Chapter 8]. Its stopping rule: add tests only where prediction intervals are too wide, residuals are systematically biased, or the case lies outside the validated domain.
terms.why: The purpose of the prototype tests is parameter identification and independent falsification, not replaying every virtual scenario on the machine [Chapter 8]. The booklet recommends pre-booking this campaign for the first six weeks after hardware delivery and using existing machines before 2027 to learn the distributions of brake delay, grade response and load effects in advance [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Decision logic (when to warn, when to brake)
terms.oneSentence: Decision logic is the set of rules inside the system that turns "there is an object over there" into "do nothing", "warn the operator" or "apply the brakes".
terms.explained:
A lifeguard applies decision logic without naming it: a swimmer near the deep end is noted, a swimmer struggling gets a shout, a swimmer going under gets a rescue. The system does the same with distances, speeds and time. Its inputs are the object's position and movement from the sensors; the machine's speed, direction, steering or articulation and load; and the predicted stopping distance. Its outputs are the stages of intervention.

Road systems mostly use time-based rules: brake when the time to collision (distance divided by closing speed) falls below a threshold, staged by phase, or when the distance to the object equals the required stopping distance ("time to brake"), with extra conditions to suppress false alarms [Chapter 8]. These transfer poorly to job sites: near zero closing speed, time to collision becomes huge or unstable even when a person is centimeters away; two machines with the same time to collision need very different distances on grade or mud; articulation and track counter-rotation can collide with no forward closing speed; and a stationary machine about to start has no time to collision at all [Chapter 8].

Off-road, the international standard ISO 21815-3 sizes a collision-risk area from the machine's kinematics: the collision-system distance must cover detection, confirmation and determination, action, machine stopping and a safe distance, and intervention happens at collision-risk level 4 or above, with a warning permitted before it [Chapters 3, 8]. The booklet's practical version is a margin, `M = R - (D_perception + D_decision + D_action + D_stop + D_safe)`, where R is the distance along the predicted path to the collision point and the bracket is everything the machine needs. Positive M means margin remains; a falling or negative M raises the risk level. D_stop should be a conservative prediction that includes grade, speed, load, surface, brake state and articulation [Chapter 8].

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Object detected and confirmed near the predicted path"] --> B["Compute the stopping margin M from speed, grade, load, surface and delays"]
    B --> C{"Is the margin healthy?"}
    C -->|Yes| D["Information only: show the object and keep monitoring"]
    C -->|No, but the operator still has time| E["Urgent warning: sound, light or seat vibration"]
    E --> F{"Is the operator already slowing enough?"}
    F -->|Yes, measured deceleration is enough| G["Stand down and keep monitoring"]
    F -->|No| H["Automatic slowing, then partial braking"]
    H --> I{"Collision otherwise unavoidable?"}
    I -->|No| J["Keep partial braking and re-evaluate"]
    I -->|Yes| K["Maximum safe braking, then hold until the operator acts"]
    L["Machine stationary with an object in the projected path"] --> M["Motion inhibit: refuse the move command"]
```

*The warn-or-brake flow the booklet describes, built on a stopping margin rather than on time to collision alone [Chapter 8].*
terms.why: The booklet's clearest recommendation is to freeze the decision architecture before the hardware arrives: a primary trigger based on the predicted swept volume against a stopping-distance envelope, `s = v x (t_sense + t_actuate) + v^2 / (2 x a_worst)`, with time to collision as a secondary layer for haul-speed traffic and operator-reaction suppression as a third [Chapter 8]. No standard or peer-reviewed study gives tuned time-to-collision or deceleration values for off-road machines, so the numbers inside the logic must come from the program's own models and tests [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Time to collision (TTC), time headway and trigger distance
terms.oneSentence: Time to collision is how many seconds remain before two things meet if nothing changes, time headway is how many seconds the machine needs to reach the spot an object occupies now, and trigger distance is the range at which the system must act.
terms.explained:
Time to collision (TTC) is the distance to the object divided by the closing speed: 10 m away, closing at 2 m/s, gives 5 s. It is the most common quantity in road-car automatic braking, where a 1.0 s trigger was used as a research convention and systems stage warning, partial and full braking at falling TTC values [Chapter 8]. Time headway divides the gap by the machine's own speed instead: 10 m at 4.2 m/s is 2.4 s, whether or not the object moves. It describes following distance. The booklet meets headway only as a distance in on-road test setups, 12 to 40 m between vehicles; its nearest off-road relative is a 50 m following distance in a Chinese underground regulation [Chapter 3].

Trigger distance turns time back into meters. The booklet writes it as `D_trigger = D_detect + v x T_action + D_stop + D_safety`: the distance spent detecting and confirming, the distance traveled while the command takes effect, the physical stopping distance, and a safety clearance, which is the ISO 21815-3 structure [Chapter 8]. Off-road examples: an early haul-truck study derived detection ranges of 15 m to the sides, 50 m to the rear and 100 m to the front from a 0.5 s reaction time plus braking, and a mining-truck patent uses two TTC limits with 1 to 3 s added for operator reaction [Chapter 8].
terms.why: The booklet rates a fixed TTC threshold "a weak primary trigger at work-site speeds" and favors the distance-and-zone formulation, with TTC retained for faster haul traffic and as a diagnostic input [Chapter 8]. Assumed reaction times in the sources range from 0.5 s to 2.5 s, so the same TTC rule can mean very different trigger distances [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Zones (warning zone, braking zone, detection zone)
terms.oneSentence: Zones are areas drawn around the machine in which the system reacts in a particular way: it must see objects anywhere in the detection zone, it warns when one enters the warning zone, and it brakes when one enters the braking zone.
terms.explained:
Picture the machine from above with bands around it like ripples: an outer band where the sensors must see everything, a middle band where an object produces a warning, and an inner band where it produces a brake command. The bands are longer in the direction of travel and grow with speed, because a faster machine needs more room to stop. ISO 21815-3 calls the inner area the collision-risk area, requires the detection zone to be "the same or larger than the collision risk area", and allows the area to be reduced using current speed, turning angle, physical or virtual barriers and the expected path [Chapters 3, 8].

The geometry comes from the stopping distance: the braking zone must reach at least the trigger distance, and the warning zone must reach further by the distance covered during the operator's reaction time, 2.5 to 3.0 s before intervention in the South African MOSH specification (MOSH is the Mining Industry Occupational Safety and Health learning hub) [Chapter 3]. Machine length, width, articulation center and attachments change the zones, and very low-speed work can need a zone that is large when measured in stopping distances yet small in meters, especially at blind corners and when reversing [Chapter 8].

Installed zones vary a great deal. In nine NIOSH underground tests the stop zones of continuous miners differed between sites by 1.4 m on average and up to 3.6 m, while repeat measurements at one site agreed within about 13 cm [Chapter 8]. The MOSH specification sets stop gaps of 1.0 to 4.0 m at 10 km/h or less and 15 m plus or minus 5 m above 10 km/h [Chapter 3]. One supplier reported adjusting its detection zones for braking distance, speed, real-time payload and haul-road grade after field tests [Chapters 1, 2].
terms.why: Zones expressed as functions of speed, latency, deceleration (mass, slope, surface), sensor position and machine envelope turn per-model tuning into per-model measurement, which is how settings can be carried across machine models without copying constants [Chapter 9]. The booklet also warns of a "false sense of protection" from idealized clover-leaf detection zones that real sensors do not deliver [Chapter 7].

terms.title: Thresholds and filters
terms.oneSentence: Thresholds are the numbers at which the system changes its behavior, and filters are the rules that stop it from reacting to a single noisy measurement.
terms.explained:
A smoke alarm has a threshold (how much smoke) and, in better models, a filter (the smoke must persist for a few seconds, so burnt toast does not wake the house). Collision systems have the same two kinds of setting [Chapter 9]:

Detection confidence threshold: how sure the perception software must be before an object counts.

Confirmation, or N-of-M frames: the object must appear in, say, 3 of the last 4 sensor frames before it is accepted. ISO 16001 asks for detection "unambiguously with an uninterrupted sequence of the signal" and allows at most 300 ms of detection time [Chapter 3].

Persistence and debounce times: how long a condition must hold before the system acts, and how long before it stands down.

Risk determination: the step that combines the confirmed object, its position and movement, and the machine's own motion into a collision-risk level. ISO 21815-3 places intervention at level 4 or above [Chapter 8].

Hysteresis: the system switches on at one value and off at a different, safer value, so it does not flicker between states. The booklet applies this after an automatic stop: use hysteresis and an explicit release condition, and on slopes never release the brake because the object disappeared for one sensor frame [Chapter 8].

Every filter trades speed for reliability. More confirmation frames mean fewer false alarms but a later brake; at 15 km/h and 10 frames per second, each extra frame costs about 0.4 m.
terms.why: These settings are what gets tuned. The booklet lists them as the decision variables of the tuning problem (confidence thresholds, zone dimensions per speed, N-of-M filters, persistence and debounce times, time-to-collision triggers, filter constants) and the outcomes they trade against each other: missed or late interventions, false warnings per hour, unnecessary brake events per hour, intervention timing and time stopped [Chapter 9]. The transition from partial to full braking should depend on the remaining stopping margin and its uncertainty, not on range alone [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Staged interventions in the decision logic
terms.oneSentence: Staged intervention means the system escalates step by step, from information to warning to slowing to partial braking to maximum safe braking and, for a stationary machine, to refusing to move, rather than jumping straight to a full stop.
terms.explained:
A good teacher does not shout first: a look, then a word, then a consequence. Staging gives the operator a chance to act before the machine acts, and it saves the harsh actions for the moments that need them. The booklet's ladder for earth-moving machines [Chapter 8]:

Information: an object is present and the stopping margin is healthy; a visual or spatial indication.

Urgent warning: risk is rising while the operator still has adequate margin; a distinct sound, light or haptic cue.

Automatic slowing: the operator has not reduced the risk; reduce propel, use the retarder or hydrostatic slowing, or apply light braking.

Partial service braking: margin approaching its minimum; controlled deceleration below stability and traction limits.

Maximum safe collision-mitigation braking: collision otherwise unavoidable; the hardest braking the current stability and control limits allow.

Stopped-state hold: speed zero while the hazard remains; keep the brake on.

Motion inhibit from standstill: an object is already in the projected path before the machine moves; reject or limit the propel or articulation command.

The booklet's state diagram writes these as compact names, UrgentWarning, Slowing, PartialBraking, MaximumSafeBraking, Hold and MotionInhibit, in the style of the ISO 21815 standards. The standards themselves speak of speed reduction, stopping and motion inhibit; ISO 21815-1 rules out automatic steering, and ISO/TS 21815-2 defines the network commands to "slow down, stop or prevent motion of the machine" [Chapter 8]. The industry body EMESRT (Earth Moving Equipment Safety Round Table) places awareness at Level 7, advisory controls at Level 8 and intervention controls that slow and stop the vehicle at Level 9 [Chapter 8]. South African law prescribes the sequence detect, warn, retard to a safe speed, then brake [Chapter 3]. Road systems stage warning, a brief haptic brake jerk, partial braking and full braking [Chapter 8].
terms.why: Staging is what makes an automatic brake acceptable to the people who work around it: mine leaders preferred an integration that slowed to a crawl before setting the brake, "not an abrupt stop" [Chapter 4]. Each stage needs its own acceptance tolerance, because an unnecessary advisory is not the same as an unnecessary emergency stop of a loaded machine [Chapter 3].

terms.title: Deceleration limits and how regulators specify them
terms.oneSentence: A deceleration limit is a rule about how hard a machine must, or may, slow down, and regulators write such rules in several different and not directly comparable ways.
terms.explained:
Brake regulations set floors: the machine must be able to slow at least this hard, or stop within this distance. The booklet's main off-road examples [Chapter 8]:

ISO 3450:2011, for wheeled and fast rubber-tracked machines with top speeds of 20 km/h or more, prescribes maximum stopping distances by machine type, measured from brake-control actuation to standstill in the worst-case load configuration, and summarizes performance as a mean deceleration from `a = v^2 / (2d)`.

The New South Wales guidance proposes a minimum mean net deceleration of 0.60 m/s² for service brakes in service (0.30 for secondary brakes), raised to 0.75 and 0.40 for type testing, with grade and mass corrections. It is a proposal, not an adopted rule.

The US mining rule (30 CFR 56.14101, Table M-1) assumes a constant deceleration of 9.66 ft/s², about 2.94 m/s², plus a system response time of 0.5 to 2.5 s by weight class and 1 s of operator time, and requires brakes that can stop and hold the loaded machine on the steepest grade it travels.

The South African MOSH specification sets emergency-stop decelerations of 1.9 m/s² for machines faster than 20 km/h and 1.0 m/s² for others, controlled-stop decelerations of 1.0 or 0.5 m/s², no wheel lock and limited veer, tested unloaded on gradients of 1 percent or less [Chapter 7].

UN Regulation No. 152 for road cars requires a braking demand of at least 5.0 m/s²: a floor, and a demand rather than a measured deceleration [Chapter 8].

Ceilings are another matter. No published maximum automatic-braking deceleration for earth-moving machines was found, and ISO 21815 leaves the intervention profile to the machine manufacturer [Chapter 8]. The one on-road ceiling the booklet quotes is in the US rule FMVSS No. 127, where a false activation fails if peak deceleration exceeds manual braking by 0.25 g or more [Chapter 3]. The booklet's recommended rule is to command the minimum of several limits, `a_command = min(a_need, a_traction, a_stability, a_machine, a_load)`, ramped with a jerk limit, held after the stop, and released only on operator action where rollaway is possible [Chapter 8].
terms.why: The floors tell the program how little deceleration it may assume; the missing ceiling means the safe maximum must be derived per machine family from stability and traction analysis and tests [Chapter 8]. Because the sources mix definitions, the program must convert them to one definition of stopping distance and one time origin before pooling them [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Operator-already-reacting detection
terms.oneSentence: This is the part of the logic that notices the operator is already braking or steering away, so the machine does not brake on top of a person who is handling the situation.
terms.explained:
If a passenger grabbed the wheel every time you slowed for a corner, you would stop driving with them. An automatic brake that fires while the operator is already stopping is just as unwelcome, and it can be dangerous: on a loaded machine the extra jolt shifts the load. A system that stands down too easily is worse still.

Road rules handle this with override: UN Regulations R131 and R152 let a conscious action such as an accelerator kick-down or a swerve interrupt the automatic braking, and test protocols watch pedal force to confirm whether the driver braked [Chapter 8]. Off-road, ISO 21815-3 says the system must not override operator braking that is stronger than the system's own demand, and may allow intentional operator control to override an intervention where appropriate. A mining-truck patent checks brake-pedal stroke after the second alarm to decide that avoidance has begun [Chapter 8].

The booklet lists the signals a production system should combine: brake pedal or lever demand and brake pressure; the hydrostatic or propel lever returning toward neutral; retarder request; steering or articulation command and rate; accelerator released; a direction-change request; measured deceleration; and the predicted path moving away from the object. The core rule is to credit the operator for the deceleration actually achieved, not for a control that moved: suppress the intervention when measured deceleration already exceeds what is required to stop short, plus a margin [Chapter 8].
terms.why: The failure the booklet warns about is a startled operator who briefly releases the accelerator or touches the brake, the system standing down, and the margin collapsing; a downhill machine can even accelerate after the throttle is released [Chapter 8]. No off-road validation of such logic was found, so it belongs in the operator-reaction state machine the program must define before the hardware arrives and test in operator-in-the-loop and physical trials [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Nuisance braking from the decision side
terms.oneSentence: Nuisance braking is an automatic brake application that was not needed, and "from the decision side" means the cases where the sensors saw something real but the logic should have known not to brake.
terms.explained:
Not every false stop is a sensor error. The sensor correctly sees a berm, a wall, a rock pile or a spotter standing where spotters stand; the mistake is deciding that the object is a collision. The booklet lists the everyday tasks that look like collisions: backing toward a rock pile to load, using a dump berm as a bump stop, dozers and trucks sharing a tip head, working close to walls and stockpiles, ground crew and spotters near the machine, parking and workshop maneuvers with small clearances, and the machine detecting its own tires [Chapter 4]. A South African guideline notes that with a fixed stop gap, machines being loaded "will not be able to come close enough to be loaded or the CPS will have to be switched off" (CPS is a collision prevention system) [Chapter 4].

The decision side has tools for this. Risk areas can be reduced using speed, turning angle, barriers and the expected path [Chapter 8]. Road regulations include false-activation tests, such as driving between two stationary vehicles or over a steel plate without braking [Chapters 3, 8]. One wheel-loader system on the market remembers the last slope the machine climbed so that reversing down a stockpile does not trigger it, a targeted fix for one false-activation case [Chapter 2]. But there are limits: a system cannot suppress the whole loading zone, because a second truck or a person can enter the same space, and it should not "learn away" repeated berm alarms, because berm contact is also how fatal dump-edge accidents begin [Chapter 4].
terms.why: The booklet calls nuisance interventions "the main documented field failure" of deployed proximity systems and the main reason operators switch them off, and it says the nuisance-intervention rate should be an acceptance metric equal in weight to missed interventions [Chapter 8]. No off-road false-activation rate per operating hour was found anywhere, so the acceptance threshold has to come from the program's own shadow-mode data [Chapters 3, 13].

terms.title: Required detection range
terms.oneSentence: The required detection range is how far the sensors must reliably see, worked out backwards from how far the machine needs to stop plus a safety margin.
terms.explained:
You cannot stop for what you cannot see. On a foggy road you slow down until your stopping distance fits inside the distance you can see; a collision system does the same sum in reverse. Start from the speed the machine will be allowed to travel, work out the full stopping distance including every delay, add the clearance you want left, add the sensor's own measurement error, and that is how far the sensor must detect objects in every condition the system is approved for. ISO 21815-3 puts it as a requirement: the detection distance "shall be large enough to allow a machine to stop" [Chapter 8].

Continuing the glossary's example of a 40 t machine at 15 km/h (4.2 m/s) on a 10 percent downgrade: the delay chain is 1.0 s, so 4.2 m at full speed; braking at a net 2.0 m/s² takes 4.3 m; the residual safe distance is 1.0 m; and suppose the sensor places objects within 0.5 m. The required detection range is 4.2 + 4.3 + 1.0 + 0.5 = 10 m. Now change one input at a time. At 30 km/h (8.3 m/s) the delay distance doubles to 8.3 m and the braking distance quadruples to 17.4 m, so about 27 m is needed. A slower brake system with 2.0 s of delay at 15 km/h needs 8.3 + 4.3 + 1.5 = about 14 m. A machine on mud with only 1.0 m/s² of net deceleration needs 4.2 + 8.7 + 1.5 = about 14 m at 15 km/h. The required range is therefore not one number but a surface over speed, grade, load, surface and delay, and the system must either see that far or limit the speed.

The booklet's figures show the spread: an early haul-truck study derived 15 m to the sides for people, 50 m to the rear and 100 m to the front from a 0.5 s reaction time plus braking; the South African MOSH specification requires 200 m machine-to-machine detection on surface mines; and the US rule for rear sensing on surface coal equipment says only that the area must give an endangered person adequate time to leave [Chapters 3, 8]. Two cautions follow. Range must be reliable range, not best-case range: on-road field measurements in heavy rain and in fog with visibility under 50 m showed metal targets not observed at 20 to 30 m [Chapter 8]. And the detection zone has to cover the collision-risk area in shape as well as reach; if it is smaller, ISO 21815-3 requires the limitation to be stated in the operator's manual [Chapter 3].
terms.why: The booklet's list of blind spots begins here: "ISO's distance budget starts at detection. If dust, fog, darkness, glare, mud on a sensor, self-occlusion, vibration or poor mounting cut reliable detection range below the required stopping distance, no brake model can recover the lost margin" [Chapter 8]. The required range is also the link between perception validation and braking validation: sensor simulation must deliver detection delay, range and error distributions into the braking simulation [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Residual safe distance
terms.oneSentence: Residual safe distance is the gap deliberately left between the stopped machine and the object, so that a stop is a near miss and not a light touch.
terms.explained:
When you park behind another car you leave a meter, because your judgment of distance is not perfect and the other car may roll. The collision system needs the same allowance. ISO 21815-3 defines a "safe distance" as a safe offset set by an authorized person plus the measurement error, and makes it the final term in the collision-system distance after detection, determination, action and machine stopping [Chapter 3]. In the booklet's formulas it appears as D_safe or D_safety, the last item in the trigger distance [Chapter 8].

How big should it be? The standard leaves the value to the site. The South African MOSH specification uses stop gaps of 1.0 to 4.0 m at 10 km/h or less and 15 m plus or minus 5 m above 10 km/h, with a position accuracy of 1.5 m or 10 percent [Chapter 3]. Field measurements show why a margin is needed: installed stop zones varied between sites by up to 3.6 m, while repeat measurements at one site agreed within about 13 cm [Chapter 8]. The residual distance must absorb sensor position error, the uncertainty in the predicted stopping distance, and small movements of the object. The booklet's acceptance list includes "minimum stopping margin" and "residual impact speed" as quantities every test should report [Chapter 3].
terms.why: The residual safe distance is the tolerance the simulation must be more accurate than: if the risk area leaves X meters of margin, the model-form, numerical and input uncertainty must be demonstrably smaller than X [Chapter 10]. A larger margin protects against error but brings more nuisance stops in close-proximity work, so it is a tuning decision, not a fixed constant.

terms.title: Secondary hazards of an automatic stop
terms.oneSentence: Secondary hazards are the new dangers an automatic stop creates by itself: being struck from behind, blocking an escape route, stalling or rolling back on a grade, spilling the load, or hurting the operator.
terms.explained:
Stopping is not automatically safe. A machine that halts without warning in a line of haul trucks can be hit by the one behind; in US insurance data, forward collision warning with automatic braking raised the rate of being struck from behind by 20 percent, a road result the booklet quotes as a caution [Chapter 4]. A machine that stops in a narrow underground roadway can block the escape route of the workers it was protecting, and workers reported "walking backwards into the tailgate" of stopped haulage [Chapter 4]. A machine stopped on a ramp may be unable to restart smoothly, and when the automatic brake releases it can roll back or roll forward: ISO 21815-3 warns that discontinuing an intervention must not create rollaway and recommends an operator action, such as applying the parking brake, before release [Chapter 8]. Hard braking can spill rock, swing a suspended load or tip a high-loaded machine, and sudden stops jar the operator; MSHA engineers estimate that three to four miners' lives a year could be saved by seat belts, one reason restraint matters for an automatic stop [Chapter 8].

The booklet also names immobilization in an unsafe location, loss of traction or control, operator counteraction, production loss, and the long-run hazard that operators disable a system that stops them too often [Chapters 1, 4, 8]. Off-road, none of these has been measured: spilled loads, slope instability and rear-end strikes caused by automatic braking were not found in the mining sources, and no injury or jerk threshold exists for haul trucks, loaders or dozers [Chapter 4].
terms.why: The safety goal cannot be "stop before the object". The transition from warning to intervention needs its own hazard analysis, and the simulation matrix needs hazardous-unintended-intervention cases as well as failure-to-intervene cases [Chapters 1, 10]. Hold-and-restart tests on grade and stability tests belong in the physical campaign for this reason [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Mixed motion and prediction of movement
terms.oneSentence: Mixed motion is the case where both the machine and the person or vehicle are moving, so the system must predict where each will be, not just where they are now.
terms.explained:
Catching a ball means running to where it will land, not where it is. Most collision tests use a stationary target or a target on a fixed path; real sites have people who step out from behind a stockpile, trucks that reverse into a loading position while a loader swings, and dozers that change direction at a tip head [Chapter 4]. The logic must therefore work with a predicted path. ISO 21815-3 allows the risk area to be shaped by the machine's "projected or expected path", and the booklet's margin formula uses the predicted path distance R to the collision point [Chapter 8]. The machine's own path is predictable from speed, steering and articulation; the other party's is not, and a worker or another machine may also react to the braking machine [Chapter 7].

Three further points from the booklet. Time to collision assumes straight-line closing and fails when motion is sideways, rotating or starting from rest [Chapter 8]. Research at the University of Pretoria samples plausible steering-rate trajectories to predict collisions and cut false interventions, with simulation-only initial results [Chapter 8]. And validated off-road behavioral models of workers and equipment operators were not found, so a simulation that moves a virtual pedestrian is making an assumption that needs its own validation [Chapters 7, 12].
terms.why: Mixed motion is listed among the controlled whole-machine tests that cannot be delegated to an unvalidated model [Chapter 1], and replay of recorded data cannot answer it, because after the brake acts the recorded movements of other actors are no longer valid [Chapter 7]. Low-speed work needs comparatively large zones at blind corners and where people enter the path from the side [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Tuning thresholds in simulation before field tests
terms.oneSentence: Tuning in simulation means adjusting the decision thresholds, zone sizes and filters on a computer model of machine, sensors and site, so that field tests confirm settings rather than discover them.
terms.explained:
A piano is tuned before the concert. For a braking system the "pitch" is the balance between stopping in time and not stopping needlessly, and simulation is where that balance is first set. The booklet is careful about what the evidence supports and what it does not [Chapter 8].

What has been done, on roads: a 2019 study swept time-to-collision triggers and latencies against US pedestrian crash data and estimated how many crashes each combination would avoid; the 2015 grade study showed a trigger that worked on level ground and collided at 11 and 17 percent; and the 2026 round robin showed that tools disagreed by 0.033 s and 0.314 m even with a prescribed trigger and brake profile, so the simulator itself needs verification [Chapter 8]. Off-road: NIOSH built a stopping-distance model to check whether detection zones covered the stopping distance of faster underground vehicles, varied six inputs at five values each, and said validation was still needed; ISO 21815-3 includes examples of configuring parameters from stopping performance; excavator and collision-prediction studies report simulation-only results. "No published off-road case compares simulation-tuned thresholds with field results quantitatively" [Chapter 8].

What can be tuned virtually, in the booklet's view: the structure of the trigger (stopping margin plus zones), the sensitivity of the outcome to each input, the grade and payload dependence, the staging logic, and first estimates of zone sizes per speed and machine family, using measured brake delays and deceleration maps as inputs [Chapter 8]. What cannot: the actual brake delays and deceleration limits of the production machine, the friction of real site surfaces, sensor behavior in snow, glare and darkness, and the nuisance rate in real work, which must come from measurements and shadow-mode logs [Chapter 8].
terms.why: The booklet's plan is to freeze the decision architecture and run the scenario sweeps before the hardware arrives, pre-book the physical anchor campaign for the first six weeks after delivery, re-run the sweeps with calibrated parameters, and spend the remaining weeks in shadow mode measuring nuisance rates before braking is enabled [Chapter 8]. It also says to treat the model "as a test-selection and uncertainty-propagation machine, not as proof by itself", and to set explicit pass criteria for calibration and stop to recalibrate if they fail [Chapter 8].

terms.title: Test space and the combinatorial explosion
terms.oneSentence: The test space is the set of every situation the braking system could meet, and the combinatorial explosion is the way that set grows so fast, when conditions are multiplied together, that nobody can test it all.
terms.explained:
Think of ordering a meal from a menu with five courses and ten choices for each course. There are 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 100,000 possible meals. Nobody could taste them all. Each new course multiplies the total; it does not add to it. Engineers call this the combinatorial explosion.

For the automatic braking system, the "courses" are the conditions that can change from one situation to the next: the type of job site, the task the machine is doing, the weather, the light, the machine model, where the sensors sit, the speed, and what kind of object is in the way. The booklet's program must cover more than 100 site types, more than ten operating scenarios per machine, seven or so weather and light conditions (rain, snow, fog, dust, dusk, darkness, glare) and many machine models. Multiplying only the first three gives 100 × 10 × 7 = 7,000 cells before any machine model, speed or object type is counted. Chapter 7 makes the same count and notes that no program can fill each cell with the 59 to 299 physical trials a statistical claim would need [Chapter 7].

A plain grid of every combination (a "full Cartesian product") is therefore not a plan. Chapter 9 recommends structuring the space in three layers instead: an operating-domain taxonomy that sets the boundaries, a scenario catalog that guarantees known fatal-accident patterns are always tested, and parameterized scenario families with a probability distribution over their variables. The decisive choice is to describe sites by their safety-relevant attributes (rough terrain, dusty air, bright sun, an 8 percent grade, frequent crossings) rather than as 100 unrelated site names. Two quarries with different names may be the same test case. Many combinations are also impossible and can be removed: there is no direct sun glare underground, and an ultrasonic-only sensor set has no camera exposure settings [Chapter 9].
terms.why: The size of the space is the reason the validation has to move largely into simulation, and the reason the choice of which combinations to test becomes a safety decision. Chapter 13 lists "compute and scenario explosion" as a standing objection to the plan and notes that published compute costs for virtual validation of off-road safety functions were not found [Chapter 13].

terms.title: Parameter, parameter range and parameterized scenario family
terms.oneSentence: A parameter is one adjustable quantity in a test (such as machine speed), its range is the span of values it may take, and a parameterized scenario family is one scenario description with those quantities left open so that thousands of concrete tests can be generated from it.
terms.explained:
A recipe that says "bake for 20 to 30 minutes at 160 to 180 degrees" is parameterized: time and temperature are the parameters, the numbers are the ranges, and each bake picks one value for each.

The booklet follows a three-level ladder from automated-driving research. A functional scenario is in words: "machine reversing toward a person." A logical scenario adds ranges: person distance 0 to 30 meters, machine speed 0 to 15 kilometers per hour, approach angle, dust density. A concrete scenario fixes every value. Chapter 9's example family, "machine reverses toward an initially visible or occluded human-shaped object while the operator does not brake", has variables such as speed, initial distance, the person's path, slope, load, sensor installation, illumination, visibility, system latency and braking friction. A concrete test is one chosen vector of these values [Chapter 9].

Two features make a family more than a list of ranges. Each family carries a probability distribution over its parameters, taken from field data or expert estimates: how often is the person 5 meters away rather than 25? That distribution is what later makes rate estimation possible. And constraints and dependencies are written down: dust correlates with dry, windy, high-traffic conditions, and a distribution that ignores this misweights the strata [Chapter 9].
terms.why: Instead of storing 10,000 copies of "reverse toward worker", the catalog stores one family, and every sampling, search and estimation method in this part operates on such families. The booklet warns that defensible distributions are the weak point, and that the only off-road scenario library found was built for intelligent off-road vehicles, not collision avoidance [Chapter 9].

terms.title: Test selection method
terms.oneSentence: A test selection method is a rule for choosing which of the countless possible tests to actually run, and each rule can honestly answer only certain kinds of question.
terms.explained:
A doctor who can order only ten blood tests chooses them to answer a specific question. The right ten for "is anything wrong at all?" differ from the right ten for "how severe is this known condition?" Test selection for a braking system works the same way: the method follows the question.

Chapter 9 explains that "coverage" has four incompatible meanings, and that no single method delivers all four: coverage of discrete configurations (has every site type been tried with every weather type?), coverage of a continuous parameter space (have speeds and distances been spread across their ranges?), discovery of failures (where does the system break?), and estimation of field rates (how often will it miss or brake unnecessarily in real operation?).

The booklet maps methods to these questions. Combinatorial designs guarantee discrete coverage. Space-filling designs cover continuous parameters and train surrogate models. Falsification and adaptive search find failures. Importance sampling estimates small probabilities, but only when the real-world distribution is known. A frozen stratified random sample is the only basis for a release rate claim. Each method also has things it cannot claim: a search that hunts for failures cannot report a failure rate, and a design that spreads points evenly says nothing about how often each point happens in a real quarry [Chapter 9].
terms.why: The booklet's position is blunt: "Do not try to make one design perform all three jobs." The program should use a portfolio: coverage designs for understanding, search for discovery, and a separate frozen sample for the statistical claim [Chapter 9].

terms.title: Design of experiments (DOE)
terms.oneSentence: Design of experiments (DOE) is the branch of statistics that plans which combinations of settings to test so that the effect of each factor, and of factors acting together, can be measured with the fewest runs.
terms.explained:
Suppose a baker wants to know whether oven temperature, baking time or flour type matters most. Changing one thing at a time is slow and misses interactions, such as a high temperature that only matters with a long time. DOE varies several factors in a planned pattern so that one set of runs answers several questions.

The booklet names the classic designs from the statistical handbook of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). A full factorial tests every combination of a few factors at a few levels; its run count grows exponentially. A fractional factorial tests a chosen fraction and cuts the run count sharply, at the price of "aliasing": some higher-order effects become indistinguishable from others. Screening designs identify the influential factors. Response-surface designs then map curvature in the smaller space of influential factors, which suits fine tuning of thresholds and zones. D-optimal designs help when constraints make a regular grid impossible [Chapter 9].

DOE can claim main effects and low-order interactions on a continuous response, for example how detection range changes with dust density and illumination. It cannot claim a failure probability in the field, because its points are not weighted by how often each condition occurs, and it cannot find a narrow failure region hidden between design points: a fractional factorial showing no main effect for fog cannot rule out a localized failure at one combination of fog density, glare and sensor contamination [Chapter 9].
terms.why: The booklet places DOE in the coverage stream and in the calibration step after prototype arrival, where modest DOE or D-optimal tests estimate sensor, latency and braking residuals. No off-road collision-avoidance study using DOE was found [Chapter 9].
aliases: National Institute of Standards and Technology

terms.title: Combinatorial testing (t-way testing, pairwise testing, covering arrays)
terms.oneSentence: Combinatorial testing chooses a small set of tests that still guarantees every combination of values of any t factors (for pairwise testing, any two) appears at least once.
terms.explained:
Imagine a clothing shop that offers 5 items, each in 4 colors, and wants to photograph outfits so that every pair of items appears together in every color combination at least once. Trying every full outfit would take 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 × 4 = 1,024 photos. A cleverly chosen set of 16 photos can show every pair of items in every pair of colors. That set is a covering array of strength 2, and the trick is called pairwise testing. Strength 3 (t = 3) covers every triple and needs more tests; in general, "t-way testing" covers every combination of t factors.

The reason this is worth doing comes from software research. NIST (the National Institute of Standards and Technology) found that "most software bugs and failures are caused by one or two parameters, with progressively fewer by three or more", up to about six. It reports fault detection equal to exhaustive testing with a 20 to 700 times reduction in test-set size. Its generator, ACTS (Automated Combinatorial Testing for Software), is public domain; PICT (Pairwise Independent Combinatorial Testing) is an open-source generator; commercial test-design tools do the same job [Chapter 9].

For the braking system, the discrete factors are site type, weather, light, object type, machine model and sensor configuration. A covering array guarantees that, for example, every machine model has been tested in every weather type with every object type, without running the full grid. What it cannot do is also important. It says nothing about continuous ranges (a speed of 7.3 kilometers per hour is not a "level"), nothing about rates, and nothing about failures that need more than t factors to line up [Chapter 9].
terms.why: Chapter 9 recommends covering arrays for "machine by sensor by weather by scenario configuration coverage". It also flags a caution: the evidence that low-order interactions explain most bugs comes from software, not from camera, radar or lidar failures caused by coupled weather, contamination, geometry and signal processing. Whether the "interaction rule" carries over to perception is listed as uncertain, so t-way designs should be supplemented by physics-guided interaction hypotheses and by failure-seeking search [Chapter 9].

terms.title: Random sampling, stratified sampling and probability-weighted sampling
terms.oneSentence: Random sampling picks tests by chance according to how often each situation occurs in real operation, stratified sampling first divides the situations into groups (strata) and samples each group deliberately, and probability-weighted sampling keeps track of each test's real-world frequency so that results can be scaled back to the field.
terms.explained:
An opinion poll does not ask everyone. It asks a random sample, and if the sample is drawn fairly, the answer is close to the whole population's answer, with a known margin of error. If a pollster worries that a small but important group would be missed by chance, they make sure to interview enough of that group (a stratum) and then weight its answers back down to its true share of the population. That is stratified sampling.

For the braking system, the "population" is every encounter the machine will have in real operation: each reverse toward a worker, each approach to a light vehicle, in each weather and light condition, on each machine model. A random sample drawn from the parameterized scenario families, using their probability distributions, gives an unbiased estimate of the detection rate and the false alarm rate, with a classical confidence interval. Stratification is usually better: deliberately ensure enough samples from dust at night, from each machine family, from each critical scenario, then weight the strata back to how often they occur [Chapter 9].

The method has one hard condition. The estimate is only valid if the assumed distribution of situations matches reality. If dust at dusk happens three times more often than the model assumed, the estimated rate is wrong. The booklet notes a second limit: plain random sampling is extremely inefficient for rare dangerous events, because most random runs are uneventful [Chapter 9].
terms.why: The booklet states that a frozen, stratified random sample, drawn from the declared operating-domain distribution before tuning starts and never used for tuning, is the only basis for the release rate claim. The field distribution needed to weight it is not available in public sources, which is why the booklet urges shadow-mode logging on the existing warning fleet to begin now [Chapter 9].

terms.title: Space-filling designs (Latin hypercube)
terms.oneSentence: A space-filling design spreads test points as evenly as possible across the ranges of several continuous parameters at once, so that no region of the space is left unexplored.
terms.explained:
If you had 20 soil probes to place across a field, you would not drop them at random, because random placement leaves clumps and gaps. You would space them out. A space-filling design does the same in many dimensions.

The Latin hypercube is the best-known example. Each parameter's range is cut into n equal slices, and the design places n points so that every slice of every parameter is used exactly once, like a sudoku grid where each row and column holds each number once. Sobol sequences and other quasi-random designs achieve a similar even spread in a different way. The booklet notes that these designs cover continuous parameters more evenly than naive random draws and are useful for exploration and for training surrogate models, which are fast approximate models of the simulator's response [Chapter 9].

The limit is that even spread is not probability. A uniformly covered box of parameters is not a picture of a real quarry's traffic, where most approaches are slow and most weather is clear. Space-filling designs treat unrealistic regions exactly like realistic ones unless constraints and distributions are added. So they can claim "even geometric spread through the chosen region" and cannot claim rates, worst cases or operational frequency [Chapter 9].
terms.why: The booklet puts space-filling designs in the coverage stream alongside combinatorial designs: good for understanding how detection range varies with dust, glare and speed, and for feeding surrogate-guided search, but never for the release claim [Chapter 9].

terms.title: Falsification (failure-seeking search)
terms.oneSentence: Falsification is a test method that treats "find a case where the system fails" as a search problem and uses optimization to steer the simulator toward the most dangerous combinations of conditions.
terms.explained:
A safety inspector checking a railing does not push gently in the middle. They push hard at the joints and corners, where failure is most likely. Falsification is the automated version. Instead of testing many ordinary situations, it looks for the worst ones.

The method defines a measure of how close the system came to failing, for example the time to collision at the moment of detection, the stopping margin left when the machine halts, or the detector's confidence. An optimizer then adjusts the scenario parameters (speed, distance, dust, glare, the person's path) to make that measure as bad as possible. When the margin reaches zero, a failure has been found and can be replayed. The booklet names the tools S-TaLiRo, Breach and VerifAI, and puts evolutionary search, Bayesian optimization, fuzzing, surrogate-guided search, reinforcement-learning adversaries and Adaptive Stress Testing in the same family. VerifAI used with the Scenic language reported up to a 5 times speed-up from running several objectives in parallel, in on-road work from 2021 [Chapter 9].

Falsification can claim that a counterexample exists, that it is reproducible, and where the failure boundaries and worst cases lie inside the simulated space. It cannot claim a failure rate, because the search concentrates on failures, so the proportion of failing runs is biased by design. Not finding a failure is not proof of absence. The search can also exploit flaws in the simulator rather than in the system, and an objective written for one kind of failure may miss a qualitatively different one [Chapter 9].
terms.why: Falsification is the heart of the booklet's discovery stream, aimed at stopping boundaries, partial visibility, high closing speed, the edge of the field of view and sensor degradation. The booklet's rule for what happens next is central: a found failure becomes a new logical scenario or a permanent regression test, its frequency is estimated separately, and the failure fraction of a search campaign "must never be reported as an operational failure rate". The evidence is on-road and aerospace; no off-road demonstration was found [Chapter 9].

terms.title: Rare-event methods (importance sampling)
terms.oneSentence: Rare-event methods deliberately make dangerous situations happen more often in simulation, then mathematically correct the results so that the estimated rate still refers to normal operation.
terms.explained:
To estimate how often a rare disease occurs, a researcher might study a hospital where cases are concentrated, then scale the count back by how much more common the disease is there than in the general population. Importance sampling works the same way. Each simulated run is weighted by the ratio between how likely the situation is in reality and how likely it was under the accelerated sampling. Dangerous runs are sampled often, but each counts for little.

The booklet lists importance sampling, cross-entropy methods, subset simulation, multilevel splitting, accelerated evaluation and naturalistic-and-adversarial environments in this family. The on-road results are striking: accelerated evaluation of lane changes (2017) showed very large speed-ups, and dense deep reinforcement learning (D2RL, published in Nature in March 2023) reported evaluation "10^3 to 10^5 times faster" while remaining unbiased [Chapter 9].

The conditions are strict. The method is unbiased only if the ratio between the real and the accelerated distribution is known and the accelerated sampling actually reaches the failure region. When the real distribution is unknown or has many dimensions, the weights become unstable and their variance can be huge. All the on-road successes rest on behavior models learned from very large naturalistic driving datasets, and no off-road dataset of comparable scale was found. The booklet's point is that a poorly modeled quarry operation cannot be rescued mathematically by importance sampling [Chapter 9].
terms.why: The booklet's rule is to use importance sampling in the estimation stream only where a defensible field distribution exists; otherwise the campaign counts as discovery. How far rare-event acceleration can replace real exposure is listed among the points where experts disagree [Chapter 9].

terms.title: Adaptive and Bayesian test selection
terms.oneSentence: Adaptive test selection chooses each new test based on the results of the tests so far, often using a Bayesian model that keeps track of what is still uncertain.
terms.explained:
A good teacher giving an oral exam adapts: if the student answers an easy question well, the next question is harder, and the exam homes in on the boundary of what the student knows. Adaptive test selection does the same with a braking system. After each run it updates a model of where the system passes and fails, and picks the next test where that model is least sure.

The "Bayesian" part refers to the model. A surrogate model (a fast approximation of the simulator) predicts the outcome at untested points and gives an uncertainty for each prediction. An acquisition rule then picks the next point, for example where the prediction is closest to the pass or fail boundary and the uncertainty is high. This is called active learning when the aim is to learn the boundary, and Bayesian optimization when the aim is to find the best or worst setting [Chapter 9].

The strength is efficiency: fewer runs to map the boundary between detection and miss. The weakness follows directly. Because the sampling is intentionally biased toward interesting regions, a naive binomial confidence interval computed from adaptively selected tests is invalid, and the surrogate's own uncertainty estimate can be wrong [Chapter 9].
terms.why: The booklet classes adaptive selection as a discovery method that can "learn decision boundaries efficiently", not as a basis for a rate claim [Chapter 9].

terms.title: Monte Carlo methods
terms.oneSentence: A Monte Carlo method answers a question by running the same experiment many times with randomly chosen inputs and counting what happens.
terms.explained:
If you wanted to know the chance that two dice total seven, you could work it out, or you could roll them 10,000 times and count. The counting approach is Monte Carlo, named after the casino. It works for problems far too tangled to work out by hand, as long as the experiment can be run cheaply many times.

In simulation, each run draws its parameters (speed, distance, dust, the person's path) at random from the scenario family's probability distribution, and the outcome is recorded. After many runs, the fraction of misses estimates the miss rate. The booklet's estimation stream is a Monte Carlo campaign on a frozen sample. Chapter 2 notes that aircraft collision-avoidance logic (ACAS X) was evaluated with encounter-model Monte Carlo runs equivalent to "billions of flight hours" [Chapter 2].

The limit is rare events. If the true miss rate is one in 10,000, a plain Monte Carlo campaign sees about one miss per 10,000 runs and needs tens of thousands of runs before it has seen enough misses to say anything precise. The booklet states that pure Monte Carlo is "extremely inefficient for rare dangerous events" and, in the planning chapter, that naive Monte Carlo cannot reach low failure rates in four months [Chapter 9, Chapter 12].
terms.why: Monte Carlo is the honest default for estimating rates, and its hunger for runs is the reason the booklet's sample-size tables and rare-event methods exist.

terms.title: Sample size, confidence level and confidence interval
terms.oneSentence: The sample size is how many independent trials you run, the confidence level is how sure you want to be, and the confidence interval is the range of values for the true rate that the data support at that level of sureness.
terms.explained:
Suppose you test a new type of lock by trying to pick it 20 times and fail every time. You might be tempted to say the lock is unpickable. A statistician would say: with 20 failures, you can be 95 percent confident the pick-success rate is below about 14 percent. That is not nothing, but it is far from "never". The confidence level (95 percent) says how often this kind of statement would be right if you repeated the whole exercise many times. The confidence interval (0 to about 14 percent) is the range of true rates that 20 clean trials cannot rule out. A bigger sample gives a narrower interval.

The booklet's statistics rest on one formula for the zero-failure case. If each trial is an independent detection opportunity and none is missed, the claim "the miss probability is at most q" holds at confidence 1 minus alpha when (1 - q)^n is at most alpha. Here q is the largest miss probability you are willing to claim, alpha is the chance of being wrong (0.05 for 95 percent confidence), and n is the number of clean trials. Solving gives n = ln(alpha) / ln(1 - q), where ln is the natural logarithm. At 95 percent one-sided confidence: a miss rate of at most 5 percent needs 59 clean trials; at most 1 percent needs 299; at most 0.1 percent needs 2,995; at most 0.01 percent needs 29,956. At 99 percent confidence the figures are 90, 459, 4,603 and 46,050 [Chapter 9].

Three further points shape every claim. First, the unit must be an independent trial. A ten-second encounter produces about 300 camera frames, but it is one encounter, not 300 chances; counting frames inflates the sample and makes intervals "grossly overconfident". Second, if some misses occur, an exact binomial (Clopper-Pearson) interval or another pre-declared interval should be used, rather than testing until a pleasing percentage appears. Third, estimating a rate precisely costs more than showing it is below a threshold: a generic 95 percent estimate within plus or minus 1 percentage point needs about 9,604 observations in the worst case, and plus or minus 0.5 point needs about 38,415 [Chapter 9].
terms.why: Chapter 9 calls the statistics "the binding constraint". Each claim about a separate population needs its own sample: a 1 percent claim in each of 20 critical strata needs about 6,000 zero-miss trials, which is only feasible in simulation or hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing. The booklet also notes that no standard sets these numbers; they follow from the claim, the confidence level and the population definition, and should be fixed before the data are collected [Chapter 9, Chapter 7].

terms.title: Binomial claims and the rule of three
terms.oneSentence: A binomial claim is a statement about the probability of a yes-or-no outcome (detected or missed) based on a count of trials, and the rule of three is the shortcut that says: with zero failures in n trials, you can be about 95 percent confident that the true failure probability is below 3 divided by n.
terms.explained:
"Binomial" simply means two outcomes. Each staged approach of a worker toward a reversing haul truck ends in one of two ways: the system detects and stops, or it misses. If the trials are independent and the conditions are the same, the number of misses in n trials follows the binomial distribution, and standard formulas turn the count into a confidence statement about the underlying miss probability.

The hardest case to reason about is zero misses, because nothing has been observed. The rule of three gives the answer. Worked example: the program wants to claim "the miss rate in reverse worker encounters is at most 1 percent" with 95 percent confidence. The rule says n must be about 3 divided by 0.01, which is 300 clean trials. The exact formula n = ln(0.05) / ln(0.99) gives 299. Check it: 0.99 raised to the power 299 is about 0.0495, just under the 5 percent chance of being wrong. If the program wants at most 0.1 percent, the rule gives 3 divided by 0.001 = 3,000 trials, and the exact figure is 2,995. If the claim is only at most 5 percent, 59 clean trials suffice [Chapter 9, Chapter 7].

Failures raise the bill. Allowing one miss while still claiming at most 1 percent needs about 474 trials; allowing two needs about 630. The rule of three is the zero-failure special case of exact binomial inference, and the booklet names Clopper-Pearson intervals as the conservative default when misses occur, with the Wilson interval as a less conservative alternative at moderate sample sizes [Chapter 9].

The arithmetic has a hidden multiplier. The 299 trials prove one claim about one defined population. If separate claims are demanded for rain, darkness, dust, each machine family and each scenario type, each needs its own 299, or a justified statistical model that pools them. The booklet's example is a 1 percent claim in each of 20 critical strata: about 6,000 zero-miss trials. Physical tests then validate the simulation in each stratum and give a smaller independent confirmation, for example 59 trials per stratum for a bound of at least 95 percent detection [Chapter 9].
terms.why: Three to four years of physical testing previously produced the evidence; the rule of three shows why four months of physical testing cannot. It also explains why the booklet treats "we ran 20,000 scenarios with 99.8 percent success" as meaningless until the population and the selection method are stated: the formula applies only to independent trials drawn from a defined population [Chapter 9].

terms.title: Bayesian methods and sequential testing
terms.oneSentence: Bayesian methods combine what you believed before the test (the prior) with the test results to produce an updated belief, and sequential testing lets you stop testing early once the evidence is clearly good or clearly bad.
terms.explained:
A mechanic who has seen a hundred trucks of one model has a strong opinion before opening the hood of the next; a few observations update that opinion rather than replace it. Bayesian statistics formalizes this: a prior distribution expresses what is believed before the data, the data update it, and the result is a posterior distribution. For yes-or-no trials the beta-binomial model does this with simple arithmetic.

For the braking system the attraction is clear: thousands of simulation runs could serve as the prior, and a few hundred physical trials would update it, so the physical sample could be smaller than the rule of three alone demands. The booklet warns that the result is very sensitive to the strength of the prior. A conservative Bayesian analysis of autonomous-vehicle road testing (2019) found that a strong prior with 90 percent prior confidence cut the RAND requirement of 275 million fatality-free miles to 69 million, while a weak prior raised it to 476 million. Assessors will challenge the prior, so conservative methods should be used [Chapter 9].

Sequential testing is a separate idea. In a sequential probability ratio test (SPRT), the evidence is checked after each trial or batch, and testing stops as soon as the result is clearly above or below the required level. This saves trials, which is attractive in a four-month window, but the stopping rules must be fixed in advance; stopping when the numbers happen to look good cheats the statistics [Chapter 9].
terms.why: The booklet lists "Bayesian priors from simulation" among the points where experts disagree: proponents report large reductions in physical testing, critics point to the prior sensitivity. Any Bayesian combination also depends on a documented credibility assessment of the simulation [Chapter 9].
aliases: In a sequential probability ratio test

terms.title: Hypothesis testing basics (null hypothesis, significance, McNemar test)
terms.oneSentence: A hypothesis test asks whether an observed difference is too large to be a coincidence, by assuming at first that there is no real difference (the null hypothesis) and computing how surprising the data would then be.
terms.explained:
A coin that lands heads 6 times out of 10 is not clearly biased. One that lands heads 60 times out of 100 is suspicious; a fair coin does that less than 5 percent of the time. The null hypothesis is "the coin is fair". The significance level is the surprise threshold, usually 5 percent, below which the null is rejected. Power is the chance that the test detects a real difference of a given size; too few trials means low power.

Chapter 7 uses these ideas to size a test that must separate an acceptable miss probability from an unacceptable one. Chapter 9 warns about multiple testing: if hundreds of machine, weather and scenario cells are each checked at 95 percent confidence, some will pass or fail by chance alone, so primary claims should be predefined and multiplicity methods applied where many claims must hold together [Chapter 7, Chapter 9].

McNemar's test is the booklet's tool for comparing the old warning system with the new one. Both systems see the same hazards, recorded in parallel on the same machine, and each hazard yields a pair: hit or miss for the old, hit or miss for the new. Pairs where both hit or both miss say nothing. The test looks only at the discordant pairs, for example 12 hazards the new system caught and the old missed against 3 the old caught and the new missed, and asks whether 12 against 3 is more lopsided than chance would produce. It is valid only when both systems faced the same events; separate deployments confound site, operator and weather [Chapter 7].
terms.why: "The new system is better than the old one" is a hypothesis, and the booklet's advice is to make it testable through paired recording rather than averages from different sites and seasons [Chapter 7].

terms.title: Base rate and exposure-based rates (events per 1,000 hours)
terms.oneSentence: A base rate is how often something happens in normal operation, and an exposure-based rate expresses it per unit of exposure, such as false alarms per 1,000 operating hours, rather than per staged test.
terms.explained:
A smoke detector that never misses a real fire but goes off twice a day while cooking will be unplugged. To judge it, you need to know how often it alarms during ordinary life, not how it performs when someone holds a match under it. That everyday count is its base rate of false alarms, measured against the hours it was switched on. The hours are the exposure.

Detection and false alarms need different denominators. Detection is measured per encounter: of 300 staged approaches, how many were detected? A false alarm or an unnecessary brake happens when there is no object or no danger, so there is no encounter to count it against. The booklet therefore measures them per operating hour, per work cycle or per object-free encounter, and insists that the hours be representative operation, usually gathered by shadow mode on customer sites. In Ruff's study for NIOSH (the United States National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health) of a radar system on a haul truck, 580 alarms sounded over seven days and 618 reversals; 102 were false, 243 were nuisance alarms about known objects, and only 235 (41 percent) warranted action. Staged tests with targets would never have revealed that ratio [Chapter 4, Chapter 7].

The zero-event mathematics for rates mirrors the rule of three. If false alarms occur at a steady random rate (a homogeneous Poisson process) and none is seen in T hours, the 95 percent upper bound on the rate is about 3 divided by T. So 300 hours with no unnecessary brake supports "fewer than 1 per 100 hours", and 3,000 hours supports "fewer than 1 per 1,000 hours".
