| ISO/TS 21815-2:2021 | On-board J1939 communication interface | Published technical specification, July 2021; confirmed December 2024 | Defines the SAE International J1939 network messages (SLOW_DOWN, CONTROLLED-STOP, EMERGENCY-STOP, capability discovery, keep-alive) by which a collision device (CxD) asks the machine to slow, stop or stay still; "not intended for plug-and-play" |
| ISO 21815-3:2023 | Risk area and risk level for forward and reverse motion | Published, edition 1, August 2023 (the booklet reviewed the 2022 draft) | Defines the CxS distance (CxS being the standard's shorthand for a collision warning or avoidance system): detection, decision, action and stopping distance plus a safe distance; the manufacturer must declare system delays; worked examples for surface and underground machines; type-C under ISO 12100 |
| ISO 21815-4 | Risk area and risk level for swing and rotation | Under publication (stage 60.00) since September 2026; scheduled October 2026 | Rotation of excavators and similar; motion inhibit before rotation starts; expressly "does not cover avoidance by automatic application of the braking" |
| ISO/PRF 21815-5 | Risk area and risk level for other forms of motion | Proof stage (50.20) since September 2026; scheduled November 2026 | Articulation, four-wheel steering, towed trailers in reverse, skid-steer turning, telescopic and vertical motions |

Standards Australia published AS 21815.1:2023, a modified adoption of Part 1 whose changes the booklet could not read, and SA TS ISO 21815.2:2023 for the interface; neither is law unless incorporated [Chapter 3].

On simulation the series says nothing that was found. Part 3 relies on calculation of the CxS distance, which "supports analytical evidence for stopping-distance margins but is not simulation-based acceptance"; Parts 1 and 3 expect physical tests, and an ISO 21815 physical test cannot be declared satisfied because a simulation passed [Chapter 3]. Part 3 notes that false positives "could create alarm fatigue", and its safe offset is set "by the authorized person" at the worksite, so configurable site parameters must be validated too [Chapter 3].
terms.why: ISO 21815 is "the core off-road standard family, and it is still being completed" [Chapter 3]. The booklet's plan uses Part 3 as the backbone: calculate the CxS distance per machine model from ISO 3450 brake data and declared delays, build the scenario catalog around its risk areas, and present simulation as coverage evidence beside the physical tests the standard prescribes [Chapters 2, 3]. Its separate parts for forward and reverse, swing and articulation are also evidence that off-road motion types need their own hazard models, one reason road scenarios do not transfer directly [Chapter 3].

terms.title: ISO 19014 series (functional safety for earth-moving machinery)
terms.oneSentence: ISO 19014 is the family of standards that tells a maker of earth-moving machines how to make sure the electronic control system behind a safety function, such as an automatic brake, is designed, built, tested and programmed so that its faults do not cause harm.
terms.explained:
Performance asks "does the system brake when it should?"; functional safety asks "what happens when a wire breaks, a chip fails, the software has a bug or the sensor is caked in mud, and how sure are we that the failure does not cause an accident?" The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) has a generic machinery method for this (ISO 13849) and road vehicles have ISO 26262. For earth-moving machines the sector framework is ISO 19014, and the booklet is clear that this, not ISO 26262, is the right one [Chapter 3].

The series uses the Machine Performance Level (MPL). A hazard and risk analysis assigns a required level, MPLr, to each safety function; the design is then evaluated to show an achieved level, MPLa, at least as high. The method for MPLr is the Machine Control System Safety Analysis (MCSSA) [Chapter 3]. Part 1 gives the MCSSA method and MPLr; Part 2 covers hardware, architecture and MPLa; Part 3 sets environmental tests (vibration, temperature, electrical robustness) for the safety-related electronics; Part 4 covers software and data transmission; Part 5 gives tables of MPLr for common functions so a manufacturer can apply them "without performing a full MCSSA for each new model" when the tables' assumptions hold [Chapter 3].

Scope is the hinge. ISO 19014-2 covers systems that control machine motion or mitigate a hazard and excludes "awareness systems that do not impact machine motion (e.g. cameras and radar detectors)". A warning-only system is outside; a system that can command the brakes is inside [Chapter 3]. The booklet asks for two safety functions to be analyzed separately: failure to intervene when needed, and intervention when it is unsafe or unnecessary, since an unexpected full brake on a loaded truck on a slope is itself a hazard [Chapter 3].

All five parts change at once: edition 2 of Parts 1 to 4 and the first full-standard edition of Part 5 (replacing ISO/TS 19014-5:2021) reached "under publication" in August 2026, scheduled for October 2026, with a European adoption of Part 1 in approval at the European standards body CEN [Chapter 3]. ISO 19014 replaced ISO 15998, withdrawn in June 2022. Whether the Part 5 tables contain an entry for collision avoidance was not reviewed; no published MPLr for this function was found [Chapter 3]. No simulation wording was found [Chapter 12]; functional safety does rest on analytical evidence by nature, which is why the booklet treats simulation as admissible design evidence even where no standard accepts it as a replacement for a physical test [Chapter 3]. Part 4 excludes cybersecurity, whether it requires tool qualification was not found, and Part 3's environmental tests are "not the same as proving a camera, lidar or radar perception chain across visibility and weather combinations" [Chapters 3, 12, 13].
terms.why: Adding a brake command moves the product into ISO 19014's scope, so the plan needs an MPLr assignment, architecture and fault evidence, environmental qualification and software process evidence, all against editions that appear in October 2026 [Chapter 3]. The Part 5 tables are the only sourced route to reducing the per-model analysis burden when many machine models must be covered in four months [Chapter 3].

terms.title: ISO 3450 and ISO 10265 (brake performance)
terms.oneSentence: ISO 3450 and ISO 10265 are the standards that say how well the brakes of an earth-moving machine must work and how to test them, ISO 3450 for wheeled and fast rubber-tracked machines and ISO 10265 for slow crawler machines.
terms.explained:
Before anyone asks whether a machine brakes automatically, the brakes themselves must stop it. ISO 3450:2011 (edition 4, confirmed 2022) specifies minimum service, secondary and parking brake performance and tests for wheeled earth-moving machines and rubber-tracked machines with a top speed of 20 km/h or more; purpose-built underground mining machines are covered only by an annex of modifications [Chapters 3, 8]. ISO 10265:2008 (confirmed 2025) covers crawler machines at 20 km/h or less, whose tracks spread the load over a long contact patch and stop differently [Chapter 8].

From a secondary technical article, the booklet reports that ISO 3450 tests at 32 km/h or 80 percent of maximum speed and sets formula-based stopping limits by machine type, for example `v^2 / 44 + 0.1 (32 - v)` for rigid and articulated dumpers under 32 t, where v is the test speed in km/h and the result is in meters; these formulas should be checked against the standard [Chapter 3]. One definition is firm: stopping distance runs from the start of brake-control actuation to standstill, so it includes brake-system response time but excludes operator reaction time [Chapter 8]. These are physical tests; no simulation wording was found, and neither standard gives a number of calibration stops that would let a braking model be trusted across 100 or more site types [Chapters 3, 8]. ISO 17757 requires autonomous machines to pass the same physical braking tests in manual and autonomous mode [Chapter 10].
terms.why: ISO 21815-3's CxS distance (its required collision-system distance) is built on real stopping distance, so ISO 3450 brake data per machine model is an input to the collision-avoidance calculation [Chapter 3]. Passing ISO 3450 proves nothing about perception, and excellent perception cannot rescue a brake plant that fails its own stopping requirements; on gravel, mud, ice and grades of 10 percent or more, ISO 3450 is more relevant than any imported passenger-car deceleration target [Chapter 3].

terms.title: ISO 16001 and ISO 5006 (object detection, visibility aids and operator visibility)
terms.oneSentence: ISO 16001 sets performance requirements and tests for the systems that detect objects and help the operator see around an earth-moving machine, and ISO 5006 defines how the operator's own field of view is measured.
terms.explained:
ISO 16001:2017 (edition 2, confirmed 2023; also EN ISO 16001:2017 in Europe and AS ISO 16001:2020 in Australia) is "the only off-road standard found with hard detection and warning numbers" [Chapter 3]. It covers object detection systems (ODS) and visibility aids such as cameras and mirrors on ISO 6165 machines. It is about warning, not braking.

Its numbers: detection time not more than 300 ms; detection "unambiguously with an uninterrupted sequence of the signal"; an audible warning at least 3 dB above ambient noise, preferably at 500 to 3,400 Hz; a flashing red light within a 120 degree arc as the most severe visual warning; no warnings by vibration alone; self-check at start-up and continuous fault monitoring; deactivation only by "two or more separate and distinct actions"; electromagnetic compatibility to ISO 13766. False signals from fog, snow, rain, wind and dust "should be minimized", a "should" with no number [Chapter 3]. The test body is "a person or a standard measuring unit representative of a person", sized in technology annexes for CCTV, radar, ultrasonic, transponder, electromagnetic transceiver, surround view and vision systems; there is no lidar annex, and the detection zone test is a physical test on the machine or a representative configuration [Chapter 3].

ISO 5006 is the standard for measuring the operator's field of view from the cab and mapping blind areas. The booklet lists it as not verified [Chapter 3] but cites ISO 5006 and ISO 16001 visibility-type methods, with the small-cylinder method of UN R159, as the geometric approach that a digital twin of each machine can reproduce to compute coverage and blind zones before hardware arrives [Chapter 7].
terms.why: ISO 16001 supplies the only hard off-road numbers for detection latency and warnings and the only per-technology test annexes, so the booklet's plan runs its annex tests for each candidate sensor technology [Chapter 3]. Its gaps matter as much: no lidar annex, no quantified weather conditions and no false-alarm rate, so that evidence must be argued by the manufacturer [Chapter 3].

terms.title: ISO 17757 and ISO 19296 (autonomous machine safety and underground mining machines)
terms.oneSentence: ISO 17757 is the safety standard for autonomous and semi-autonomous earth-moving and mining machine systems, and ISO 19296 is the general safety standard for mobile machines that work underground.
terms.explained:
ISO 17757:2019 (edition 2, confirmed) applies to autonomous and semi-autonomous machine systems (ASAMS): machines, infrastructure, hardware and software. It requires the safety-related parts of their control systems to meet appropriate functional safety performance, notes that electronic commands control brakes and steering on such machines, and uses the idea of a "defined functional environment" within which the system is meant to operate [Chapters 1, 3]. Its braking and steering tests are physical, run in manual and autonomous mode under ISO 3450 and ISO 10265 [Chapter 10]. Whether it applies here is unclear: function-specific automated features are outside its scope unless used as part of an ASAMS, so "an isolated automatic-braking function on an operator-driven machine should not automatically be claimed to fall under it" [Chapter 3]. No simulation wording was found [Chapter 12].

ISO 19296:2018 gives general safety and foreseeable-misuse requirements for mobile machines working underground. ISO 21815-1 cites it to define the underground machines in its scope; it is "not a stand-alone collision-avoidance performance protocol" [Chapter 3]. For mining machines outside the ISO 6165 definition, ISO 19014 should not simply be assumed to apply; ISO 19296 and generic standards may apply by contract or jurisdiction [Chapter 3].
terms.why: An operator-driven machine with an intervention function sits in a gray zone between ISO 21815 (collision avoidance) and ISO 17757 (autonomy). The booklet lists this among its open uncertainties and asks that applicable standards be settled early by a qualified functional-safety specialist [Chapters 3, 12]. ISO 17757's "defined functional environment" is the off-road cousin of the operational design domain used for staged release [Chapter 1].

terms.title: ISO 6165 and ISO 20474 / EN 474 (classification and general safety of earth-moving machinery)
terms.oneSentence: ISO 6165 defines which machines count as earth-moving machinery, and ISO 20474 and its European twin EN 474 set the general safety requirements that every such machine must meet.
terms.explained:
ISO 6165 is a vocabulary standard that names and classifies earth-moving machines (loaders, excavators, dozers, dumpers, graders). Its importance is indirect: ISO 21815-1, ISO 16001 and ISO 19014 all apply to "machines as defined in ISO 6165", so whether a mining machine is inside ISO 6165 decides which rules reach it [Chapter 3].

ISO 20474-1:2017 and its machine-specific Parts 2 to 15 give baseline safety requirements for earth-moving machinery. Collision avoidance is not their specialized purpose; they sit alongside ISO 21815 and ISO 19014 rather than serving as the acceptance standard for automatic braking [Chapter 3]. EN 474 is the European version, in the 2022 family (EN 474-1 plus machine-specific parts), and is a machine-specific type-C standard [Chapter 3].

EN 474's legal role is why it recurs. In Great Britain, a notice of 8 August 2026 listed the EN 474:2022 family as designated standards, giving a presumption of conformity under the Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008, though "not an automatic-braking performance matrix"; the booklet notes a small uncertainty about the notice number [Chapter 3]. Whether EN 474 will be harmonized under the European Union's new Machinery Regulation was not verified, since the list was still being prepared in 2026 [Chapter 3].
terms.why: Compliance with EN 474 will be part of the machine's declaration but does not answer the automatic-braking question; that evidence must come from ISO 21815, ISO 19014 and the safety case [Chapter 3]. ISO 6165 decides scope, so a project spanning surface and underground machines must check, machine by machine, which standards apply.

terms.title: ISO 15998 and ISO 13766 (withdrawn control-system standard and EMC)
terms.oneSentence: ISO 15998 was the former functional-safety standard for electronic machine-control systems on earth-moving machinery, withdrawn in 2022 and replaced by ISO 19014, and ISO 13766 is the standard for electromagnetic compatibility of such machines.
terms.explained:
ISO 15998:2008 ("Machine-control systems using electronic components, performance criteria and tests for functional safety") and its companion ISO/TS 15998-2:2012 were withdrawn on 14 June 2022 and replaced by the ISO 19014 series [Chapter 3]. Older documents still refer to it: ISO 16001:2017 points to ISO 15998 for environmental conditions and notes that "ISO 19014-3 can be used as an alternative" [Chapter 3]. A reader who sees ISO 15998 in a supplier document should treat it as dated and ask for the ISO 19014 equivalent.

ISO 13766 covers electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) for earth-moving machinery: the electronics must neither emit radio interference that disturbs other equipment nor be disturbed by interference from outside. ISO 16001 requires an object detection system to meet it, and the South African mining industry's MOSH laboratory phase lists EMC testing among its TRL4 bench tests [Chapters 3, 7].
terms.why: Withdrawn standards are a trap in a fast project: an old data sheet may cite ISO 15998, which no longer exists [Chapter 3]. EMC matters because a brake request travels on an electronic network and a radar shares the air with other radios; the booklet notes radio-frequency coexistence as one reason a factory emergency brake was disabled in an on-road case [Chapter 13].

terms.title: ISO 12100, ISO 13849, IEC 62061 and IEC 61508 (the machinery and functional-safety family)
terms.oneSentence: These four standards form the general toolkit for making any machine safe: ISO 12100 for assessing and reducing risk, ISO 13849 and IEC 62061 for the safety of control systems on machinery, and IEC 61508 as the parent standard for electronic safety systems in every industry.
terms.explained:
ISO 12100 is the basic ("type-A") safety-of-machinery standard: identify hazards, estimate and evaluate risk, reduce it first by design, then by safeguards, then by information for use. Machine-specific standards hang from it; ISO 21815-3 is "a type-C standard under ISO 12100" [Chapter 3].

ISO 13849-1:2023 (edition 4) is the generic machinery method for safety-related parts of control systems, including software, using the Performance Level (PL) scale. It "does not itself assign the performance level required for this collision function"; for ISO 6165 machines ISO 19014 is the sector framework, but ISO 13849 stays relevant for subsystems developed generically or machines outside the earth-moving scope [Chapter 3]. ISO 13849-2:2012 covers validation and lists simulation among validation methods and "software simulation of faults"; a draft of edition 3 was issued in 2026 [Chapter 12]. IEC 62061:2021, from the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), is the parallel machinery standard on the Safety Integrity Level (SIL) scale; the booklet lists it as current but not reviewed [Chapter 12].

IEC 61508 is the parent: a seven-part standard for electrical, electronic and programmable safety systems in any industry, from which ISO 26262 (cars), ISO 13849 and IEC 62061 (machinery) and ISO 25119 (agriculture) descend. The booklet uses two of its ideas. IEC 61508-3:2010 defines software tool classes T1 to T3, a reference for how much a tool such as a simulator must be qualified when its output is relied on [Chapter 12]. Its "proven in use" route lets a reused element claim credit from field history under strict conditions, with higher confidence demanded than the comparable ISO 26262 clause [Chapter 10]. Neither was verified in detail [Chapter 13].
terms.why: The booklet's safety-case skeleton maps the intervention chain to ISO 13849 or IEC 62061 where ISO 19014 does not reach, and the intervention path needs a performance-level or integrity assignment plus fault testing [Chapters 1, 9]. If simulation results become safety evidence, the simulator is a tool whose errors can hide defects, which is what tool qualification addresses [Chapter 13]. The warning system's field history does not transfer to the braking function as "proven in use", because adding braking changes the item [Chapter 10].

terms.title: IEC 61496, IEC TS 62998, ISO 3691-4 and ISO 18497 (safety sensors, driverless industrial trucks and agricultural automation)
terms.oneSentence: These are neighboring standards from other sectors: IEC 61496 and IEC TS 62998 certify safety sensors in factories, ISO 3691-4 covers driverless warehouse trucks, and ISO 18497 covers automated farm machines, including how to test their obstacle detection.
terms.explained:
IEC 61496 is the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) series for electro-sensitive protective equipment: light curtains, laser scanners and, in IEC TS 61496-5:2023, radar protective devices that stop a factory machine when someone enters a zone. It gives sensors an established certification basis, but the radar part states that it "does not consider the aspects of a moving RPD application", and a vendor's use of IEC TS 62998-1 (a technical specification on safety-related sensors) for a radar in mobile outdoor use is a vendor claim. Component certification "does not deliver system-level performance on a moving outdoor machine" [Chapter 1].

ISO 3691-4:2023 covers driverless industrial trucks and their systems; a draft of edition 3 was in progress and no simulation wording was found [Chapter 12].

ISO 18497:2024 is the closest published cousin of this project's function. Revised in July 2024 into four parts for partially automated, semi-autonomous and autonomous agricultural machinery (design principles, obstacle protection systems, autonomous operating zones, verification and validation), it starts from the premise that no detection technology works perfectly in all conditions and names four failure categories: failure to detect, late detection, incorrect classification and localization error [Chapter 2]. Part 4 includes braking, steering and person or obstacle detection tests, defines test objects in Annex C, and lists "Simulation (virtual evaluation of functions and performance)" among verification methods alongside inspection, measurement, test and analysis, "the closest off-road standard support found" for simulation, though no evidence was found that it authorizes replacing any share of field tests [Chapters 2, 7, 12].
terms.why: ISO 18497 shows an off-road sector writing perception test objects and simulation into a standard, and the booklet suggests building the scenario catalog around ISO 21815-3 risk areas and ISO 18497-2's four failure categories [Chapters 1, 2]. The sensor standards show the limit of buying certified parts: a certified radar still has to be proved as part of a moving machine in dust and rain [Chapter 1].
aliases: IEC 61496, IEC TS 62998, ISO 3691-4 and ISO 18497

terms.title: ISO 21448, ISO 26262 and the AI safety standards (ISO/PAS 8800, ISO/IEC TR 5469, ISO/IEC 42001, 23894, 24029)
terms.oneSentence: ISO 26262 and ISO 21448 are the road-vehicle standards for functional safety and for safety when sensors and software misjudge a situation without failing, and the ISO/PAS 8800 and ISO/IEC documents are the first, mostly unfinished, attempts to write standards for machine learning in safety functions.
terms.explained:
ISO 26262 is the functional-safety standard for electronic systems in road vehicles, with its own risk scale, the Automotive Safety Integrity Level (ASIL). ISO 21448:2022, known as SOTIF (Safety of the Intended Functionality), deals with harm that occurs when nothing is broken but the system misreads the world, for example a camera blinded by glare. The booklet is firm that both "are road-vehicle standards and do not apply by scope", and that the Machine Performance Level scale of ISO 19014 is not the ASIL scale [Chapter 3]. They remain useful as method: the booklet's safety-case skeleton borrows ISO 21448's triggering-condition logic for perception, and ISO 26262-8 is the reference for tool qualification (clause 11) and "proven in use" (clause 14), the latter resting on a 70 percent confidence level and not carrying the warning system's history over to the braking function [Chapters 1, 10, 12].

The artificial intelligence (AI) documents are younger. ISO/PAS 8800:2024 (December 2024) tailors ISO 26262 for AI in road vehicles and is road-vehicle only. ISO/IEC TR 5469:2024 (January 2024) is guidance on AI and functional safety, "not a requirements document". ISO/IEC CD TS 22440-1, -2 and -3 were committee drafts in 2026, so publication much before 2027 or 2028 is unlikely. ISO/IEC 42001 (AI management systems), ISO/IEC 23894 (AI risk management) and ISO/IEC 24029 (robustness of neural networks) are published ISO and IEC documents that the booklet lists, with UL 4600 (from Underwriters Laboratories) and the European standards bodies' committee CEN/CENELEC JTC 21, as not verified [Chapter 3].

The key finding is a gap: "Off-road and mining standards with machine-learning clauses: not found." ISO 19014 has no separate acceptance process for machine-learning perception, so training-set coverage, distribution shift, retraining, non-determinism, confidence calibration and change control "must be treated as additional safety-case subjects rather than closed by ISO 19014 compliance" [Chapter 3]. Legally, the European Union's Machinery Regulation pulls machine-learning safety components into notified-body assessment from 20 January 2027, and AI-specific machinery requirements are expected by 2 August 2028 through delegated acts not yet adopted in October 2026 [Chapter 3].
terms.why: If a neural network decides when to brake, no standard yet tells the manufacturer how to validate it for an off-road machine, and the road-vehicle documents cannot be claimed by scope. The booklet's advice is to borrow their structure as method, keep the machine-learning subjects explicit in the safety case, and consider a deterministic safety channel so that less has to be proved about the learned part; one view keeps machine learning out of the safety function entirely, the other accepts it under ISO/PAS 8800-style assurance [Chapters 1, 3].
aliases: ISO 21448, ISO 26262 and the AI safety standards

terms.title: ISO 34501 to 34505, ISO/PAS 34506, ISO/TS 5083 and ISO 19206 (scenario-based evaluation and test targets)
terms.oneSentence: The ISO 3450x series and ISO/TS 5083 are road-vehicle standards for describing, sorting and choosing the test scenarios of an automated driving system, and ISO 19206 defines the dummies and foam cars that stand in for people and vehicles in crash-avoidance tests.
terms.explained:
When a car can drive itself you cannot test "everything", so the industry wrote standards for organizing the test space. ISO 34501:2022 gives the vocabulary; ISO 34502:2022 the scenario-based safety evaluation framework; ISO 34503:2023 how to describe an operational design domain (ODD), the set of conditions a system is meant to handle; ISO 34504:2024 how to categorize scenarios with tags; ISO 34505:2025 how to evaluate and prioritize test cases, with a clause on the validity of simulation in virtual testing [Chapters 5, 9]. ISO/PAS 34506, on qualification of virtual test environments, was a draft in October 2026 and "should not be treated as a finished standard" [Chapter 10]. ISO/TS 5083:2025 covers design, verification and validation of automated driving systems [Chapter 12]. All are "explicitly scoped to road vehicles and limited-access highways"; they are "methodological precedent, not off-road compliance evidence", and they establish no physical-to-virtual ratio [Chapters 1, 10]. The series carries the three-level scenario idea from the German PEGASUS project (functional, logical, concrete), which the booklet adopts for the off-road catalog with ISO 21815 and the mining industry group EMESRT's storyboards supplying the content [Chapter 9].

ISO 19206 specifies test targets: ISO 19206-2:2018 the pedestrian dummy and ISO 19206-4:2020 the bicyclist target, used by UN R131 and the Euro NCAP consumer rating program [Chapter 3]. Their value off-road is the principle, not the objects: surrogates must represent persons in protective clothing, light vehicles under the nose of a haul truck, machines and fixed obstacles, with camera appearance, radar cross-section, lidar reflectivity and ultrasonic response matched to each sensor [Chapter 3].
terms.why: The structure transfers and the content does not. The booklet uses the ISO 3450x layering and ODD taxonomy to organize the off-road scenario space while warning that road attributes dominate and off-road taxonomies are immature [Chapter 9]. ISO 19206 shows that standardized targets are a precondition for comparable tests, and no off-road equivalent exists [Chapter 3].
aliases: ISO 34501 to 34505, ISO/PAS 34506, ISO/TS 5083 and ISO 19206

terms.title: ISO 18571, ISO 16290 and ISO 25119
terms.oneSentence: ISO 18571 defines a score for how closely two curves agree, ISO 16290 defines the technology readiness levels, and ISO 25119 is the functional-safety standard for control systems on farm machines.
terms.explained:
ISO 18571 is a road-vehicle standard giving an objective way to compare two signals over time, for example a measured deceleration curve from a track test and the simulated curve for the same run. It combines sub-scores for corridor, phase, magnitude and slope into one number, often called the "ISO score". The Euro NCAP consumer rating program's virtual-testing protocol requires manufacturers to qualify their simulation against physical tests using "the ISO score and defined KPIs", and an April 2026 test-house demonstration correlated a virtual emergency-braking setup against proving-ground tests with ISO 18571 metrics [Chapters 2, 3]. The booklet's wider point is that peaks alone mislead: in one worked example the peaks differed by 0.3 percent while the time-history error was 60.4 percent [Chapter 10].

ISO 16290:2013 standardizes the technology readiness levels (TRL), the one-to-nine maturity scale from basic principles (TRL 1) to proven in operation (TRL 9), which originated at NASA [Chapter 12]. The South African mining industry's MOSH regime uses TRL4 and TRL7 as stage gates, and the booklet uses TRLs for critical-technology maturity only, not as a measure of a whole system [Chapters 3, 12].

ISO 25119 is the agricultural counterpart of ISO 13849 and ISO 19014, functional safety for control systems on tractors and farm machinery; the booklet lists it as current but not reviewed [Chapters 3, 12].
terms.why: ISO 18571 is the kind of metric a correlation test needs if simulation is to be presented in the Euro NCAP manner [Chapter 3]. TRLs supply the vocabulary of the only published independent verification regime for mining automatic braking [Chapter 3]. ISO 25119 is a reminder that neighboring sectors have their own functional-safety standards, which may apply by contract.

terms.title: Systems and software engineering standards (ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288, 29119, 42010, 15026-2, IEEE 1012, ISO 31000, IEC 31010)
terms.oneSentence: These are the general standards for how to run an engineering project: how to organize a system's life cycle, document tests, describe an architecture, write an assurance case, verify and validate, and manage risk.
terms.explained:
None of these mentions a collision or a brake; they are the scaffolding a safety program is built on, and the booklet cites them as documented practice. ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2023 defines system life-cycle processes and, with the handbooks of the International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE) and NASA, is the backbone of verification and validation planning; IEEE 1012-2016 is the standard for system, software and hardware verification and validation [Chapter 12]. ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119-3:2021 defines test documentation (plan, design, case and completion reports) and Part 4:2021 test-design techniques; they have "no collision-avoidance content" but supply the discipline of separating test processes, techniques and documentation [Chapter 9].

ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022 covers architecture description, the idea of several views matched to the viewer's role rather than one universal diagram; the booklet applies it to the simulation toolchain, marking which elements are real, modeled, emulated or substituted [Chapter 12]. ISO/IEC/IEEE 15026-2:2022 standardizes the assurance case, the structured argument from claims through evidence [Chapter 12]. ISO 31000:2018 and IEC 31010:2019 document risk-management practice and risk-assessment techniques, the basis of the risk register; the booklet notes that outcome evidence for risk registers is thin [Chapter 12].
terms.why: The program's final question is evidentiary: can a safety board trust a virtual result enough to support a safety decision? These standards supply the structure for an evidence plan that traces each claim to its evidence, method, acceptance criterion, owner and gate [Chapter 12]. They do not say what to test; they make sure nothing tested is untraceable.

terms.title: Rail and aviation standards (EN 50126 to EN 50129, EN 50716, EN 14363, DO-178C, DO-330, DO-385, ED-256)
terms.oneSentence: These are the safety and simulation standards of two industries, railways and aviation, that have accepted simulation as evidence for longer than road or off-road vehicles have.
terms.explained:
Railways. EN 50126, EN 50128 and EN 50129 are the European railway standards for reliability and safety management, software and electronic signaling; EN 50716:2023 is the current railway software standard and successor to EN 50128. The booklet lists all four as not verified [Chapter 10]. EN 14363:2016+A2:2022, the standard for accepting the running behavior of railway vehicles, was studied closely: its Annex T covers simulation of on-track tests and Annex U extension of acceptance to vehicles of the same basic design. In the related practice, at least 24 simulation-versus-measurement comparisons are drawn from at least 12 track sections and validation limits are set on the whole set of deviations; the European Union Agency for Railways' guidance describes modifying a validated model to represent a changed vehicle and using it as evidence, and the DynoTRAIN research behind the method compared many models and tools against measurements [Chapter 10].

Aviation. DO-178C is the software standard for airborne systems and DO-330 its companion on qualifying software tools whose output is relied on without further checking; DO-330 "does not address whether a physics model is valid", and both are listed as not verified [Chapter 10]. DO-385 and its European twin ED-256 are the minimum operational performance standards for the Airborne Collision Avoidance System X (ACAS X), the new aircraft collision-avoidance system, published in October 2018 by the aviation standards bodies RTCA and EUROCAE; the system was validated largely by simulating encounters equivalent to billions of flight hours [Chapter 2].
terms.why: Rail gives the booklet its clearest model of "validation-domain extension by similarity plus bridging evidence": a family model validated at the corners of the envelope, with a documented difference and targeted extra tests when a vehicle changes, which is the shape of argument needed to cover many machine models and sensor positions [Chapter 10]. Aviation gives the tool-qualification idea and a precedent of statistical simulation accepted by standards bodies and authorities after years of building the underlying models [Chapters 2, 10].

terms.title: UL 4600 (autonomous products safety case)
terms.oneSentence: UL 4600 is a standard that tells a developer what a complete safety case for an autonomous product must cover, in the form of long lists of questions and claims to be answered with evidence.
terms.explained:
Published by Underwriters Laboratories (UL), UL 4600 "Standard for Safety for the Evaluation of Autonomous Products" is in its third edition, dated 17 March 2023 [Chapter 12]. It sets no performance numbers and prescribes no tests. It takes the safety-case approach: the developer states a top-level claim ("this product is acceptably safe for its intended use"), decomposes it into sub-claims, and supports each with arguments and evidence, while the standard's question lists let an assessor check nothing was skipped. The booklet groups it with the assurance-case standard ISO/IEC/IEEE 15026-2 and Goal Structuring Notation as structured ways to organize such an argument, and uses its question lists as one format for presenting a plan to reviewers [Chapter 12].

Its limits are noted too. UL 4600 was written for autonomous road products, appears among standards "not verified in this research" on simulation acceptance, and is among the artificial intelligence (AI) documents whose applicability was not checked [Chapters 3, 5, 10]. Safety cases have critics as well as proponents, and the booklet records both [Chapter 12].
terms.why: No regulation spells out acceptance for off-road automatic braking, so a structured safety case is the instrument that ties simulation, physical tests and analysis to claims an assessor can judge. UL 4600 is the most developed published template for such a case on a product with perception and machine learning [Chapters 1, 12].

terms.title: UN regulations (UN R152, R131, R159, R171) and UNECE WP.29, GRVA, VMAD and NATM
terms.oneSentence: The UN regulations are the shared road-vehicle approval rules written at the United Nations in Geneva, R131 and R152 for emergency braking on trucks and cars, R159 for moving-off information and R171 for driver assistance, and WP.29, GRVA, VMAD and NATM are the forum, working party, expert group and method that produce them.
terms.explained:
Most countries outside North America approve road vehicles against regulations agreed at the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE). The forum that adopts them is WP.29, the World Forum for Harmonization of Vehicle Regulations; its working party on automated, autonomous and connected vehicles is GRVA; and an informal group under it, VMAD (Validation Method for Automated Driving), developed the New Assessment/Test Method (NATM) [Chapters 2, 10]. All are road-vehicle bodies, and the booklet marks everything from them as "on-road evidence" that does not regulate a quarry loader or haul truck [Chapter 3].

UN R131 covers advanced emergency braking on heavy vehicles. Its 02 series, in force 4 January 2023, requires a warning at least 0.8 s before emergency braking, a braking demand of at least 4 m/s², tabulated impact speeds, a child pedestrian target to ISO 19206-2, a false-reaction test between two parked cars 4.5 m apart at 50 km/h, and no more than 10 percent failed runs in robustness testing [Chapter 3]. UN R152 covers cars and vans, with car-to-car tests at 10 to 60 km/h and pedestrian tests at 20 to 60 km/h; supplements adopted by WP.29 in 2025 permit virtual testing as an alternative to some physical tests, with the number of physical confirmation tests "defined in agreement between" manufacturer and authority, after a January 2024 GRVA paper found an earlier proposal short of the full credibility framework [Chapters 3, 10]. UN R159 (2021) covers moving-off information systems that warn truck drivers of pedestrians and cyclists in front; the booklet cites its small-cylinder visibility method and road users moving at 3 to 5 km/h [Chapter 7]. UN R171 (2025) covers driver control assistance systems: validation "may include the use of virtual testing", in which case "a credibility assessment as described in Annex 5 shall be provided to the Type Approval Authority", with the manufacturer demonstrating the tool's scope, its validity for the scenario and the toolchain's validation [Chapter 3].

NATM has five pillars (audit and assessment, virtual testing, track testing, real-world testing, in-service monitoring) and a credibility framework covering toolchain management, analysis, verification, validation and uncertainty, with the rule that "the outcome of the credibility assessment will define the envelope in which the virtual tool can be used" [Chapters 10, 12]. The European Union's Implementing Regulation 2022/1426 on automated-vehicle approval carries a related annex and states that simulation "shall not be a substitute for physical tests" [Chapter 13].
terms.why: These are the most developed rules anywhere for accepting simulation as safety evidence, and the booklet adopts their structure: qualify the toolchain, state the envelope, keep physical tests as the default and spot-check [Chapters 3, 10]. Their content does not transfer (road geometry, car targets, asphalt and the type-approval regime itself are absent off-road), and no off-road body has adopted an equivalent [Chapter 3]. The on-road false-reaction tests are the model for off-road false-activation tests with berms, dust plumes and parked machines [Chapter 3].
aliases: United Nations Economic Commission for Europe

terms.title: FMVSS 127, NHTSA, NTSB and IIHS
terms.oneSentence: FMVSS 127 is the United States rule requiring automatic emergency braking on new cars, NHTSA is the agency that writes such rules and investigates defects, NTSB is the independent board that investigates accidents, and IIHS is the insurer-funded institute that tests and rates vehicles.
terms.explained:
In the United States, road-vehicle safety rules are Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS), written by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA); manufacturers self-certify to them and NHTSA checks afterward. FMVSS No. 127 is the automatic emergency braking (AEB) rule for light vehicles up to 4,536 kg: final rule 9 May 2024, compliance from 1 September 2029. It requires no-contact avoidance of a lead vehicle up to 62 mph, pedestrian AEB in daylight and darkness, and forward-collision warning, with two false-activation tests, a steel trench plate at 80 km/h and a pass-through between parked vehicles, failing if peak deceleration exceeds manual braking by 0.25 g or more [Chapter 3]. Car makers petitioned against it citing false-activation risk and sued in January 2025; in March 2026 the Department of Transportation said it was preparing to extend the lead time by two years; and NHTSA rejected judging compliance over several trials instead of each trial, a debate the booklet expects off-road too [Chapters 2, 3].

NHTSA also runs defect investigations in two stages, Preliminary Evaluation (PE) and Engineering Analysis (EA). The booklet's record of unnecessary braking comes from these: Honda, Nissan, Tesla (closed June 2026 with no defect finding) and Daimler heavy trucks [Chapter 2]. Its New Car Assessment Program adds consumer ratings with AEB tests at 40 to 80 km/h [Chapter 3].

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is independent of NHTSA and investigates accidents rather than writing rules. Its 2019 report on the 2018 Uber automated-vehicle fatality found that the factory emergency brake had been disabled, that the system recognized the emergency 1.2 s before impact while planned braking was held back by a one-second action suppression, and that safety risk management and culture were deficient [Chapters 2, 13].

The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) is funded by insurers and publishes crash tests and effectiveness studies; the booklet cites its findings that rear automatic braking with camera and sensors cut backing crash involvement by 78 percent and that 93 percent of drivers keep AEB switched on [Chapter 4].
terms.why: FMVSS 127's false-activation tests and 0.25 g limit are the clearest published definition of an unacceptable unnecessary brake, which no off-road document provides [Chapter 3]. NHTSA's investigations show that false braking, not missed detection, is the dominant documented field failure of production AEB [Chapter 2]. The NTSB case shows that intervention-timing decisions and organizational oversight become central evidence after an accident [Chapter 13].

terms.title: Euro NCAP and its virtual-testing protocol
terms.oneSentence: Euro NCAP is the European consumer program that crash-tests cars and awards star ratings, and its virtual-testing protocol is the first published procedure under which an outside assessor accepts a manufacturer's simulation results for crash avoidance, subject to correlation and random physical checks.
terms.explained:
The European New Car Assessment Programme (Euro NCAP) is not a regulator. It is an independent consumer-assessment body backed by governments, motoring clubs and insurers; its stars are not legal approval and "its score is not regulatory evidence for any machine" [Chapters 2, 3]. For 2026 to 2028 it made what it calls its largest overhaul since 2009, adding robustness testing with varied speed and offset, real-world driving assessment prompted by complaints about "annoying warnings or intrusive interventions", and virtual testing with spot checks; the 2026 protocols hold more than 1,200 scenarios and use ISO 19206 targets [Chapters 2, 3].

The virtual-testing supporting protocol (version 1.00, March 2025, in force January 2026) works in steps. The manufacturer submits a simulation dossier of vehicle, sensor, target and environment models, qualifies its simulation in-house against physical tests using "the ISO score and defined KPIs calculated using the Euro NCAP scripts", and submits color-coded predictions for the whole scenario grid. Euro NCAP physically tests randomly selected grid cells. The virtual results are accepted for a scenario cluster only if at least 75 percent of the verification tests in that cluster meet the qualification criteria; otherwise the dossier is rejected for that cluster and the manufacturer may re-simulate or test physically [Chapter 3]. Virtual sensor positions, opening angles and ranges must match the physical car, function logic must be similar, and targets and environment models must match the physical tests [Chapter 3].

Two cautions. The protocol allows "perfect perception" to be assumed, "which limits its value as a precedent for sensor robustness": it cannot establish that a camera works in dust or glare [Chapter 3]. And several of its tolerances are printed in square brackets as provisional, so they should not be copied into an off-road specification as final thresholds [Chapter 3]. Per-manufacturer build time was not found [Chapter 2].
terms.why: This is "the clearest collision-avoidance example of simulation evidence accepted by an external assessor" [Chapter 2]. The booklet recommends presenting the project's simulation in the Euro NCAP manner (qualify the models, predict the grid, let an independent party pick physical spot checks, requalify after material software, sensor-position or machine changes) and offers its governance split, developer predicts and independent organization verifies, as a template for the internal safety board [Chapters 2, 3]. The 75 percent criterion and the perfect-perception assumption are both reasons it is a structure to borrow, not a number to copy [Chapter 3].

terms.title: EU Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, the AI Act, the Product Liability Directive and the Data Act
terms.oneSentence: These four European Union laws set the legal ground for a machine sold in Europe from 2027: the Machinery Regulation governs its safety and conformity, the AI Act and its 2026 amendment govern artificial intelligence in it, the Product Liability Directive governs who pays when it causes harm, and the Data Act governs access to the data it produces.
terms.explained:
The Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, adopted 14 June 2023, applies from 20 January 2027 and replaces the Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC, which covers machines placed on the market until 19 January 2027 [Chapter 3]. For a product arriving in mid-2027 it is "the core market-access law". It requires risk reduction, safe and reliable control systems, protection against corruption (cybersecurity) and technical documentation, and contains no automatic-braking test matrix [Chapter 3]. Three changes matter here. Annex I Part A lists "safety components with fully or partially self-evolving behaviour using machine learning approaches ensuring safety functions" and machinery embedding them, both needing a notified body. Annex II makes "software ensuring safety functions" a safety component. And it reportedly requires logging of safety-related decisions and software versions for some machinery [Chapters 3, 7]. Whether a frozen trained model is "self-evolving" is disputed and unsettled, the harmonized-standards list was still being prepared in 2026, and no wording accepting simulation as evidence was found [Chapters 3, 12].

The AI Act (EU) 2024/1689 is the general law on artificial intelligence. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the "Digital Omnibus on AI", adopted 8 July 2026 and in force 27 July 2026, rewrote its timeline and amended the Machinery Regulation directly: high-risk obligations for AI embedded in products now apply from 2 August 2028; machinery is taken out of direct AI Act high-risk classification; AI health and safety requirements for machinery are to arrive through delegated acts under the Machinery Regulation by the same date; and a "safety function" is defined as one that prevents or mitigates risks to health, safety or property. Those delegated acts had not been adopted by 1 October 2026, and the booklet warns that machine learning cannot be treated as "unregulated until 2028", because the general machinery and functional-safety duties exist in 2027 [Chapter 3].

The Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853 applies to products placed on the market after 9 December 2026. Software, including updates, is a product; courts may order disclosure of evidence; and a defect is presumed if the defendant fails to disclose or where technical complexity makes proof "excessively difficult" [Chapters 12, 13]. The booklet's product-liability review concludes that "the assumptions and gaps of a disclosed simulation safety case become the claimant's exhibit" [Chapter 13]. The EU Data Act gives users rights to data from connected products; its application dates, and those of the Cyber Resilience Act, were not verified [Chapter 13].
terms.why: Three dates fall inside the program window: 9 December 2026 (liability), 20 January 2027 (machinery) and 2 August 2028 (AI requirements for machinery) [Chapter 12]. If machine learning performs the braking function, the conservative plan budgets for a notified body from 2027 and expects machinery-specific AI rules by 2028 [Chapter 3]. Every simulation assumption in the safety case should be written as if a court will read it [Chapter 13].

terms.title: United Kingdom rules (HSE, Supply of Machinery Regulations, UKCA)
terms.oneSentence: In Great Britain the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) enforces workplace safety, the Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008 govern what machines may be sold, and UKCA is the British conformity mark that replaced CE marking after the United Kingdom left the European Union.
terms.explained:
Great Britain kept the European machinery law it already had. The Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008 (SI 2008/1597), as amended, impose general essential health and safety requirements and conformity obligations; amendments in SI 2026/867 take effect on 20 January 2027, the day the EU's new Machinery Regulation applies [Chapter 3]. In place of harmonized standards Britain has "designated standards"; the notice of 8 August 2026 designated the EN 474:2022 earth-moving machinery family. No dedicated off-road automatic-braking regime and "no UK collision-avoidance mandate" were found [Chapter 3]. Northern Ireland is different: under the Windsor Framework EU product law applies there, so one declaration route should not be assumed to cover both [Chapter 3].

UKCA (UK Conformity Assessed) is the mark placed on a product sold in Great Britain to declare compliance, the counterpart of the CE mark, with "approved bodies" as the counterpart of notified bodies. The booklet does not discuss the mark itself; it treats the British route as a parallel declaration path [Chapter 3].

The HSE is the workplace regulator that inspects sites and prosecutes after accidents. The booklet uses its statistics and guidance: in 2025/26, 126 workers were killed in Great Britain and being struck by a moving vehicle was the second most common cause with 24 deaths; HSE's workplace transport guidance says "nearly a quarter of all deaths involving Workplace transport occur during reversing"; and its quarry guidance states that "transport accounts for 40% of all accidents in quarries and 60% of all deaths" [Chapter 4]. The Quarries Regulations 1999 and HSE's quarry guidance documents were not verified [Chapter 3].
terms.why: Britain adds a second declaration, a separate standards-designation calendar and separate treatment for Northern Ireland, with no automatic-braking mandate to meet [Chapter 3]. HSE's figures are part of the evidence that reversing and workplace transport dominate the harm the system is meant to prevent [Chapter 4].

terms.title: United States rules (OSHA 29 CFR 1926.601, MSHA 30 CFR, NIOSH)
terms.oneSentence: In the United States, OSHA writes and enforces construction safety rules, MSHA does the same for mines, and NIOSH is the research institute whose studies and tests inform both; none of their rules requires automatic braking.
terms.explained:
The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) regulates construction sites. Rules 29 CFR 1926.601(b)(4) and 1926.602(a)(9)(ii) require a reverse signal alarm audible above surrounding noise, or an observer, when a machine's rear view is obstructed. OSHA interpretation letters accept alternatives: a camera can remove the "obstructed view" trigger if it truly provides a clear view, and radar warning can satisfy the rule where it warns in time. There is no numeric range and no automatic-brake mandate [Chapter 3].

The Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) regulates mines under title 30 of the Code of Federal Regulations. 30 CFR 77.410 (surface coal) requires, for loaders, trucks, graders and similar equipment, a reverse alarm or discriminating detection "using infrared, ultrasonic, radar, or another effective device", with a sensing area large enough for an endangered person to escape; lidar is not named, so it should not be called "approved" [Chapter 3]. 30 CFR 56.14132 and 57.14132 (metal and non-metal mines) require a reverse-activated alarm, alternatives or an observer. 30 CFR 75.1732 (2015) requires proximity detection on continuous mining machines underground: warn, then stop before contacting a miner, with no numeric distance after the proposed 3 ft and 5 ft values were dropped [Chapter 3]. The Safety Program for Surface Mobile Equipment rule (compliance from 17 July 2024) requires mine-specific written programs that evaluate "currently available and newly emerging feasible technologies"; it does not mandate collision avoidance, and 863 citations had been issued by April 2026 [Chapter 3]. A federal rule requiring a machine to command its own brakes after an ignored warning was not found [Chapter 3].

The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) researches rather than regulates, and the booklet relies on it heavily: its 2000 haul-truck tests defining "reliable" detection as an alarm within 200 ms, its 2007 finding that 67 percent of blind-area fatalities occurred in the rear blind area of reversing equipment, its 2022 rapid review of collision-avoidance technology and its field studies of false alarms [Chapters 1, 3, 4].
terms.why: The United States "requires warnings and risk programs, not automatic braking", and MSHA's technology-neutral wording supports arguing against the hazard rather than by sensor label [Chapter 3]. NIOSH's measurement definitions and accident analyses supply much of the booklet's evidence on what gets hit and how [Chapter 4].

terms.title: Canada and Australia rules (CSA M424, WHS laws, NSW Resources Regulator, RSHQ QGN 27 and QGN 33, DMIRS)
terms.oneSentence: Canada regulates mining province by province with CSA M424 as the relevant national standard, and Australia uses model Work Health and Safety laws plus state mining regulators in New South Wales, Queensland and Western Australia, none of which mandates automatic braking.
terms.explained:
Canada. A federal collision-avoidance or automatic-braking rule was not found; requirements are provincial. CSA M424 is the CSA Group standard series for mining machinery; the booklet did not verify it or the provincial regulations and advises a province-by-province matrix before claiming Canadian compliance [Chapter 3].

Australia. The model Work Health and Safety (WHS) Regulations bind only once a state or territory adopts them. Regulation 215 (powered mobile plant) requires, "so far as reasonably practicable", control of the risk of collision with pedestrians and other mobile plant and a warning device where collision is possible, with no prescribed braking, speed or distance; the Model Code of Practice "Managing the risks of plant in the workplace" (June 2023) is the official explanatory material [Chapter 3]. Standards Australia has adopted ISO 21815-1 as AS 21815.1:2023 (modified) and ISO 16001 as AS ISO 16001:2020; none is law unless incorporated [Chapter 3].

State regulators add guidance. The New South Wales (NSW) Resources Regulator issued a discussion paper on vehicle interaction controls (September 2023) and is developing a draft Technical Reference Guide [Chapter 3]. Its 2023 paper reported "no meaningful reduction in the number of incidents being reported year on year" and no proximity technology in NSW mining yet "reliably capable of correctly discriminating between potentially hazardous or spurious conditions" [Chapter 4]. Resources Safety and Health Queensland (RSHQ) publishes guidance notes: QGN 27 on collision prevention (2017) states that 26 percent of mineral mine and quarry fatalities from 1998 to 2016 were collisions, gives a worked stopping example (22.2 m covered at 40 km/h during a 2 s reaction-plus-delay period) and warns of a "false sense of protection" from idealized detection zones; QGN 33 on autonomous mobile machinery says of itself that it "is not a Recognised Standard" [Chapters 3, 4, 7]. In Western Australia the mines regulator (DMIRS, now DEMIRS) followed up the 2019 autonomous-truck collisions at Fortescue and BHP sites; its codes were not verified [Chapters 2, 3].
terms.why: Australia is a major mining market with risk-based duties, modified adoptions of the ISO standards and active regulator guidance, but "no prescriptive collision-avoidance mandate was found", so the destination state's WHS adoption and mine legislation must be checked site by site [Chapter 3]. The NSW and Queensland material is also evidence of the industry's unsolved false-alarm problem [Chapter 4].

terms.title: South Africa rules (MHSA, DMRE, Chapter 8 regulations, MOSH, CPS verification specifications)
terms.oneSentence: South Africa is the only country the booklet found that legally requires automatic slow-down and braking on mining machines, through regulations under the Mine Health and Safety Act, with the industry's MOSH specifications and independent test regime filling in the numbers the law leaves out.
terms.explained:
The Mine Health and Safety Act 29 of 1996 (MHSA) is the governing law, administered by the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy (DMRE, since renamed the Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources). Its Regulations Chapter 8 covers machinery, and Regulation 8.10 covers trackless mobile machinery (TMM). The regulations were promulgated on 27 February 2015, but the two critical sub-regulations, 8.10.1.2(b) for machine-to-pedestrian risk underground and 8.10.2.1(b) for machine-to-machine risk, commenced only on 21 December 2022 by Government Gazette No. 47790, Notice 2908, with no transitional period [Chapters 2, 3]. They require diesel-powered TMMs to detect and warn automatically and, "in the event where no action is taken to prevent potential collision", to be retarded "to a safe speed where after the brakes... are automatically applied", and the system "must fail to safe without human intervention" [Chapter 3]. The law sets no detection percentage, distance, false-alarm limit or stopping test, and whether battery-electric machines fall within its "diesel powered" wording is unclear [Chapter 3]. Mines must also write mandatory codes of practice that address braking systems and their testing [Chapter 3]. A 2019 task team had judged the technology immature, yet the clauses came into force; the nearly eight-year lag shows how long the industry needed [Chapters 2, 3].

The Minerals Council South Africa, through its MOSH learning hub (Mining Industry Occupational Safety and Health), wrote the engineering layer: the Surface Collision Prevention System (CPS) Functional and Technical Performance Requirements (F&TPR, Rev 1), a Requirements Verification Regime with technology readiness level (TRL) gates at TRL4 and TRL7 (11 October 2025), a Surface TMM CPS Independent Verification Test Specification (29 August 2025), a TRL7 Stage Gate specification (20 January 2026) and a fail-to-safe addendum [Chapters 1, 3]. Their numbers are the most concrete in mining: 200 m minimum detection range, a 2.5 to 3.0 s warning before intervention, stop gaps of 1.0 to 4.0 m at 10 km/h or less and 15 m plus or minus 5 m above, fail-to-safe within 500 ms, and "no false interventions and false warnings" at the TRL4 gate [Chapter 3]. Independent verification is carried out by the University of Pretoria [Chapters 2, 7]. One consultant's opinion piece questions whether the MOSH blueprint is valid unless mandated by the regulator [Chapter 3].

One acronym can confuse: MCSSA, which appears near these documents, is not a South African body but the Machine Control System Safety Analysis method of ISO 19014-1 [Chapter 3].
terms.why: South African compliance is "a design input even if South Africa is not the launch market", because it is the strongest explicit off-road automatic-braking mandate found anywhere, and the MOSH numbers with the scenarios of the mining industry group EMESRT are "the most concrete acceptance targets available" for mining customers [Chapter 3]. The MOSH regime requires physical independent verification at TRL gates, with no simulation substitute [Chapter 3].

terms.title: South America and Asia rules (NR-22, NR-12, DS 132, SERNAGEOMIN, DS 024-2016-EM, DGMS, GB standards, JARI)
terms.oneSentence: Brazil, Chile, Peru, India, China and Japan each have general mining or machinery safety rules, and in none of them did the booklet find a dedicated rule with numeric tests for automatic braking on off-road machines.
terms.explained:
South America has no continent-wide machinery regime. Brazil's NR-22 (occupational safety and health in mining, last modified 29 January 2026) and NR-12 (machinery safety) set general machine, mining, brake and operating requirements; an automatic-braking mandate with prescribed tests was not found [Chapter 3]. Chile's Decreto Supremo 132, the Reglamento de Seguridad Minera (promulgated 2002, published 2004, consolidated to 2024), gives broad mining safety controls; a dedicated braking test standard was not found, and guidance from SERNAGEOMIN, Chile's mining regulator, was not verified [Chapter 3]. Peru's DS 024-2016-EM is the mining occupational safety regulation, a general risk framework with no collision-braking acceptance regime found [Chapter 3]. For all of these the answer on numeric items is "not found", not "not required" [Chapter 3].

India. The Directorate General of Mines Safety (DGMS) issues circulars under the Coal Mines Regulations 2017, with regulation 216(2) as the legal hook: Circular No. 03 of 2024 (21 August 2024) on wheeled trackless machinery in opencast coal mines calls for proper proximity-warning or anti-collision devices, a 2025 technical circular refers to fail-safe braking before tippers are deployed, and a cited circular sets a 30 km/h maximum speed. These were read through secondary summaries, so confidence on details is low [Chapter 3].

China. A peer-reviewed article states that the Coal Mine Safety Regulations require trackless rubber-tired vehicles traveling in the same direction underground to keep at least 50 m apart; the regulation text was not reviewed, and whether GB or GB/T (Chinese national) adoptions of ISO 21815, ISO 16001, ISO 17757 or ISO 19014 exist was not found [Chapter 3].

Japan. No dedicated off-road automatic-braking rule was found. The Japan Automobile Research Institute (JARI) appears in the booklet not as a regulator but as one of the weather test facilities, with CEREMA, CARISSMA and NIED, whose fog chambers provide ground truth for sensor models [Chapters 3, 6]. Korea and Indonesia were not verified [Chapter 3].
terms.why: A machine sold worldwide meets risk-based duties everywhere but a numeric braking test almost nowhere, so the project's own acceptance criteria will be judged against general obligations in these markets [Chapter 3]. India's circulars and China's following-distance rule are the kind of site-specific expectations a configurable system must be able to meet.

terms.title: EMESRT and PR-5A (Earth Moving Equipment Safety Round Table, vehicle interaction performance requirement)
terms.oneSentence: EMESRT is a group of mining companies that writes shared safety requirements for the makers of mining machines, and PR-5A is its requirement for controlling collisions between vehicles and people, which gives the industry its nine-layer model of controls and its catalog of collision scenarios.
terms.explained:
The Earth Moving Equipment Safety Round Table (EMESRT) was formed by large mining companies to speak with one voice to equipment manufacturers about design-related safety problems. It is an industry body, not a regulator; its documents are a "risk-control philosophy, not law, and not proof that a product passes a mine's acceptance test" [Chapter 3]. Because mining fleets mix machines from many makers with third-party detection systems, EMESRT's requirements shape what mining customers ask for worldwide.

Performance Requirement PR-5A, Vehicle Interaction Systems, is the document that matters here. It exists in Rev 1.0 (April 2016), Rev 2.0 (August 2019, a version dated 2 September 2019) and Rev 3.0 (September 2024, as cited in a vendor white paper) [Chapters 3, 5]. It does two things. First, it defines the nine levels of vehicle interaction controls: site requirements, segregation controls, operating procedures, authority to operate, fitness to operate, operating compliance, operator awareness (Level 7), advisory controls (Level 8) and intervention controls (Level 9), where the system takes control from the operator [Chapter 5]. Levels 1 to 7 are the site's own defenses; Level 8 warns; Level 9 slows or stops the machine. EMESRT and its partners insist that "Level 9 intervention is not a standalone product" but a machine-control capability resting on a strong Level 1 to 7 baseline [Chapters 3, 8].

Second, PR-5A sets out the surface vehicle interaction scenarios as "storyboards": following on straight roads and curves, overtaking, head-on, junctions, congested dump and park areas, light vehicle against heavy equipment and so on. The booklet records two counts: 24 scenarios according to a 2019 trade article and 17 published surface storyboards according to EMESRT's own 2024 Activity Report, and it does not resolve the difference [Chapters 1, 5]. An agricultural research paper calls PR-5A "a replicable model for ODD definition and validation", ODD meaning operational design domain [Chapter 5].
terms.why: PR-5A supplies the only sector-specific scenario list and the control vocabulary that mining customers use, so the booklet maps the project's requirements and scenario catalog to the PR-5A storyboards and the South African MOSH numbers as "the most concrete acceptance targets available" [Chapters 3, 9]. Its nine-layer model also warns against validating the brake in isolation from roadway design, segregation, procedures and advisory controls [Chapter 1].

terms.title: ICMM, the nine-layer control model and the ICSV program (International Council on Mining and Metals, Innovation for Cleaner Safer Vehicles)
terms.oneSentence: ICMM is the international association of the largest mining companies, and its Innovation for Cleaner, Safer Vehicles program set the industry goal of making collision avoidance technology available by 2025, using EMESRT's nine-layer model of controls.
terms.explained:
The International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM) is a membership body of major mining companies and associations that publishes shared commitments on safety, environment and community matters. Its Innovation for Cleaner, Safer Vehicles (ICSV) program brought mining companies and equipment makers together around the goal to "make collision avoidance technology available to mining companies by 2025", using the requirements of EMESRT (the Earth Moving Equipment Safety Round Table) as the technical basis [Chapter 3].

The nine-layer control model is EMESRT's, and ICMM adopted it. In April 2024 ICMM and EMESRT published the Vehicle Interaction Leading Sites Program, which treats intervention as one layer within design, operating, advisory and intervention controls, insists on a Level 1 to 7 baseline before Levels 8 and 9, and states plainly that "there are no silver bullets" [Chapters 1, 3]. ICMM material also warns that unqualified Level 9 deployment can hurt production and accelerate brake wear [Chapter 3]. The booklet labels all of this expert opinion from an industry group; it did not review the ICSV program in depth and lists it as not verified in several chapters [Chapters 10, 12, 13].
terms.why: ICMM's position is the clearest statement from customers that an automatic brake is a last layer, not a substitute for site controls, which argues against validating the brake in isolation and for measuring nuisance as carefully as misses [Chapters 1, 8]. The 2025 availability goal also explains why mining customers expect intervention systems now.
aliases: ICMM, the nine-layer control model and the ICSV program

terms.title: ACARP and its two-tier test approach (Australian Coal Association Research Program)
terms.oneSentence: ACARP is the research fund of the Australian coal industry, and its project C26028 proposed a two-tier framework for testing proximity detection systems: first prove that the system detects objects, then prove that its advisory or intervention action works.
terms.explained:
The Australian Coal Association Research Program (ACARP) is funded by a levy on coal production and commissions applied research for the industry. Two of its projects appear in the booklet. Project C26028, delivered by the research company Mining3 in January 2021, is a proximity detection system testing framework. Its two tiers are object detection first (Tier 1) and Level 8 or Level 9 advisory or intervention second (Tier 2). The framework states its own limits: the baseline covers "limited choreographed test scenarios" and ignores "pre-existing site controls" and "complex, multi-variate dynamic vehicle interactions" [Chapter 1]. The booklet lists it, with the Mining3 toolkit, evaluations by the United States research institute NIOSH and the South African MOSH regime, among the industry-shared frameworks that give comparability and credible independent evidence [Chapter 1].

Project C24028, by the University of Queensland (2017, with follow-on work to 2019), used a modified haul-truck simulator to study the design of proximity-advisory interfaces. A richer schematic display reduced collision risk and braking force and shortened travel time; the project explicitly listed "acceptable false alarm rate" among the questions still requiring research [Chapter 4].
terms.why: The two tiers are a sensible shape for the project's own physical campaign: detection first, intervention second, with the stated caution that choreographed tests cannot stand in for site-specific, multi-variable dynamics [Chapter 1]. The simulator study is the booklet's main off-road evidence that operator-in-the-loop testing works, and its open question on acceptable false alarms is still open [Chapter 4].
aliases: ACARP and its two-tier test approach

terms.title: MOSH and its TRL stage gates (Mining Industry Occupational Safety and Health learning hub)
terms.oneSentence: MOSH is the learning hub of the Minerals Council South Africa that turned the country's automatic-braking law into engineering specifications and a staged, independently verified test regime organized by technology readiness level.
terms.explained:
South Africa's Regulation 8.10 says that a mining machine must warn, slow and brake automatically, but gives no numbers. The Minerals Council South Africa, through its Mining Industry Occupational Safety and Health (MOSH) learning hub, wrote the missing engineering: functional and technical performance requirements for surface collision prevention systems, a requirements verification regime and independent test specifications [Chapter 3].

The regime uses technology readiness levels (TRL) as stage gates. At TRL4, the laboratory phase, a system is bench-tested: the ISO/TS 21815-2 interface test, log keeping, self-diagnostics, radio spectrum approval and electromagnetic compatibility, with the requirement of "no false interventions and false warnings" [Chapters 3, 7]. At TRL7 the system is verified on machines at a representative site, under a stage-gate specification dated 20 January 2026 [Chapter 1]. At TRL9, in production, statistical monitoring continues, with data "collected over an extended period (e.g., 3 months or 2000 hours)" and a requirement of "no significant production loss" [Chapters 3, 7]. The MOSH specification also requires fail-to-safe within 500 ms of a critical failure, a supplier FMECA (failure mode, effects and criticality analysis), 10 Hz logging during interventions and defined override rules [Chapter 3].

Independent verification is done by the University of Pretoria. Its reported results show how hard the gates are: pass rates of 62 percent for detection devices, 42 percent for machine-side systems and 83 percent for third-party interfaces across 189 tests, at 1.6 tests per week and with an 18-week lead time (October 2025) [Chapter 7]. Hexagon's intervention system passed TRL4 in March 2026 and Komatsu South Africa reported in August 2026 that it was the first surface mining machine maker to achieve TRL4 [Chapters 2, 7].
terms.why: MOSH is "the one published independent verification regime for automatic slow-down and stop in mining", and it shows high first-pass failure and long queues, so review and retest time can become the critical path [Chapter 7]. Its gates are physical; it offers no simulation substitute [Chapter 3].
aliases: Mining Industry Occupational Safety and Health
MOSH and its TRL stage gates

terms.title: NIOSH, MSHA, BLS and CPWR (US bodies that publish accident data)
terms.oneSentence: These four United States bodies produce the accident statistics the booklet relies on: NIOSH researches workplace safety, MSHA regulates mines and records their accidents, BLS counts all workplace deaths and injuries, and CPWR analyzes the construction figures.
terms.explained:
The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) is the federal research institute for workplace safety; it has no enforcement power. Its mining research is the booklet's richest source: an analysis of fatality reports from 2000 to mid-2006 found 22 blind-area deaths, with dump trucks (38 percent) and front-end loaders (33 percent) the machines most involved and 67 percent of victims "in the rear blind area of reversing equipment"; a 2022 analysis of 54 haul-truck deaths from 2005 to 2021 found 21 berm-related, 13 collisions, 12 at dump points and 8 other, with 12 of the 13 collisions involving a forward-moving truck; and underground studies concluded that 82 percent of 39 continuous-miner fatalities might have been prevented by proximity systems [Chapter 4]. NIOSH also documented false and nuisance alarm rates in the field and reviewed collision-avoidance technology in 2022 [Chapters 4, 1].

The Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) regulates mines and publishes their fatality and injury counts: in 2025 powered haulage caused 13 of 33 mining deaths and 426 of 4,792 nonfatal injuries, and from 2003 to 2018 surface mobile equipment was involved in 109 deaths and 1,543 injuries at mines with six or more miners [Chapter 4].

The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) runs the national census of fatal occupational injuries. The Center for Construction Research and Training (CPWR) analyzes those data for construction: vehicles and mobile heavy equipment caused 7,681 construction deaths from 1992 to 2010, about 404 a year, with 131 road-site deaths from backing equipment; in 2019 struck-by incidents caused 170 construction deaths, 47.1 percent involving transport vehicles [Chapter 4].
terms.why: These figures tell the project which collisions to prevent first: reversing loaders and small dump trucks at quarries and construction sites, forward-moving or starting haul trucks hitting light vehicles and pedestrians at mines [Chapter 4]. The booklet also warns that databases record fatalities far better than property damage or near misses, and that figures from different agencies must not be added into one rate [Chapter 4].
aliases: US bodies that publish accident data

terms.title: WorkSafe New Zealand, WorkSafe Western Australia (SIR 286), HSE and EU-OSHA
terms.oneSentence: These are workplace-safety regulators and agencies whose incident reports and statistics the booklet uses: WorkSafe New Zealand for mines and quarries, WorkSafe Western Australia for the Significant Incident Reports on autonomous haul trucks, Britain's HSE for national figures, and EU-OSHA, the European agency, mainly as a source of legislation summaries.
terms.explained:
WorkSafe New Zealand is the national regulator; its extractives inspectorate covers mines and quarries. Its August 2017 alert was triggered by "numerous" interactions involving heavy mobile plant: a dozer reversing into a loaded dump truck at a tip head, a night-shift truck clipping a dozer, a loader bucket tipping a loader onto its side during stockpile loading. Its quarterly data for late 2019 split vehicle events as 46 percent overturning, 27 percent unintended movement or brake failure and 11 percent collision with other plant, with an explicit warning that reporting was incomplete [Chapter 4].

WorkSafe Western Australia is a different regulator with a similar name, and it is the source of the Significant Incident Reports (SIR) the booklet cites. SIR 286 records operators who approached autonomous haul trucks during a recovery without recognizing that the trucks were in exception mode rather than suspended; when communications were restored the trucks resumed moving. Contributory factors were lack of understanding of system modes, limited communications redundancy, the ability to override safety controls, failure to observe status lights and desensitization after prior communication problems [Chapter 13]. SIR 226 describes an autonomous truck colliding with a manned water cart at night after a route was released in the control system but not marked on the ground [Chapter 13].

The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is Great Britain's regulator; its figures appear under the United Kingdom entry [Chapter 4]. EU-OSHA, the European Agency for Safety and Health at Work, is an information agency rather than a regulator; the booklet cites its summary of the Machinery Regulation and notes that EU-OSHA breakdowns of machine collisions by movement type were not found [Chapters 4, 10].
terms.why: SIR 286 is the booklet's direct warning that degraded and recovery modes can be more dangerous than normal operation and that repeated faults desensitize people, so test plans must include communications loss, blocked sensors, restart and recovery cases [Chapter 13].
