The New Zealand events show that ordinary production tasks at tip heads and stockpiles produce the collisions [Chapter 4].
aliases: WorkSafe New Zealand, WorkSafe Western Australia

terms.title: PEGASUS, VVM, SET Level, VaViM and EVIDENT (German and European research programs on scenario-based validation)
terms.oneSentence: These are the publicly funded research programs, mostly German and Swedish, that worked out how to validate automated driving with scenarios and simulation, and whose durations show how long building such a capability takes.
terms.explained:
PEGASUS was the German project that defined a method for validating a Level 3 highway automation function. It ran from 1 January 2016 to 30 June 2019, 42 months, with 17 partners, about EUR 34.5 million (EUR 16.3 million public subsidy) and about 1,791 person-months, roughly 149 person-years. It produced a method, not a certified product: a scenario database built from field recordings, simulation, proving-ground and field tests, and the three-level scenario idea (functional, logical, concrete) that later entered the ISO 3450x standards [Chapters 2, 9]. Its partners included car makers, suppliers, simulation vendors and test laboratories [Chapter 2].

VVM (Verification and Validation Methods) was the follow-on for urban Level 4 and 5 automation, July 2019 to June 2023, with a EUR 47 million project volume and the stated goal of a "significant shift from real tests to simulation" [Chapter 2]. SET Level, a sister project, published the Credible Simulation Process (August 2021), which embeds simulation credibility in product development with credibility levels tied to the criticality of the simulation task; the booklet treats it as a process template, not proven off-road [Chapter 10].

Two Swedish programs addressed credibility directly. VaViM (February to August 2022; Volvo Autonomous Solutions and Blekinge Institute of Technology, funded through Vinnova and Drive Sweden) studied validation of virtual models for autonomous vehicles in fenced areas, built a feasibility model, planned simple comparative physical tests, and concluded that validated models and real tests must be used side by side; six months "sufficed for a pre-study, not an accepted capability" [Chapter 2]. EVIDENT (April 2022 to December 2024, about 33 months, SAFER and Vinnova) researched credible virtual verification, correlation and the replacement or complementing of real recordings, and EVIDENT 2 was still running in 2026 [Chapter 2].
terms.why: The booklet's central timeline finding rests on these programs: "building the capability took years in every documented case", so a four-month window must be a validation window, not a capability-construction window [Chapter 2]. VaViM is the nearest precedent for off-road machines and supports using automotive credibility concepts without assuming automotive sensor and environment models are valid off-road [Chapter 2]. The booklet also uses these programs as a reference class for schedule forecasting [Chapter 12].
aliases: PEGASUS, VVM, SET Level, VaViM and EVIDENT

terms.title: Waymo and Motional collision-avoidance validation methods (on-road precedents)
terms.oneSentence: Waymo and Motional are developers of self-driving road vehicles whose published safety methods show how simulation, replay, closed-course tests, public roads and shadow mode are layered, and whose material the booklet treats as vendor evidence from on-road.
terms.explained:
Waymo published a collision avoidance testing methodology in 2022 and documented city-by-city release, in which the vehicles' operating area is widened only as evidence accumulates [Chapter 1]. Its material distinguishes open-loop replay of recorded data from closed-loop simulation, and its Open Dataset illustrates what a reproducible reference needs: synchronized lidar and camera data, calibration, vehicle poses and tracked 3D labels [Chapters 1, 7]. A Waymo study on automatic labeling found that "human labels do not have the consistency one may expect", a caution for anyone building ground truth [Chapter 7]. Its 2026 "world model" for generating driving scenes is a vendor claim with no off-road qualification [Chapter 5].

Motional's 2026 safety material describes a progression from synthetic simulation and re-simulation of recorded data through closed-course and public-road testing to deployment, with daily testing that includes shadow-mode deployment of features before broader roll-out [Chapter 1]. Shadow mode means the new software runs on the vehicle and produces decisions "which are not executed by the actuator system", so its behavior can be measured without risk [Chapter 1].

Both are vendor sources, both are on-road, and neither discloses validation durations or physical-test shares that would count as verified sign-off [Chapters 1, 2].
terms.why: The booklet uses these programs to show that the best-documented developers use simulation, replay and shadow mode as filters before scarce physical time, not as substitutes for it, and that staged release with a limited operating domain is standard practice [Chapter 1]. Shadow mode on the existing warning-only fleet is the booklet's single most valuable lever for gathering false-positive evidence before the prototype arrives [Chapter 2].
aliases: Waymo and Motional collision-avoidance validation methods

terms.title: Auto-GCAS (Automatic Ground Collision Avoidance System for fighter aircraft)
terms.oneSentence: Auto-GCAS is the system on F-16 and F-35 fighter aircraft that takes control and pulls the aircraft up when it is about to fly into the ground, a precedent for an automatic intervention that had to be proven both effective and free of nuisance activations.
terms.explained:
The Automatic Ground Collision Avoidance System (Auto-GCAS) grew out of research by NASA, the US Air Force Research Laboratory and Lockheed Martin dating to the early 1980s. Retrofits on F-16 Block 40 and 50 aircraft began in September 2014, and F-35 integration followed in 2019, which the manufacturer says came "seven years earlier than previously planned" thanks to reuse of the F-16 work, with eight F-16 pilots' lives credited as saved by then [Chapter 2]. A 2007 NASA release reported 98 percent effectiveness [Chapter 2].

Its design requirement is the reason it appears in the booklet: the system had to be "nuisance free". The test lead put the order of priorities plainly: "It's only if we can make sure we're not going to do any harm, and not be a nuisance, only then will we worry about providing protection" [Chapter 2]. Flight testing remained part of the program throughout. Auto-GCAS is an automatic flight-control recovery, so it is an analog for intervention rather than for object-triggered braking, and its acceptance came from the US Air Force, not a civil regulator [Chapter 2].
terms.why: Auto-GCAS is a real case of validation time compressed by reuse, but only after about three decades of foundational work, which supports the booklet's conclusion that reuse is fast and first construction is slow [Chapter 2]. Its nuisance-first philosophy is the one the booklet recommends for a machine brake: prove it does no harm and does not annoy, then prove it protects [Chapters 2, 4].

terms.title: ACAS X and TCAS (aircraft collision avoidance, encounter models)
terms.oneSentence: TCAS is the long-standing system that warns airline pilots of a possible mid-air collision and tells them to climb or descend, ACAS X is its successor, and the encounter model is the statistical description of near-collisions that let ACAS X be validated largely by simulation.
terms.explained:
The Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) has flown on airliners for decades. Its replacement, the Airborne Collision Avoidance System X (ACAS X), chooses its advice from a table computed by optimization, and its minimum operational performance standards, DO-385 and ED-256 from the aviation standards bodies RTCA and EUROCAE, were published in October 2018 [Chapter 2]. Both systems are advisory: the pilot remains in the loop and flies the maneuver, so they are a precedent for warning logic rather than for automatic braking [Chapter 2].

The validation method is what the booklet draws on. An encounter model is a statistical model of how aircraft come close to each other, built from years of radar data; the MIT Lincoln Laboratory model used nine months of radar recordings, and the European CREME model was built "based on twelve million flight[s]". Validation of the threat-resolution logic "involved simulation of close encounters equivalent to billions of flight hours", with pilot assessment of individual advisories alongside. Acceptance came through the RTCA and EUROCAE standards and aviation authorities [Chapter 2]. A caution survives in the record: in March 2022 committee minutes, European results suggested ACAS Xa induced more near mid-air collisions than TCAS, the US laboratory "didn't see the same disparity", and participants noted that sensor noise had not been assessed [Chapter 2].
terms.why: ACAS X shows that a standards body and regulators can accept statistical simulation as primary evidence for a safety-critical collision function, but only on encounter models built over years from real data, and even then with unresolved disagreements about sensor noise [Chapter 2]. For the project, the lesson is that a credible statistical argument needs field data about real interactions first, which is one reason the booklet presses for logging on the existing warning fleet [Chapter 2].

terms.title: Honda CMBS investigations (NHTSA PE22-003, EA24-002, EA25-002) as a precedent for unnecessary braking
terms.oneSentence: The Honda investigations are the United States regulator's inquiries into cars whose Collision Mitigation Braking System braked hard with nothing in the way, the largest documented case of unnecessary automatic braking reaching a production fleet.
terms.explained:
Honda's Collision Mitigation Braking System (CMBS) is the maker's name for its automatic emergency braking (AEB). The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened Preliminary Evaluation PE22-003 on 21 February 2022 with 278 complaints (107 Accord, 171 CR-V) of inadvertent activation, six alleging a collision, "some with large speed changes, occurring with nothing obstructing the vehicle's path" [Chapter 2]. In April 2024 it upgraded the case to Engineering Analysis EA24-002, covering 2,997,604 vehicles (2018 to 2022 Accord and 2017 to 2022 CR-V, including hybrids) and 1,294 complaints. Crash and injury counts differ by outlet, from 31 crashes and 50 injuries to 47 crashes and 93 injuries [Chapter 2]. A further analysis, EA25-002, added 295,125 Insight and Passport vehicles in January 2025; Honda cited about 412 reports, dealer technicians who could not replicate the fault told customers it was "normal AEB operation", and the agency reviewed 475 reports in total [Chapters 2, 13]. Honda's own review concluded that some customers did not understand the system or its limits; no recall had been ordered as of 2026 according to secondary sources [Chapter 2].

The booklet is careful about what the case proves. None of the investigations shows that weak pre-production validation caused the field problem; they establish that unnecessary braking reached very large fleets and kept the regulator busy for years [Chapter 2]. The Tesla investigation closed in June 2026 is the counterexample: about 25,900 reports, zero crashes, and reports that fell steeply after firmware updates [Chapter 2].
terms.why: "Unnecessary braking is the dominant documented failure mode" of production automatic braking, so a validation campaign measured only by collisions avoided is incomplete [Chapter 2]. The dealer episode shows that complaints which cannot be reproduced in the workshop are an early warning sign to watch for in field pilots [Chapter 13].

terms.title: Rail, port, forklift and agriculture precedents (Wabtec and others)
terms.oneSentence: These are the neighboring industries the booklet searched for cases of automatic braking validated with less physical testing, and in each it found products on the market but no published validation method, duration or share of physical testing.
terms.explained:
Rail. Bosch's tram collision assistance combines camera and radar to detect vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists, warn the driver and brake automatically; radar is presented as adding detection in fog, rain and at night, the technology was adapted from automotive systems, and approval for public transport was reported by 2016. Development duration and the split between physical and virtual validation were not found, and positive train control and other rail systems were not researched in depth [Chapter 2]. Wabtec, a company known for railway equipment, appears in the booklet for its mining work: its Level 9 collision awareness system tested on Komatsu 730E and 860E haul trucks in December 2021 showed controlled deceleration at speeds up to 30 km/h, and detection zones were then adjusted through further physical tests for braking distance, speed, payload and haul-road grade [Chapters 1, 2].

Port equipment. A June 2024 case at a container terminal describes straddle carriers with area awareness and active obstacle detection giving visual and audible warnings; automatic braking is not stated, so it is customer acceptance of a warning system [Chapter 2].

Forklifts. Toyota's SEnS+ (August 2021) uses a rear stereo camera to tell people from objects and slows by cutting power; the maker states it "does not have function in using the brake to decelerate and automatically stop". Linde's Reverse Assist Radar slows and can stop the truck, with an optional camera recognizing work and protective clothing. Validation methods and field problems were not found [Chapter 2].

Agriculture and forestry. The ISO 18497 standards exist, but no agricultural or forestry case of simulation-reduced validation with a stated timeline was found, and no currently sold farm system with documented object-triggered emergency braking and a public operating envelope was found [Chapter 2].
terms.why: The search across sectors is what supports the booklet's headline: "no case exists, in any sector, of a new automatic braking function being taken from first representative hardware to accepted validation in about four months" [Chapter 2]. Where products exist, physical testing still dominated at integration, as Wabtec's zone adjustments show [Chapter 2].
aliases: Rail, port, forklift and agriculture precedents

terms.title: The Pretoria process and MineSim (mining research precedents)
terms.oneSentence: The Pretoria process is the University of Pretoria's step-by-step method for independently verifying mining collision-avoidance systems, and MineSim is an open-source simulation test system for autonomous trucks in open-pit mines.
terms.explained:
The University of Pretoria's Vehicle Dynamics Group acts as the independent verifier for the South African mining industry's MOSH regime. Its methodology, described in 2020, starts with controlled laboratory tests and progresses to interaction tests in a representative mine, using high-precision satellite positioning as ground truth on surface and combinations of lidar, cameras and automotive radar underground; the group opened an underground test facility in December 2020 and has worked with mining organizations and an ISO working group [Chapter 2]. Its reported pass rates (62 percent for detection devices, 42 percent for machine-side systems, 83 percent for third-party interfaces across 189 tests, at 1.6 tests per week with an 18-week lead time) are the only published independent results for automatic slow-down and stop in mining [Chapter 7]. Its 2024 research found that mining collision-avoidance systems "tend to be very conservative" and suffer "false positive interventions leading to production losses, increased wear, and resistance to adopt", and investigated adding steering rate to collision prediction, modeling South African mining scenarios in a scene-building tool [Chapters 2, 7].

MineSim (published April 2025 in Accident Analysis & Prevention) is an open-source, peer-reviewed, scenario-based simulation test system and benchmark for autonomous trucks in open-pit mines. It incorporates scenarios from two real mines and represents mining-specific features such as unstructured roads, noting that urban simulators "lack coverage of unstructured road environments in open-pit mining" [Chapters 1, 5]. The booklet calls it proof that mine-specific closed-loop scenario simulation is feasible today, "not to be confused with validated sensor physics" [Chapter 1].
terms.why: Pretoria's process shows that off-road validation is still far more physical than the automotive state of the art and that independent gates have long queues, which bears directly on a four-month schedule [Chapters 2, 7]. MineSim shows that the scenario and planning layer of a mining simulator can be built now, while sensor models in dust, snow and fog remain the unsolved part [Chapter 1].

terms.title: RAND Corporation and GAO (the Driving to Safety report and the US Government Accountability Office cost and schedule guides)
terms.oneSentence: RAND is an independent American research institute whose 2016 report showed that road miles alone cannot prove a self-driving car is safe, and GAO is the audit arm of the United States Congress whose guides and program reviews show what makes cost and schedule estimates credible.
terms.explained:
RAND's report "Driving to Safety" (Kalra and Paddock, April 2016) calculated that autonomous vehicles "would have to be driven hundreds of millions of miles and sometimes hundreds of billions of miles" to demonstrate their reliability: 275 million failure-free miles to show, with 95 percent confidence, a fatality rate no worse than the human rate of 1.09 per 100 million miles, and about 11 billion miles to show a 20 percent improvement [Chapter 9]. The booklet states that the logic transfers to off-road machines and the numbers do not, and that off-road machines accumulate far less exposure per unit than cars, "so the gap is worse on a job site, not better" [Chapters 1, 9]. The report is the statistical reason virtual testing is pursued at all [Chapter 12]. RAND also developed assumption-based planning in the 1990s, which the booklet adopts for tracking load-bearing assumptions [Chapter 12].

The Government Accountability Office (GAO) audits federal programs. Its long series of acquisition reviews links immature technology at the point of commitment to cost growth and delay: in 2006 most of 23 major defense programs began development with immature technologies and 10 already expected more than 30 percent cost growth or a year's delay; a July 2026 report on 104 programs found "almost half" entered with immature technologies and average delivery time above 12 years [Chapter 12]. GAO's guides turn this into practice: the Schedule Assessment Guide (2015) with ten best-practice areas and schedule-risk analysis, the Cost Estimating and Assessment Guide (2020), the Technology Readiness Assessment Guide (2020) and a 2025 recommendation of iterative minimum viable products [Chapter 12]. The booklet notes that GAO's evidence is correlational and sometimes small-sample [Chapter 12].
terms.why: RAND's argument is why the project cannot rely on field hours to prove a rare-event safety function and must combine simulation, statistics and targeted tests [Chapters 1, 9]. GAO's principle of "knowledge before commitment" underlies the booklet's gate-based plan, its use of ranges instead of dates and its warning that immature technology at commitment is the most consistently documented cause of schedule failure [Chapter 12].

terms.title: DARPA RACER program (off-road autonomy research)
terms.oneSentence: RACER is a program of the United States defense research agency DARPA to make military ground vehicles drive themselves fast across rough off-road terrain, and its simulation arm built a very large virtual off-road environment.
terms.explained:
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) funds high-risk research for the United States military. Its RACER program (Robotic Autonomy in Complex Environments with Resiliency) pursues high-speed autonomous driving over unstructured off-road terrain. The companion RACER-Sim effort, announced in January 2022 with Duality Robotics and Intel Federal as the two prime contractors and a reported Phase 1 budget of about USD 6 million, tasked one team with building an 80 square kilometer (20 km by 4 km) virtual off-road environment on a digital-twin simulation platform; NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory contracted the same platform for RACER Phase II in September 2024 [Chapter 11]. The booklet records this as documented government use of an off-road simulator, with a focus on high-speed military driving rather than on close-quarters work with people [Chapter 11].

For validation precedent the booklet found nothing: no publicly documented military ground-vehicle automatic-braking safety case with quantified simulation substitution, and RACER itself was "not found" as a validation case in Chapter 2 and "not verified" as a lead in Chapter 13 [Chapters 2, 13].
terms.why: RACER shows that large off-road virtual environments can be built and that a government customer has paid for one, which supports the feasibility of virtual job sites; it offers no evidence about accepting simulation as safety evidence for braking [Chapter 11].

terms.title: Columbia Accident Investigation Board (why a space shuttle accident appears in a mining booklet)
terms.oneSentence: The Columbia Accident Investigation Board was the body that investigated the loss of the space shuttle Columbia in 2003, and its findings about a computer model used far outside the range it had been tested on are the textbook case of false confidence from simulation.
terms.explained:
During Columbia's launch in January 2003 a piece of insulating foam struck the wing. Engineers assessed the damage with Crater, an empirical model of impact penetration. The debris was about 400 times the size of anything in the model's test database (an early briefing said 640 times). Crater actually predicted penetration deeper than the tile, but because the model had tended to overpredict in its small-impact calibration data and was considered conservative, engineers "used their judgment" to conclude the damage would not penetrate, and the in-flight assessment reported no safety-of-flight issue. Columbia broke up on re-entry on 1 February 2003 [Chapter 10].

The Columbia Accident Investigation Board reported in August 2003. Finding F6.3-10 said the assessment used "an impact simulation that was well outside Crater's test database" and that the analyst was inexperienced; finding F6.3-11 recorded the override of the model's prediction by judgment. The Board also criticized the briefing slides for burying key information in vague words such as "significant" [Chapter 10]. A former shuttle program manager has dissented, arguing that Crater gave a correct warning and the failure was management's override of it; the booklet records both views [Chapter 10].
terms.why: Columbia is "the canonical false-confidence case", and the lesson is extrapolation: a model's known bias cannot be assumed to hold outside the domain where it was validated, so every simulation claim needs an explicit validity envelope and margin [Chapter 10]. The booklet also draws from it the rule to present results in plain charts and words rather than slides that bury caveats [Chapter 10]. For a program that will simulate machines, sensors and weather it has not physically tested, the case is a standing warning.

terms.title: Tool chain
terms.oneSentence: A tool chain is the set of separate software programs and hardware boxes that are connected together so that one virtual test can run from start to finish.
terms.explained:
No single program does everything that virtual testing needs. One program describes the test situation (a loader reversing toward a person in dust). Another builds the three-dimensional job site. Another calculates how the machine moves, how its tires sink into gravel and how fast its brakes act. Another pretends to be the camera, radar or lidar and produces fake sensor data. The braking software under test reads that data and decides to brake. Then something has to run thousands of these tests, collect the results and store them. Each of these jobs is done by a different tool, often from a different company. Linking them is the tool chain. A kitchen is a fair comparison: oven, refrigerator and mixer from different makers all have to fit the same counter and the same power outlet.

The booklet maps the market into eight categories: complete platforms, sensor simulation, vehicle and machine dynamics, terrain and soil, environment creation, scenario generation and test management, data replay and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL), and cloud execution. Its central finding is that the market is modular. Road-vehicle tool chains have strong sensor and scenario tooling but thin soil physics; heavy-machine physics tools have strong terrain and hydraulics but thin sensor and scenario tooling. No single tool, open-source or commercial, has public evidence of validating automatic braking for earth-moving machines across many job sites and all weather [Chapter 11].

The "glue" between tools is a set of open standards: the Functional Mock-up Interface (FMI, supported by about 250 tools by mid-2025), the ASAM Open Simulation Interface (OSI), OpenSCENARIO and OpenDRIVE for scenarios and roads, OpenUSD for scenes, and Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) for robotics software. Standards reduce the work but do not remove it. The hard parts are making two programs agree on coordinate systems and clocks, feeding the machine's position to the sensor program at exactly the same time step, matching surface materials across programs, representing an articulated machine and its attachment, and proving that a software update has not changed results. The booklet quotes the Project Chrono developers that common tire models silently do not work on deformable terrain: "plugging together" tools can quietly break the physics. No benchmark of integration effort in engineer-weeks was found; the booklet ranks it only relatively, from same-vendor modules (lower) through standards-linked components (medium) to a separate sensor renderer plus third-party dynamics plus soil plus a hardware bench (high) and raw-signal sensor benches (highest) [Chapter 11].

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S["Scenario generation and test management"] --> E["Environment: virtual job site and materials"]
    E --> R["Sensor simulation: camera, radar, lidar, ultrasonic"]
    D["Machine dynamics, terrain and soil"] --> R
    R --> F["Braking function under test"]
    F --> D
    F --> X["Execution: workstation, cloud or HIL bench"]
    X --> T["Results, verdicts and archived records"]
    T --> S
```

*The categories of a simulation tool chain and the main flow of data between them; the loop from the braking function back to the machine dynamics is what makes the test closed-loop.*
terms.why: The organization has no virtual testing capability and about nine months before hardware arrives, so the integration work, not the choice of any one tool, is the schedule risk. The booklet notes that the ASAM project refining OSI for high-fidelity sensors runs until March 2027, exactly when this program would be integrating its first chain [Chapter 11].

terms.title: Complete and near-complete simulation platforms
terms.oneSentence: A complete simulation platform is a commercial or open-source product that tries to cover several layers of the tool chain at once: scenarios, environments, sensors, vehicle motion and test execution.
terms.explained:
Think of a complete platform as a whole kitchen bought from one supplier instead of appliances from several. The booklet warns that "complete" is relative: these products usually still rely on a separate machine model, controller, asset pipeline or hardware bench [Chapter 11].

The table lists the platforms named in Chapter 11. "Demonstrated" means a documented customer use, peer-reviewed study, government program or shipped example; "claimed" means a vendor statement only; "on-road only" means proven for road vehicles with no off-road evidence found. "Not found" is a finding, not a gap.

| Platform | Type and license | What the booklet reports on off-road use | Public price |
|---|---|---|---|
| MathWorks MATLAB and Simulink with the Offroad Autonomy Library and RoadRunner | Commercial, annual or perpetual per product | Demonstrated as shipped examples: an autonomous excavator, a backhoe loading a truck, an open-pit haul truck (release R2026b); Volvo CE built a human-in-the-loop excavator simulator with it | Quote only; an unofficial January 2024 price list exists |
| Applied Intuition | Commercial | Demonstrated: a Komatsu partnership announced September 2025 covering collision avoidance on staffed sites; also sells an autonomy stack, which the booklet flags as a possible conflict; owns CarSim and TruckSim | Not found |
| Cognata | Commercial | Claimed: a construction and mining use-case page; camera, radar, lidar and thermal marketed | Not found |
| Duality AI Falcon | Commercial | Demonstrated in military off-road work (DARPA RACER-Sim, NASA JPL), not construction or mining | Education license USD 20 per month; commercial price not found |
| Cadence (formerly Hexagon) Virtual Test Drive (VTD) and VTDx | Commercial | On-road only; ownership moved to Cadence in February 2026 | Not found |
| IPG Automotive CarMaker and TruckMaker with an off-highway stack | Commercial | Claimed with named applications: a lidar accident-prevention application with Linde and tractor vehicle-in-the-loop; targets construction, agriculture and mining | Not found |
| dSPACE AURELION with SIMPHERA | Commercial | On-road only; camera, ray-traced radar, lidar, infrared and ultrasonic models; integrates with dSPACE benches | Not found |
| Siemens Simcenter Prescan | Commercial | On-road only; camera, radar, lidar and ultrasonic models | Not found |
| CARLA | Open source (MIT code) | A mining earth-mover vehicle asset exists (release 0.10.0, December 2024); no soil physics | Free |
| NVIDIA Isaac Sim | Open source (Apache 2.0) with separate asset terms | Not found for construction or mining; 25 RTX lidar models and one radar model listed | Free for internal research; enterprise price not found |
| Project Chrono | Open source (BSD-3) | Demonstrated in off-road mobility research; wheeled, tracked and articulated vehicles on deformable terrain | Free |
| BeamNG.tech | Commercial business license | Off-road driving feasible, but the vehicle model is car-scale, not an excavator or haul truck | Not found |
| MORAI | Commercial | Not found | Contact for price |
| rFpro | Commercial | On-road only; detailed camera pipeline | Not found |
| Gazebo | Open source (Apache 2.0) | Not found (general robotics) | Free |

Two names in common use do not appear as platforms. Ansys sensor simulation is now Synopsys AVxcelerate Sensors, covered under sensor simulation tools; NVIDIA DRIVE Sim is mentioned only as a tool whose frame rates were not found [Chapter 6]. AVL appears as an engineering service company with its own vehicle models and scenario tool, not as a complete platform [Chapter 11].
terms.why: Only a few platforms publicly position for construction or mining, and most of that is claimed rather than independently demonstrated; independent validation of any platform for automatic braking on heavy machines was not found. The booklet also records that nearly every commercial product is quote-only, so a budget must be built from vendor quotations [Chapter 11].

terms.title: Open-source simulators
terms.oneSentence: An open-source simulator is a simulation program whose source code anyone may read, change and use without paying a license fee, under conditions set by its license.
terms.explained:
Most software is sold as a sealed box. Open-source software comes with the recipe, under a license that states the conditions. The licenses the booklet names are all "permissive": MIT (CARLA's code), BSD-3 (Project Chrono) and Apache 2.0 (Isaac Sim, Gazebo). In plain terms, all three let a company use, modify and redistribute the software, including inside a commercial product, as long as the original copyright notice is kept; Apache 2.0 also includes an explicit patent grant. None requires the company to publish its own changes.

The open-source simulators the booklet names: CARLA (a driving simulator on the Unreal game engine, with a mining earth-mover asset since December 2024), NVIDIA Isaac Sim (robotics simulation with ray-traced lidar and radar), Project Chrono (a physics engine for wheeled, tracked and articulated vehicles on deformable terrain), Gazebo (a robotics simulator with a long-term release supported to 2031), Scenic (a scenario language), MineSim (a test system for autonomous trucks in open-pit mines, built from two real mines), AutoDRIVE (a digital-twin framework used in an off-road braking study) and MAVS, a university off-road simulation library [Chapters 1, 5, 11].

Three cautions. "Open" can be mixed: Isaac Sim's core is Apache 2.0, but some assets carry other terms, redistribution with certain components needs a paid enterprise license, and vendor staff described free use for teams of up to two people. Open-source projects change fast; CARLA changed game engine between release lines, so a frozen, qualified build is advisable. And the research did not examine who funds and maintains these projects or how quickly they patch security problems [Chapter 11].
terms.why: The booklet concludes that open source is viable for a low-license-cost core but is not the lowest total cost: someone must still build and maintain the coupling, the assets, the scenario database and all the validation evidence, with no vendor support [Chapter 11].

terms.title: Sensor simulation tools
terms.oneSentence: A sensor simulation tool produces artificial camera images, radar returns, lidar point clouds or ultrasonic echoes from a virtual scene, so the braking software can be tested without a real sensor.
terms.explained:
A sensor turns the world into data. A sensor simulation tool does the reverse: it starts from a described world and produces the data a sensor would have produced. The booklet insists on the difference between sensor presence and sensor credibility. A checkbox saying "radar supported" may mean anything from a perfect list of objects, to simple geometric ray casting, to tuned statistical detections, to simulation of the raw radio signal, and for automatic braking those levels are not interchangeable [Chapter 11]. The ladder of realism runs: ideal object lists; geometric ray casting; phenomenological models tuned to measurements; physics-based raw-signal models using ray tracing and material properties; and full-wave electromagnetic solvers, far too slow for whole job sites [Chapter 6].

Commercial tools named: dSPACE AURELION (camera, ray-traced radar, lidar, infrared, ultrasonic, with a material database); Synopsys AVxcelerate Sensors, formerly Ansys (camera, lidar, radar, thermal; co-simulation with CarMaker and CARLA documented); Simcenter Prescan sensor models; rFpro's camera pipeline; and Persival, which builds sensor models to the ASAM Open Simulation Interface (OSI) standard, packaged as Functional Mock-up Units (FMUs), and correlates them against real sensor output. Open-source options are the RTX sensors in Isaac Sim, Chrono::Sensor and CARLA's sensors; physics-based ultrasonic simulation in these was not found. None of the commercial tools had public off-road validation [Chapter 11].

Research tools discussed: RadaRays, a real-time radar ray tracer whose authors mounted a radar on a wheel loader in a hall, the most directly relevant heavy-machine result found; RadSimReal and Sim2Radar, on the radar gap between simulation and reality; SplatAD and the NVIDIA NuRec engine, which rebuild scenes from recordings with Gaussian splatting; LiDARsim-style meshing from machine logs; and Boreal3D, synthetic forest lidar plots [Chapters 5, 6].
terms.why: Sensor and environment fidelity is the hardest uncertainty in the whole program, and it is weakest exactly where the risk is: dust, fog, snow, rain, glare and darkness [Chapter 13]. ASAM itself states that no standardized metrics exist to assess the quality of sensor simulation [Chapter 11].

terms.title: Vehicle and machine dynamics tools
terms.oneSentence: A vehicle and machine dynamics tool calculates how a machine moves: how it accelerates, steers, tips, sinks into soft ground and stops when the brakes act.
terms.explained:
A braking test is only as good as the model of the machine. A 40-ton loader on wet gravel, with a full bucket raised, does not stop like a car. Dynamics tools calculate the forces on every body of the machine (frame, boom, bucket, wheels or tracks), the hydraulics that move them and the contact with the ground, many times per second.

The booklet separates two families. Heavy-machine physics tools built for mobile machinery: Mevea (real-time multibody dynamics with hydraulics and soil, used for crane digital twins and training simulators; it claims over 100 simulator models for more than 50 customers); Algoryx AGX Dynamics (modules for terrain, tires, tracks, hydraulics and granular material; a peer-reviewed 2025 paper calibrated an AGX wheel-loader twin against a real machine; its Unity version added a reverse auto-brake example with a lidar module in April 2025); CM Labs Vortex Studio (real-time physics for earthmoving and cranes, documented mainly for operator training); and Project Chrono (open source; wheeled, tracked and articulated vehicles; its developers report that common handling tire models do not work on its deformable terrain). Road-heritage tools: CarSim and TruckSim (owned by Applied Intuition; a 2022 press release claimed expansion into off-road, agricultural, construction and mining use); IPG TruckMaker; MSC/Cadence Adams (high-end multibody dynamics, not an environment simulator); MathWorks Vehicle Dynamics Blockset and Simscape, with articulated steering since R2025a; and Altair MotionSolve, cited for a tracked-vehicle tutorial with soft soil [Chapters 8, 11]. RecurDyn is not discussed in the booklet.
terms.why: Surface friction, slope, mass, payload, attachment position, tire or track state and brake and hydraulic delay dominate stopping distance and must be in the model; the booklet finds that heavy-machine physics vendors are mature in dynamics and demonstrated off-road, but their sensor physics is not independently validated in weather [Chapters 8, 11].

terms.title: Terrain and soil tools
terms.oneSentence: Terrain and soil tools calculate how the ground deforms under a machine, how a bucket digs into a pile and how loose material flows, because soft ground changes how a machine stops.
terms.explained:
On a paved road the ground is a fixed surface. On a job site the ground is part of the machine: gravel shifts, mud ruts, a berm collapses. Three mathematical approaches appear in the booklet, each available inside several tools. The Soil Contact Model (SCM) is a fast, semi-empirical method from Bekker and Wong that treats the ground as a deformable mat with pressure-sinkage rules. The Discrete Element Method (DEM) simulates thousands or millions of individual grains and their collisions, which is realistic for piles and digging but very slow. Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) and related continuum methods treat the soil as a flowing material represented by particles; Chrono calls its version CRM [Chapters 8, 11].

The tools: EDEM, a DEM program for bulk material such as soil, ore and coal that couples with multibody tools (Chapter 11 lists it as Simcenter EDEM; Chapter 8 cites an Altair MotionSolve tutorial that couples a tracked vehicle to EDEM); Fraunhofer ITWM Demify, DEM-oriented soil-tool interaction for heavy machinery, a research and service product; Project Chrono's terrain models (SCM, CRM and DEM), where the developers report CRM running 50 to 200 times slower than real time and needing a graphics processing unit (GPU) from one specific maker; AGX Terrain and AGX Granular; Mevea's soil simulation; and MAVS, with a tire-soil model for sand and clay [Chapters 5, 8, 11].
terms.why: The booklet finds high-detail soil simulation far too slow for scenario sweeps and notes that uncertain soil inputs can overwhelm fidelity. It recommends a multi-fidelity approach: use DEM or deformable terrain to learn how stopping distance depends on soil, slope and payload, fit simpler parameterized models for the large regression, and confirm the parameter envelope with targeted physical tests [Chapters 8, 11].

terms.title: Environment creation and reconstruction tools
terms.oneSentence: Environment creation and reconstruction tools build the three-dimensional virtual job site, either by designing it by hand and by rules or by rebuilding a real site from photographs, laser scans and machine recordings.
terms.explained:
Before a virtual loader can reverse toward a virtual pile, someone must make the pile, the ramp, the parked truck and the person, and give every surface the properties a camera, a radar and a lidar would see. The booklet identifies eleven families of method, from hand-built models and rule-based (procedural) generation to drone photogrammetry, lidar survey, reconstruction from the machine's own recordings, neural reconstruction and reuse of mine plans. It stresses that the combination matters more than any one authoring package: a quarry model might start from a mine plan, replace the active pit with a drone mesh, fill gaps by hand and then generate hundreds of variants by rules [Chapter 5].

The named tools: MathWorks RoadRunner with Scene Builder, which imports map data and point clouds and exports to CARLA, dSPACE and IPG CarMaker, but whose base editor remains road-oriented; the Fraunhofer ITWM VMC Road and Scene Generator, which builds scenes from fused real measurements; OpenUSD and Omniverse tooling, a domain-neutral way to describe scenes (an open standard plus one vendor's components); Unreal Engine editors inside Falcon, CARLA and the MathWorks stack; photogrammetry software such as COLMAP, with quarry examples from drone surveys; neural reconstruction such as NuRec, SplatAD and LiDAR-EVS, which rebuild appearance from logs but struggle when the sensor viewpoint moves; Boreal3D for forest plots; CropCraft, an open-source generator for farm fields; AgriGen, which generates large agricultural scenes in Isaac Sim; and MAVS, which generates off-road terrain with controllable roughness and haze. ASAM OpenMATERIAL 3D (version 1.0.0, April 2025) standardizes the material properties sensors react to; it excludes dirt on the sensor itself [Chapters 5, 11].
terms.why: The booklet calls job-site reconstruction a bottleneck: a reusable representation of sites is needed before scenario volume matters, and the open road formats assume lanes, so stockpiles, berms and ruts often need custom representations. Every captured environment also needs a capture date and revision history, or "the quarry model" becomes ambiguous [Chapters 5, 11].

terms.title: Scenario generation and test management tools
terms.oneSentence: Scenario generation tools describe and vary the test situations; test management tools decide which runs to execute, run them, and keep track of the results.
terms.explained:
A scenario is a short story for a test: "loader reverses at 8 km/h, person steps out from behind a truck 12 m away, light rain, dusk." A scenario generation tool lets engineers write that story in a standard language, then vary its numbers (speed, distance, weather) to create thousands of related tests. A test management tool is the bookkeeper: it schedules the runs, records every result and shows which situations have been covered.

The standard languages are ASAM OpenSCENARIO (the story) and OpenDRIVE (the road), supported by VTD, the dSPACE chain, CARLA, RoadRunner, Prescan and MORAI. OpenDRIVE assumes roads, so job sites without lane geometry fit poorly [Chapter 11]. Named tools: Foretellix Foretify (coverage-driven generation with constrained random variation and large-scale validation management; a 2021 partnership with Volvo Autonomous Solutions adapted it for mines and quarries, and the vendor sells a mining suite); AVL SCENIUS (scenario lifecycle from requirements to reporting); RoadRunner Scenario; the VTD 2025.2 ScenarioEngine; dSPACE SIMPHERA; and Scenic, an open-source probabilistic scenario language that places objects without needing lanes and connects to several simulators. Scenic integrates with VerifAI, and together with S-TaLiRo and Breach these are falsification tools that search for the parameter combinations where a function fails [Chapters 9, 11]. The open-source editor esmini was not assessed [Chapter 11].

For test management, the booklet names no single product. It describes what a neutral implementation needs: a requirements platform for hazards and traceability, version control and continuous integration, a database and object store, and a campaign service that generates runs and computes verdicts and coverage; ASAM ATX for test metadata and ASAM MDF for measured data are named as neutral formats [Chapter 9].
terms.why: Scenario count is not coverage; the booklet warns that the brief confuses the two and that interface standards are still being revised during the program [Chapters 11, 13].

terms.title: Data replay and HIL hardware
terms.oneSentence: Data replay feeds recorded real sensor data back into the braking software, and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) hardware is the real-time computer and signal equipment that lets the real control unit run against a simulated machine.
terms.explained:
Replay is like showing a trainee a video of yesterday's near miss and asking what they would have done. Recorded camera, radar or bus data from real machines is played into the software and its decisions are compared with what happened. Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) goes further: the real electronic control unit (ECU) is wired to a computer that pretends to be the rest of the machine, in real time, down to the millisecond. Data injection means pushing simulated or recorded signals into the sensor path, for example raw camera data behind the imager or radar detections, together with recorded J1939 or CAN (controller area network) bus traffic and "restbus" models of the rest of the network [Chapter 7].

The hardware the booklet names: dSPACE SCALEXIO (real-time HIL systems), VEOS (PC-based virtual ECU simulation) and AURELION; NI VeriStand with PXI and CompactRIO (a PXIe-8842 controller is listed at about USD 5,200, but that is only a controller, not a bench); Speedgoat with Simulink Real-Time; OPAL-RT 4DV-SIM and the OP5707XG2, which combines a CPU with a field-programmable gate array (FPGA), with named off-highway and defense users; IPG's model-, software- and hardware-in-the-loop (MIL, SIL, HIL) and vehicle-in-the-loop; Mevea, Vortex and Applied Intuition HIL; and RoadRunner with the Automated Driving Toolbox for reconstructing and replaying recorded scenarios. ISO/TS 21815-2:2021 defines the J1939 command interface (stop, slow down, motion inhibit) that a bench can emulate between the collision-avoidance device and the machine [Chapters 7, 11]. Vector tools are not discussed in the booklet.
terms.why: HIL is the only way to test ECU timing and interfaces before the machine exists, but sensor injection is sensor- and ECU-specific and raw-signal benches are the highest integration effort. The booklet suggests a HIL bench on the ISO/TS 21815-2 interface as a mid-2027 target that should not be on the critical path unless interfaces stabilize early [Chapters 1, 11].
aliases: CPU with a field-programmable gate array

terms.title: Operator-in-the-loop simulators
terms.oneSentence: An operator-in-the-loop simulator is a cab, screens and controls where a real person drives a simulated machine, so that human reactions to warnings and automatic braking can be measured.
terms.explained:
Flight simulators train pilots; machine simulators train loader and excavator operators. The same equipment can be used to study behavior: how long an operator takes to react to a warning, whether a sudden automatic stop surprises them, and how many nuisance stops they will tolerate before switching the system off.

The booklet names the Fraunhofer ITWM RODOS human-in-the-loop driving simulator; CM Labs Vortex Studio, documented mainly as a training simulator for construction equipment; Mevea's training simulators for mining; and Volvo Construction Equipment's real-time human-in-the-loop excavator simulator built with Simulink and Simscape. A haul-truck proximity-interface simulator has been used in academic work [Chapters 1, 11]. The booklet's early-experiment list includes an operator clinic: expose operators to simulated or real nuisance stops and measure the acceptance threshold by scenario [Chapter 13].
terms.why: Warning-then-brake depends on the operator's reaction, and nuisance interventions are documented as the primary reason deployed proximity systems fail; the booklet lists human-in-the-loop simulators as a likely need and makes operator acceptance a release criterion [Chapters 11, 13].

terms.title: Cloud execution services
terms.oneSentence: Cloud execution means renting computers, including graphics processors, by the hour over the internet instead of buying them, so that thousands of simulations can run in parallel.
terms.explained:
"The cloud" is a large data center owned by someone else. A company rents a slice of it for as long as it needs and pays by the hour. For simulation this matters because the work comes in bursts: a few hundred computers for a week, then none. Buying that capacity would leave it idle most of the year.

The booklet reports two kinds of cloud. Vendor clouds run a specific simulator: FalconCloud, VTDx, AURELION cloud, and the large-scale services of Applied Intuition and MORAI; their prices were not found. Generic cloud rents raw machines. Third-party price trackers listed an Amazon Web Services (AWS) g6e.xlarge instance, with one NVIDIA L40S graphics processor, at about USD 1.861 per hour on demand in the US East region, rising to about USD 30.131 per hour for eight such processors; a one-year commitment brought the single-processor price to about USD 1.17, and "spot" prices for interruptible capacity fluctuated widely. Google Cloud listed a g2-standard-32 with one L4 processor at about USD 1.734 per hour. Spot pricing suits regression runs that can be paused and restarted, not deterministic hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) tests or irreplaceable long jobs. Regional availability and quotas vary, and prices should be rechecked at purchase [Chapter 11].

Orchestration, the software that hands out runs to machines and collects results, is named as Kubernetes, batch systems or high-performance computing (HPC) schedulers plus object storage. Vendor cloud terms, export control and data residency were not researched; the booklet notes that site scans, mine layouts and machine CAD are commercially sensitive and that an on-premises or private-cloud option is a mitigation [Chapter 11].
terms.why: Compute is cheap relative to engineering labor, but the four-month window caps how many runs fit: ten single-processor instances running continuously for 122 days cost on the order of USD 54,000 and deliver at most about 29,000 processor-hours [Chapter 11].

terms.title: Mining, construction, agriculture and forestry specific tools
terms.oneSentence: These are the few simulation tools, datasets and frameworks that were built for, or deliberately adapted to, off-road working machines rather than road cars.
terms.explained:
Most simulation tools grew up on roads with lanes, curbs and traffic lights. A quarry has none of these. The booklet sorts the off-road-relevant tools into three groups. Machine and terrain physics tools built for mobile machinery: Mevea, AGX Dynamics, Vortex Studio, Project Chrono, EDEM and Fraunhofer Demify. Road-vehicle validation platforms with explicit off-road packages: the MathWorks Offroad Autonomy Library, IPG's off-highway stack, Applied Intuition, Cognata, AVL's off-road engineering (its Generic Off-Road Automation System demonstrated on a tractor) and Foretellix (a 2021 partnership for mines and quarries). Research and military programs: Duality Falcon (DARPA RACER-Sim), Fraunhofer ITWM (InVerS construction-site digital twins, RODOS, VMC), Fraunhofer IVI (agricultural and construction machinery testing), Southwest Research Institute (off-road scene tools for military, space and agriculture) and OPAL-RT 4DV-SIM (off-highway and defense users). CARLA has a mining earth-mover asset only [Chapter 11].

From other chapters: MineSim, an open-source, peer-reviewed scenario-based test system and benchmark for autonomous trucks in open-pit mines (April 2025), built from two real mines and modeling unstructured roads and heavy-truck response lag; SimMining-3D, a synthetic lidar dataset that varies sensor height because detection degrades when viewpoint changes on mine benches; CropCraft, AgriGen and Boreal3D for agricultural and forest scenes; a Robotec.ai digital twin for Boliden; and the Mining3 and ACARP proximity-detection testing framework (project C26028, January 2021), a shared physical test protocol rather than a simulator [Chapters 1, 5, 9]. KomVision is not a tool: it is Komatsu's human detection and collision mitigation product on excavators, used in the booklet as a market precedent [Chapters 2, 13]. CSIRO was not assessed as a provider, so its status is "not found" rather than "does not offer" [Chapter 11].
terms.why: Independent validation of any of these for automatic braking on heavy machines was not found; the booklet treats MineSim as proof that mine-specific closed-loop scenario simulation is feasible, "not to be confused with validated sensor physics" [Chapter 1].

terms.title: Engineering service companies and research institutes
terms.oneSentence: Engineering service companies sell engineering work by the hour or by the project, and research institutes sell applied research, test facilities and independent assessment; both can do parts of virtual validation for a manufacturer.
terms.explained:
A company that has never built a simulation capability has three kinds of outside help available. An engineering service company (like hiring a builder) does the integration, modeling and testing work under contract. A research institute (like hiring a specialist laboratory) brings methods, measurement facilities and people who have done similar work for others. An independent test or assessment body (like a building inspector) checks the result without having built it.

Service companies in the booklet: AVL (its Generic Off-Road Automation System demonstrated on a retrofitted tractor, VSM vehicle models with a vendor-claimed correlation "up to 97%", the SCENIUS scenario tool, and scenario-based validation services; explicit agriculture, forestry, construction and mining work); IPG Automotive (consulting around CarMaker, TruckMaker and the off-highway stack); OPAL-RT (real-time hardware-in-the-loop or HIL benches); Mevea (modeling services and digital twins); MathWorks Consulting; Persival (sensor-model development and validation); Speedgoat engineering services; FEV.io (virtual validation, with an automotive case study); EDAG and Bertrandt (not assessed in depth); and IAV and Capgemini Engineering (not assessed). Test houses: IDIADA (vehicle-in-the-loop services; a 2026 demonstration with MathWorks correlating simulated and proving-ground automatic braking), UTAC (proposals on virtual testing methods to the United Nations working group on automatic emergency braking), and TÜV SÜD (independent simulation and model validation; it played the test-lab role in the PEGASUS program) [Chapters 1, 2, 10, 11].

Research institutes: Fraunhofer ITWM (construction-site digital twins, the RODOS simulator, real-data scenes, Demify soil simulation), Fraunhofer IVI (agricultural and construction machinery testing), Fraunhofer IESE (modular co-simulation and fault injection), VTT in Finland (sensor simulation and digital twins for non-road mobile machinery), TNO in the Netherlands (scenario-based testing, mostly road), Southwest Research Institute (off-road autonomy tools), Mining3 (the ACARP proximity-detection testing framework) and CSIRO (not assessed). The German aerospace center DLR and the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) appear only as authors of cited technical work, not as assessed providers [Chapters 7, 10, 11].

Weather facilities are a special case: the CEREMA fog and rain tunnel in France, CARISSMA in Germany, and NIED and JARI in Japan are named as the main ground truth for weather models, because a fog model is tuned by matching a real sensor's output in real fog. The booklet did not examine their booking lead times, capacity or suitability for machines of this size [Chapter 6].
terms.why: The booklet's preferred option is a hybrid in which a partner accelerates the first correlated sensor model while the manufacturer keeps the operating-domain definition, scenario catalog, acceptance criteria and correlation data in-house. No public contract values or delivery timelines were found for any provider [Chapter 11].

terms.title: Build, buy or partner
terms.oneSentence: Build, buy or partner is the decision between writing the simulation capability in-house on open-source parts, buying commercial products, or paying an outside company to deliver it.
terms.explained:
It is the same choice a household faces with a kitchen renovation: do it yourself, buy fitted units, or hire a contractor. Each trades money against time, control and dependence.

The booklet compares five options. Build in-house on open source (CARLA or Isaac Sim or Gazebo, Chrono, Robot Operating System 2 or ROS 2): lowest license cost, highest internal labor, full ownership of source and models, but no vendor support, key-person dependence and the organization owns all the credibility evidence. Buy an integrated commercial stack: lower integration burden, but domain modeling and correlation remain substantial, the core cannot be owned, and there are off-road gaps, license dependence and roadmap risk. Buy specialist tools and integrate internally: high flexibility, high interface and version complexity. Partner-led implementation: potentially fastest, but knowledge and models stay with the partner and the dependency can become permanent. Hybrid: an internal owner plus a partner plus commercial or open-source tools, which the booklet judges the best balance of retained knowledge and outside specialization, provided the contract has unusually clear ownership clauses [Chapter 11].

The evidence gap is explicit: no independent 2024 to 2026 benchmark states total cost, team headcount or time to a first useful result for any option; vendor case studies report large gains but are not controlled measurements. Whatever the choice, the booklet says a partner contract should require delivery of editable machine models, scene and source assets, parameter provenance, correlation datasets, test definitions, continuous-integration scripts, simulator version manifests, known-limitation registers and interface specifications, not only test reports [Chapter 11].
terms.why: With no internal capability and nine months before hardware, the booklet calls the hybrid the most defensible choice and warns that outsourcing alone "solves the 2027 deadline while creating a larger long-term dependency" [Chapter 11].

terms.title: License types and pricing models
terms.oneSentence: A software license is the permission to use a program under stated conditions, and the pricing model is how the vendor charges for it: per computer, per shared pool, per year, per person, or not at all.
terms.explained:
Common license forms, in plain words. Node-locked: the license is tied to one named computer. Floating (or concurrent): a pool of licenses on a server; any computer may use one until the pool is empty. Per-seat: one license per named user. Subscription: paid yearly, stops working when payment stops. Perpetual: paid once, often with a yearly maintenance fee for updates. Runtime or OEM licenses: permission to ship the software inside a product. Academic or education licenses: cheap but limited to non-commercial use. Open source: free to use under the license conditions.

The booklet found public prices almost entirely absent. The only dated price points: an unofficial January 2024 copy of a MathWorks price list showing MATLAB at 980 (annual) or 3,920 (perpetual), Simulink 1,480 or 5,920, RoadRunner 4,680 or 9,360 and RoadRunner Scenario 3,400 or 13,600, presumed US dollars and indicative only; a Duality Falcon education license at USD 20 per month, non-commercial; an NI PXIe-8842 controller at about USD 5,200; and cloud graphics-processor rates. AGX Dynamics sells a yearly subscription per seat in three tiers at "price upon request", with separate runtime, OEM (original equipment manufacturer) and academic licenses. Isaac Sim is free for internal research, but redistribution needs a paid enterprise license and staff described free use for teams of up to two people. AURELION requires a valid maintenance contract for new versions [Chapter 11].
terms.why: License limits are a listed risk: parallel cloud execution, build servers, hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) nodes, subcontractor access and geography are often licensed separately and terms are not public. The booklet advises pricing peak concurrent workers, continuous-integration and cloud rights, subcontractors and disaster-recovery environments in the request for proposal, not only desktop seats [Chapter 11].

terms.title: The three example tool chains at different cost levels
terms.oneSentence: The booklet sketches three ways to assemble a tool chain, from an open-source core to a fully commercial chain with a partner, and labels them lowest, middle and highest by relative cost and integration posture, not by dollar figures.
terms.explained:
Because almost every commercial vendor is quote-only, the levels are relative. All three are expert assessment built from the tool entries, the integration findings and the compute figures [Chapter 11].

Lowest cost, an open-source core plus in-house integration: CARLA, Isaac Sim or Gazebo for sensors and environments; Project Chrono for machine dynamics and Soil Contact Model (SCM) terrain; Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2); in-house scenario scripts or Scenic; J1939 emulation to ISO/TS 21815-2; on-premises RTX graphics cards or spot cloud. It can do camera and lidar sensor-in-the-loop, articulated and tracked dynamics on deformable terrain and scripted job-site scenarios, with full control of intellectual property. Without major work it cannot provide validated radar, physics-based ultrasonic, weather effects with correlation evidence, vendor support or tool-qualification evidence, and it depends on hiring scarce skills.

Middle, a model-based engineering stack plus heavy-machine physics: MATLAB and Simulink with the Offroad Autonomy Library, RoadRunner and RoadRunner Scenario, Unreal and the sensor toolboxes; Mevea or AGX Dynamics coupled through the Functional Mock-up Interface (FMI) for terrain, hydraulics and machine variants; one externally validated sensor model packaged to the ASAM Open Simulation Interface (OSI) as a Functional Mock-up Unit (FMU); Speedgoat or NI for later hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing; cloud graphics processors (GPUs) for batch runs. It gives credible machine dynamics, explicit construction and mining workflows, camera and lidar sensing and HIL with real electronic control units (ECUs), but not broad validated multi-sensor weather physics or large-scale coverage-driven scenario management; module prices are not public.

Highest, an integrated commercial chain plus a partner: a commercial validation platform (for example dSPACE AURELION with SIMPHERA, VEOS and SCALEXIO; Applied Intuition; Cognata; VTD; or Foretellix); heavy-machine dynamics from IPG TruckMaker, Mevea, AGX or Vortex; specialist sensor simulation (AURELION or AVxcelerate); dSPACE or NI benches; cloud execution; and an engineering partner such as AVL, IPG or Fraunhofer for integration and correlation. It offers physics-based simulation of all four sensor types, large-scale regression and partner capacity for the four-month window, but cannot guarantee off-road sensor realism, avoid multi-vendor dependence or remove the manufacturer's own physical correlation tests. No public evidence shows this chain validated end to end for off-road automatic braking.
terms.why: The booklet adds a fourth architecture that applies at every cost level: do not make one simulator carry every test. Use fast functional tests for millions of logic combinations, medium-fidelity dynamics for broad regression, high-fidelity rendering and soil only for sensitive subsets, HIL for timing, and targeted physical tests for correlation, with the allocation decided by sensitivity and correlation work, not assumption [Chapter 11].
aliases: Speedgoat or NI for later hardware-in-the-loop
three example tool chains at different cost levels

terms.title: CPU, GPU, FPGA, VRAM and real-time computers
terms.oneSentence: These are the kinds of computing hardware a simulation program needs: the central processor for general work, the graphics processor for massively parallel work, the programmable chip for exact timing, the graphics memory that holds the scene, and computers built to answer on a fixed schedule.
terms.explained:
A central processing unit (CPU) is the general-purpose brain of a computer. It has a few very capable cores that handle one complex task each, very fast. Think of a few expert chefs. A graphics processing unit (GPU) has thousands of small cores that all do the same simple operation on different pieces of data at once. Think of a hall of line cooks all chopping. GPUs were built to draw pictures, which is why they are good at rendering camera images, tracing light rays or radar rays through a scene, and simulating millions of soil grains. VRAM is the GPU's own memory. A whole job site, its textures and its material properties must fit in it; the booklet reports CARLA on Unreal Engine 5 needing at least 16 GB, cloud GPUs with 48 GB, and workstation cards with 96 GB [Chapter 11].

A field-programmable gate array (FPGA) is a chip whose internal wiring can be reconfigured for one job. It is used where timing must be exact to the microsecond, for example to generate bus signals toward a real control unit. A real-time computer is a machine whose software is guaranteed to finish each calculation step within a fixed time, every time. For hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing, where a real control unit expects a sensor message every 50 milliseconds, missing a deadline would be a false test result. The booklet names OPAL-RT's CPU and FPGA systems and the dSPACE, Speedgoat and NI real-time products as this class [Chapter 11].

The booklet's workload table shows that one program needs all of them in different places. Braking-logic tests on object lists are CPU work, very parallel, suited to commodity servers. Rigid vehicle dynamics is CPU work, often faster than real time. Camera photorealism and lidar are GPU work, where VRAM and ray tracing matter. Physics-based radar can be very GPU-intensive. Discrete-element soil is highly compute-intensive and suits dedicated GPU or high-performance computing workers; Chrono's continuum terrain runs 50 to 200 times slower than real time. HIL needs deterministic real-time CPU, FPGA and input-output hardware, where timing matters more than throughput. Campaign orchestration and results are CPU, database and storage heavy [Chapter 11].
terms.why: There is no single hardware requirement because the workloads differ by orders of magnitude; the real-time factor each tool reaches on the actual machine geometry and sensor set decides what the compute budget buys, and it must be benchmarked rather than assumed [Chapter 11].

terms.title: Graphics cards named in the booklet
terms.oneSentence: A graphics card is a circuit board carrying a graphics processing unit (GPU) and its memory, and the booklet names specific models because the speed of sensor simulation depends heavily on which one is used.
terms.explained:
The cards named are mostly from one maker, NVIDIA, because the simulators the booklet reviews depend on that maker's ray-tracing libraries. The booklet flags this as a dependency risk rather than a recommendation: the Chrono community itself has raised the NVIDIA-specific requirement of its high-performance modules [Chapter 11].

RTX is the maker's line of cards with dedicated ray-tracing cores, from consumer to workstation models. CARLA on Unreal Engine 5 requires at least an RTX 3000-series card with 16 GB of VRAM. The RadaRays radar simulator produced one radar image in 7.8 to 18.8 milliseconds on an RTX 2070 Super, against 25.8 to 78.5 milliseconds on a desktop CPU. A workstation card with 96 GB of memory exists (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell), but server prices were not found [Chapters 6, 11]. A100 and A40 are data-center cards: SplatAD trains a scene in about one hour on one A100, and a diffusion weather-editing network took 20.52 seconds per image on one A40 [Chapter 6]. L40S (48 GB) and L4 are the data-center cards in the Amazon Web Services (AWS) G6e and Google Cloud G2 instances whose hourly prices the booklet quotes [Chapter 11]. One non-NVIDIA figure appears: a radar signature calculation on a supercomputer with AMD MI250X cards, for an aircraft [Chapter 6]. "AGX" in the booklet refers to Algoryx AGX Dynamics, a physics engine, not to a graphics card; embedded computing boards carrying that name are not discussed.

Why the type matters: ray-tracing cores speed up the light and radio ray calculations that camera, lidar and radar simulation depend on; VRAM sets how large a scene fits; and users of one simulator reported severe frame-rate loss in multi-sensor scenes, so performance is a qualification item, not a given [Chapter 11].
terms.why: No neutral cross-vendor benchmark that holds scene, sensor and settings constant was found, so published figures are examples, not planning constants, and every candidate tool must be timed on this program's own machine geometry and sensors [Chapters 6, 11].

terms.title: High-performance computing (HPC) and cluster, versus workstation
terms.oneSentence: A workstation is one powerful desktop computer; a cluster is many computers wired together and managed as one; high-performance computing (HPC) is the largest class of cluster, built for scientific calculation.
terms.explained:
One engineer running one simulation at a time needs a workstation: a desktop with a strong central processor (CPU), a capable graphics processing unit (GPU) and a large disk. CARLA alone asks for 130 GB of disk space [Chapter 11]. A program that must run thousands of scenarios in four months cannot queue them one by one on desktops. It needs a cluster: tens or hundreds of computers in racks, with scheduling software that hands each run to a free machine and gathers the results. HPC means the same idea at supercomputer scale, usually shared by a university or national laboratory. A cloud is simply a cluster someone else owns and rents by the hour.

The booklet gives three glimpses of scale. A digital-twin off-road validation study ran on HPC clusters because sequential parameter sweeps could not explore the variability space under time constraints; the same group ran 128 simulated off-road braking cases this way. A radar signature calculation used eight supercomputer nodes with four GPUs each. A European virtual-testing study needed "800+ hours" of compute and "300+ hours" of manual case selection [Chapters 1, 5, 6]. The booklet's point is that in a four-month window, tests per wall-clock hour matter more than real-time rendering: low-fidelity models should screen the broad space and expensive models should run only where they are needed [Chapter 5].
terms.why: The compute character of the work decides the architecture: commodity servers or cloud containers for logic tests, GPU workers for sensors, dedicated GPU or HPC workers for soil, and a local real-time system for hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) testing; orchestration and storage become their own CPU and database load [Chapter 11].

terms.title: Compute cost and run time
terms.oneSentence: Compute cost is what it costs to run the simulations, and it is set by three numbers: the price per hour of the computer, how many hours it runs, and how much simulated time each hour produces.
terms.explained:
The key idea is the real-time factor (RTF): simulated seconds produced per wall-clock second. A simulator at 10 times real time produces ten minutes of virtual driving per minute of computer time; one at 0.1 times real time needs ten minutes of computer time for one minute of driving. The booklet's rule: cost per simulated hour equals the cloud price per wall-clock hour divided by the real-time factor. In symbols, `cost_sim = price_hour / RTF`, where `price_hour` is the hourly rent and `RTF` the real-time factor. A tool at 10 times real time therefore costs one tenth as much per simulated hour as one at real time, and one at 0.1 times costs ten times as much [Chapter 11].

To estimate how many runs fit a budget: hours bought equals budget divided by hourly price; simulated hours equals hours bought times RTF; runs equals simulated hours divided by the length of one scenario. The booklet's example: ten cloud instances, each with one graphics processing unit (GPU), running 24 hours a day for 122 days give about 29,000 GPU-hours for about USD 54,490 on demand. If sensor-realistic runs are near real time, that is roughly 29,000 hours of simulated driving, which caps how many of the 100-plus sites times 10-plus scenarios times weather times machine variants can run at full fidelity and forces a tiered strategy [Chapter 11]. The reference table: 1,000 GPU-hours cost about USD 1,734 to 1,861, 10,000 about USD 17,344 to 18,610 and 100,000 about USD 173,438 to 186,100, excluding licenses, storage, network traffic and support.

Two examples show how far the RTF can swing. A radar solver on a central processor (CPU) took 14 hours to simulate a 12-second scenario, an RTF of about 0.0002, while the GPU version of the same vendor's method produced a frame in about 12 milliseconds. Chrono's continuum soil runs 50 to 200 times slower than real time [Chapters 6, 11].
terms.why: Compute is cheap relative to engineering labor, which the booklet puts at roughly USD 150,000 to 260,000 per specialist per year. The larger risks it names are model preparation, correlation measurements and human triage of failures, to be benchmarked end to end before scaling infrastructure [Chapters 6, 11, 13].

terms.title: Software terms a planner meets
terms.oneSentence: These are the everyday words of software work that appear throughout the booklet: how programs talk to each other, which programming tools the simulators use, and how teams package, track and automatically test their code.
terms.explained:
An application programming interface (API) is the agreed set of commands one program accepts from another; CARLA offers a Python API, Prescan offers Python and MATLAB APIs, and RoadRunner uses gRPC, a network protocol for calls between programs [Chapter 11]. Python is a widely used programming language; many simulators and research generators (Scenic, CropCraft, Demify) are driven from it. MATLAB is a commercial numerical computing environment and Simulink its block-diagram tool for modeling control systems; MathWorks' off-road library, Simulink Real-Time and Simscape belong to that family, released twice a year (R2026b is the second 2026 release) [Chapter 11]. Robot Operating System (ROS) is open-source middleware that lets the parts of a robot's software exchange messages; ROS 2 is its current generation, integrated in CARLA, Isaac Sim, Gazebo and BeamNG [Chapter 11].

A container packages a program with everything it needs so it runs identically on any computer; the booklet advises containerizing a frozen tool-chain version and archiving the containers for the safety case [Chapter 11]. Version control records every change to code and files with a unique identifier (a commit hash) for each state; GitHub is a widely used hosting service, and the booklet requires the software build or commit in every run record [Chapter 9]. DevOps means the people who write software also run and maintain it, with heavy automation; the booklet lists it among the internal labor an open-source build requires [Chapter 11]. Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) means every change is automatically built and tested and tested software is automatically released; the booklet names cloud and CI as a skill to acquire and CI scripts as a deliverable a partner must hand over [Chapter 11].
terms.why: Evidence produced on one software version may need re-qualification after an update, so freezing versions, containerizing, and regression-testing upgrades before adopting them are listed mitigations against fast-changing tools [Chapter 11].

terms.title: Data storage, data lineage and record keeping for thousands of runs
terms.oneSentence: Record keeping for simulation means storing, for every one of thousands of runs, exactly what was run, with which versions and inputs, and where every input came from, so that any result can be reproduced and defended later.
terms.explained:
A single simulation run produces a verdict: braked in time, or did not. That verdict is worthless as evidence unless someone can later recreate the run exactly. Data lineage is the record of where each piece of data came from and what was done to it, like the chain of custody for a court exhibit. The booklet's rule is to treat every executed run as a reproducible experiment with an immutable provenance manifest [Chapter 9].

The minimum manifest stored with each run: requirement and hazard identifiers, scenario family and version, the concrete parameter values, machine configuration, sensor hardware, mounting and calibration, software build or commit, simulator or rig version, random seed, environmental measurements, timestamp, raw-data identifiers and checksums, the metric version, the verdict and any deviations. Everything that can change a result gets an immutable identifier; content hashes do this. Neutral formats named are ASAM MDF 4.3.0 for measured signals and ASAM ATX for test metadata; the implementation can be commercial, open-source or in-house, as long as the data model is stable and machine-readable [Chapter 9]. The traceability chain runs hazard, safety requirement, logical scenario, test case, run, result, evidence item in the safety case [Chapter 9].

Chapter 11 adds that tool versions, binaries or containers, drivers, graphics-processor type, assets and seeds must be archived for the safety case; Chapter 13 lists version drift making evidence irreproducible as a failure mode. Storage itself is a cost: large synchronized camera, lidar and radar programs create storage, retention, worker-imagery privacy and access-control obligations [Chapter 7].
